title: Collective dressed states for inelastic light scattering by atomic ensembles
comment: 40 pages, 21 figures, accompanied by a Python package for reproducing the data
summary: We develop a general dressed-state framework for computing fluorescence spectra, probe absorption spectra, and photon-photon correlations of light scattered by ensembles of $N_\mathrm{at}$ two-level atoms with arbitrary $J_g \to J_e$ transitions driven by intense coherent fields. The approach employs a full vectorial treatment of the electromagnetic field, handles any atomic geometries, illumination directions, and polarizations, and yields optical observables as explicit sums of Lorentzian lines whose positions, widths, and weights are directly tied to the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Lindbladian. The framework is implemented in an open-source Python package and benchmarked against exact single- and two-atom calculations. We identify geometries in which the full vectorial description is essential, and the scalar approximation fails qualitatively. Applying the method to pairs of atoms with a $J_g=0\to J_e=1$ transition, we show that elastic and inelastic scattered intensities collapse onto universal master curves controlled by a single collective saturation parameter built from the dominant superradiant mode, across several orders of magnitude in drive strength and interatomic distance. We identify collective phenomena that require a description beyond this single-mode picture. Extending the analysis to atoms with ground-state degeneracy, we find that most collective features carry over, while two qualitatively new effects emerge: an incoherent spontaneous Raman channel that modifies the scaling of inelastic emission, and a slow timescale in the time-delayed correlations $g^{(2)}(τ)$ governed by the competition between Raman scattering and subradiant decay, controlled by a single dimensionless parameter. These results provide both physical insight and practical computational tools for engineering collective optical responses in few-atom systems such as optical tweezer arrays.

AI.tldr: A general dressed-state framework is developed to compute fluorescence, probe absorption, and photon-photon correlations from ensembles of two-level atoms with arbitrary J_g→J_e transitions in intense fields, using a full vectorial treatment of light. It yields observables as Lorentzian sums tied to Lindbladian eigenpairs, is implemented in an open-source Python package, and reveals universal scaling laws, collective phenomena, and new Raman-induced effects in degenerate ground-state systems.
AI.motivation: To provide a general and computationally practical framework for accurately computing collective optical observables (fluorescence, absorption, g(2)(τ)) in few-atom systems driven by intense fields, capturing full vectorial electromagnetic effects that scalar approximations miss, and to uncover universal physics and qualitative new phenomena in degenerate atomic transitions.
AI.method: The authors develop a dressed-state (Lindbladian diagonalization) framework with full vectorial treatment of the electromagnetic field, applicable to arbitrary geometries, illuminations, and polarizations. Observables are expressed as explicit sums of Lorentzian lines whose positions/widths/weights derive from Lindbladian eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The method is implemented in an open-source Python package and benchmarked against exact few-atom calculations.
AI.result: They identify geometries where the scalar approximation fails qualitatively. For J_g=0→J_e=1 atom pairs, elastic and inelastic intensities collapse onto universal master curves parameterized by a single collective saturation parameter of the dominant superradiant mode across wide ranges of drive and distance. They also identify effects requiring beyond-single-mode descriptions. For degenerate ground states, most collective features persist, but two new effects emerge: an incoherent spontaneous Raman channel modifying inelastic emission scaling, and a slow timescale in g(2)(τ) from competition between Raman scattering and subradiant decay, controlled by a single dimensionless parameter.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers both physical insight and practical computational tools for engineering collective optical responses in few-atom systems like optical tweezer arrays, capturing phenomena that scalar approximations miss and revealing universal scaling behavior as well as novel Raman-mediated collective effects.

title: Impact of light shift inhomogeneities on the contrast of light pulse atom interferometers
summary: We study the loss of the contrast in an atom interferometer when increasing the duration of Raman mirror pulses, and find the contrast decay rate to increase with the interferometer duration. We attribute this effect to the transverse spatial fluctuations of the intensity across the Raman beams, and to the dephasing induced by the associated light shifts inhomogeneities. Simulations based on the propagation of noisy synthetic Raman beams show that the contrast decay rate increases with the distance between the wavepackets at the mirror pulse, before reaching an asymptotic limit when intensity fluctuations between the two wavepackets become completely decorrelated. Finally, simulations based on the propagation of Raman beams having their measured intensity fluctuations predict contrast loss rates consistent with our measurements, confirming the detrimental role for the interferometer contrast played by intensity fluctuations across the interferometer laser beams.

AI.tldr: The paper studies contrast loss in atom interferometry when Raman mirror pulse duration increases, finding that the contrast decay rate grows with interferometer duration due to transverse spatial intensity fluctuations across the Raman beams and associated light-shift-induced dephasing. Simulations using noisy synthetic beams and measured intensity fluctuations confirm the mechanism, linking contrast loss to intensity inhomogeneities across the interferometer laser beams.
AI.motivation: To understand and explain the mechanism behind increased contrast decay rates in atom interferometers when Raman mirror pulse durations are increased, identifying intensity fluctuations across the Raman beams as the underlying cause.
AI.method: Experimental measurement of contrast decay as a function of Raman mirror pulse and interferometer durations, combined with simulations based on propagation of noisy synthetic Raman beams and of beams with measured intensity fluctuation profiles.
AI.result: The contrast decay rate increases with interferometer duration and asymptotically saturates when intensity fluctuations between the two wavepackets become fully decorrelated. Simulations using measured intensity fluctuations accurately reproduce experimental contrast loss rates.
AI.conclusion: Transverse spatial fluctuations of intensity across Raman beams and the resultant inhomogeneous light-shift-induced dephasing are detrimental to interferometer contrast, explaining the observed increase in contrast loss with interferometer duration.

title: Polarization measurements of the $2s$--$2p_{3/2}$ VUV transition in N$^{4+}$ excited by electron collisions
summary: We present the linear polarization of the $2s$--$2p_{3/2}$ transition in Li-like N$^{4+}$ excited by electron collisions, measured at electron energies between 85 and 1000~eV. The measured polarizations are compared with theoretical values calculated using the Flexible Atomic Code (FAC). Although the overall trend that the degree of polarization decreases with increasing electron energy is reproduced, the theoretical values are systematically larger in magnitude than the experimental values. After examining possible experimental sources of depolarization, we suggest that the discrepancy likely originates from an overestimation in the theoretical model. Further theoretical and experimental investigations along the isoelectronic sequence are needed to resolve this discrepancy.

AI.tldr: This paper reports measurements of linear polarization of the 2s-2p₃/₂ transition in Li-like N⁴⁺ excited by electron collisions at energies from 85 to 1000 eV, compared against Flexible Atomic Code (FAC) calculations. The measured polarizations are systematically lower in magnitude than theory, and the authors attribute the discrepancy to a likely overestimation in the theoretical model rather than experimental depolarization sources.
AI.motivation: To test theoretical predictions of electron-impact excitation polarization in Li-like ions and identify whether discrepancies arise from experimental effects or shortcomings in the theoretical model, with the larger goal of understanding collision dynamics along the isoelectronic sequence.
AI.method: Measurement of linear polarization of the 2s-2p₃/₂ transition in N⁴⁺ produced by electron-impact excitation across an energy range of 85–1000 eV, with comparison to theoretical polarization values computed using the Flexible Atomic Code (FAC). Possible experimental sources of depolarization were examined to assess the origin of systematic discrepancies.
AI.result: The experimental polarizations follow the expected overall trend of decreasing magnitude with increasing electron energy, but the FAC theoretical values are systematically larger than the experimentally measured values across the energy range studied.
AI.conclusion: After ruling out experimental depolarization effects as the primary cause, the authors conclude the systematic discrepancy likely stems from an overestimation in the theoretical model. Further theoretical and experimental work along the isoelectronic sequence is required to resolve this issue.

title: A fully coupled electromagnetic-thermal-mechanical model for metal-insulated HTS high field magnets
summary: Ultra high field REBCO magnets operate under strongly coupled electromagnetic, thermal and mechanical conditions, where screening currents, localized heating, thermal expansion and Lorentz forces can modify both the structural state and the critical current density of the conductor. In this work, a coupled electromagnetic, thermal and mechanical model is developed for a metal-insulated nested REBCO insert designed for a 40 T class SuperEMFL magnet. The existing electromagnetic formulation resolves the non-uniform screening currents in the REBCO tapes. The thermal model is extended from an explicit Finite Difference Method (FDM) to an implicit Backward Euler scheme with Picard iteration, while a new axisymmetric mechanical FDM solver based on BiCGSTAB is introduced to calculate displacements, strains and stresses in the coil windings and G10 spacer regions. Thermal expansion and Lorentz force contributions are included, and the calculated longitudinal mechanical strain is coupled back to the electromagnetic model through a strain dependent critical current density, which also depends on temperature, magnetic field, and its orientation. A literature-informed Parabolic-Weibull model is used to model reversible and irreversible strain degradation of the REBCO conductor. The numerical methods are benchmarked, and the resulting framework provides a computationally efficient approach for investigating temperature gradients, thermo-mechanical stresses, strain-dependent critical current degradation and quench behaviour in full scale nested high field REBCO magnets.

AI.tldr: A coupled electromagnetic-thermal-mechanical model is developed for a metal-insulated nested REBCO insert in a 40 T class SuperEMFL magnet, using an implicit Backward Euler thermal solver, an axisymmetric mechanical FDM solver with BiCGSTAB, and strain-dependent critical current degradation via a Parabolic-Weibull model coupled back into the electromagnetic simulation.
AI.motivation: Ultra high field REBCO magnets experience strongly coupled electromagnetic, thermal and mechanical effects where screening currents, localized heating, thermal expansion and Lorentz forces mutually influence both structural integrity and conductor performance. Simulating these coupled phenomena in full-scale nested high field magnets is computationally challenging and has not been adequately addressed.
AI.method: The work develops a multi-physics framework combining: (1) an existing electromagnetic formulation resolving non-uniform screening currents in REBCO tapes; (2) an implicit Backward Euler thermal scheme with Picard iteration (extended from explicit FDM); (3) a new axisymmetric mechanical FDM solver based on BiCGSTAB computing displacements, strains and stresses in coil windings and G10 spacers; (4) inclusion of thermal expansion and Lorentz force; and (5) feedback of longitudinal mechanical strain into the electromagnetic model through a strain-, temperature-, field-, and angle-dependent critical current density using a Parabolic-Weibull degradation model.
AI.result: The numerical methods were benchmarked and the resulting framework demonstrates computationally efficient capability to investigate temperature gradients, thermo-mechanical stresses, strain-dependent critical current degradation and quench behavior in full-scale nested high field REBCO magnets.
AI.conclusion: The coupled multi-physics framework provides a computationally tractable approach for analyzing the intricate interplay of electromagnetic, thermal and mechanical phenomena in ultra high field REBCO inserts, enabling investigation of quench behaviour and strain-induced performance degradation in realistic full-scale magnet designs.

title: Reference-Density Hartree Screening for Gausslet Hamiltonians
summary: Gausslets are among the few electronic-structure bases that permit the four-index electron--electron interaction to be replaced by an accurate two-index integral diagonal approximation (IDA). Near a many-electron nucleus, however, the nuclear attraction and core-electron Hartree field are individually large and substantially cancel. Treating the first as a full finite-basis matrix while treating the second with IDA leaves an avoidable imbalance. We introduce reference-density Hartree screening: the Hartree field of a chosen reference density is represented accurately, and IDA is applied only to density fluctuations about it. Tests on He, Ne, atomic F, F$_2$, and Cr$_2$ show large reductions in direct Hartree errors, including transfer of fitted neutral-atom fields to molecules. For Cr$_2$, atomic-core screening prevents the spurious HF collapse found with the unscreened $q=5$ and $q=7$ Hamiltonians, whereas finite-reference matching without screening does not. Screening leaves exchange and residual correlation unchanged. We therefore also introduce a low-rank one-particle correction that uses an accurate conventional Gaussian-basis Hartree--Fock calculation to match either occupied-space exchange information or the complete occupied Fock vectors. In F$_2$ and Cr$_2$, $X_{\rm HF}$ reproduces the finite-reference energy and occupied Fock vectors to numerical precision and the selected states return after orbital perturbations. For Cr$_2$, the corrected $q=5$ basis uses one quarter as many functions as the $q=7$ control while retaining sub-mHa mean-field accuracy. Screening provides the physical improvement to the direct field; the state-specific correction then restores the remaining accuracy of the Gaussian-basis mean-field reference.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces reference-density Hartree screening for Gausslet electronic-structure bases, where the Hartree field of a reference density is treated accurately and the two-index integral diagonal approximation (IDA) is applied only to density fluctuations. This removes the imbalance between full finite-basis nuclear attraction and IDA-treated Hartree fields near many-electron nuclei. Tests on He, Ne, F, F2, and Cr2 show large reductions in direct Hartree errors, including successful transfer of fitted neutral-atom fields to molecules. For Cr2, atomic-core screening prevents spurious HF collapse. A low-rank one-particle correction (X_HF) using conventional Gaussian-basis HF data restores remaining mean-field accuracy, allowing corrected q=5 basis to use one quarter the functions of q=7 control at sub-mHa accuracy.
AI.motivation: In Gausslet bases using the two-index integral diagonal approximation (IDA), the nuclear attraction and core-electron Hartree field individually are large near many-electron nuclei and substantially cancel. Treating nuclear attraction as a full finite-basis matrix while the Hartree field is approximated with IDA creates an avoidable numerical imbalance that can lead to spurious collapse (e.g., in Cr2).
AI.method: The paper introduces reference-density Hartree screening: the Hartree field of a chosen reference density is computed accurately (not via IDA), and IDA is applied only to density fluctuations about this reference. Additionally, a low-rank one-particle correction X_HF is introduced, built from a conventional Gaussian-basis Hartree-Fock calculation to match occupied-space exchange or complete occupied Fock vectors.
AI.result: Tests on He, Ne, F, F2, and Cr2 show large reductions in direct Hartree errors, with fitted neutral-atom reference fields transferable to molecules. For Cr2, atomic-core screening prevents the spurious HF collapse seen with unscreened q=5 and q=7 Hamiltonians, whereas reference matching without screening fails. X_HF reproduces finite-reference energies and occupied Fock vectors to numerical precision in F2 and Cr2. The corrected q=5 basis uses one quarter as many functions as q=7 while retaining sub-mHa mean-field accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Screening provides the physical improvement to the direct Hartree field by accurately representing the reference density's field, and the state-specific X_HF correction restores the remaining accuracy of the Gaussian-basis mean-field reference. The two combined approaches enable accurate, compact Gausslet calculations.

title: Quasi-normal-mode signatures of periodicity and hyperuniformity
summary: Hyperuniform materials occupy an intermediate regime between periodic order and conventional disorder, characterized by a suppression of long-wavelength density fluctuations, commonly quantified by the structure factor. This characterization, however, relies on the statistical properties of an extended configuration or supercell representation and does not directly describe the resonant response of a finite structure, as typically encountered in scattering experiments. Here, we introduce the quasi-normal-mode spectrum as a complementary framework for characterizing the wave properties of finite stealthy hyperuniform materials. We analyze the complex eigenfrequencies of both periodic and stealthy hyperuniform structures over a range of the stealthiness parameter ($χ$), and investigate how the spatial organization of scatterers is encoded in both frequency and spatial profiles of their quasi-normal modes. We find systematic changes in the quasi-normal modes spectrum as the degree of hyperuniformity is varied, revealing signatures that are not captured solely by the structure factor. In particular, the evolution of the resonant states provides a direct connection between structural correlations and the scattering response of finite systems. Our results establish quasi-normal modes as a real-space and open-system characterization of hyperuniformity and provide a unified framework for comparing discrete heterogeneous materials from the perspective of their scattering and resonant dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the quasi-normal-mode (QNM) spectrum as a complementary, finite-system framework for characterizing stealthy hyperuniform materials, showing that QNM signatures reveal wave/resonant properties not captured by the structure factor alone and providing a direct link between structural correlations and scattering response in finite open systems.
AI.motivation: Traditional characterization of hyperuniformity via the structure factor relies on statistical properties of extended or periodic supercell configurations, which does not directly capture the resonant response of finite structures encountered in scattering experiments. A framework is needed that describes the wave properties of finite stealthy hyperuniform systems from the perspective of their open-system resonant dynamics.
AI.method: The authors analyze the complex eigenfrequencies of quasi-normal modes for both periodic and stealthy hyperuniform structures across a range of the stealthiness parameter χ. They examine how spatial organization of scatterers is encoded in both the frequency spectra and spatial profiles of the quasi-normal modes, comparing signatures as the degree of hyperuniformity is varied.
AI.result: Systematic changes are found in the quasi-normal-mode spectrum as hyperuniformity degree is varied, revealing signatures not captured solely by the structure factor. Specifically, the evolution of resonant states provides a direct connection between structural correlations and the scattering response of finite systems.
AI.conclusion: The results establish quasi-normal modes as a real-space, open-system characterization of hyperuniformity, offering a unified framework for comparing discrete heterogeneous materials based on their scattering and resonant dynamics.

title: Green-function Zeros Encode Competing Mott and Charge-ordering Scales
summary: While correlated insulators are devoid of low-energy quasiparticle poles, their Green functions retain clean momentum structure through zeros. However, precisely what zeros imply is not clear. By studying the extended Hubbard model both analytically and numerically, we establish a new paradigm for strongly correlated matter: the dispersion of Green function zeros is determined by both microscopic spin-spin correlations and defect kinematics. In fact, we find that the dispersion changes discontinuously across the transition between the Mott and the checkerboard charge-density wave phases as is expected for a first-order transition. This physics is robust to the inclusion of further neighbor hopping which simply fine tunes the spin-correlation or charge-defect kinematics. We conclude that it is the {\it dispersion} of the Green-function zeros that encode the physics of ordering resultant from the strong correlations.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that in correlated insulators, the dispersion of Green function zeros is governed by microscopic spin-spin correlations and defect kinematics, and changes discontinuously across the first-order Mott to checkerboard charge-density wave transition.
AI.motivation: While correlated insulators lack low-energy quasiparticle poles, their Green functions retain clean momentum structure through zeros, yet precisely what these zeros imply was not clear. The authors aim to establish a new paradigm for understanding strongly correlated matter through the dispersion of Green function zeros.
AI.method: The authors study the extended Hubbard model both analytically and numerically, examining the dispersion of Green function zeros. They also test robustness by including further neighbor hopping to fine-tune spin-correlation or charge-defect kinematics.
AI.result: The dispersion of Green function zeros is determined by both microscopic spin-spin correlations and defect kinematics. The dispersion changes discontinuously across the transition between the Mott and checkerboard charge-density wave phases, consistent with a first-order transition. The physics remains robust upon including further neighbor hopping.
AI.conclusion: It is the dispersion of Green-function zeros that encodes the physics of ordering resulting from strong correlations, providing a new paradigm for strongly correlated matter.

title: Bayesian Tracking of a Diffusing Target in Two and Three Dimensions
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 14 pages of supplemental material
summary: We study Bayesian tracking of a diffusing target monitored by a noisy distributed sensor array. Building on an earlier mapping to KPZ growth with a moving defect (or an equivalent directed polymer pinning problem) we determine the phase structure, beyond the previously-studied one-dimensional case, for both Bayes-optimal and suboptimal inference. In $d=2$, theoretical analysis and numerical simulations both give a depinning transition between a successful tracking phase and a failure phase. Weak-coupling RG shows that Bayes-optimal tracking is always successful in $d=2$, but failure can arise from overconfident (suboptimal) inference. In $d=3$, tracking can succeed, or can fail in two distinct ways: the posterior probability distribution may delocalize (no detection), or may become sharply localized, but at the wrong position (a false detection). The two possibilities correspond to Edwards-Wilkinson or Kardar-Parisi-Zhang statistics for the log-posterior. The three phases meet at a Nishimori-like multicritical point on a Bayes-optimal line in a two-parameter phase diagram. (Model misspecification alone can drive depinning into either unpinned phase: underconfidence gives diffuse failure, while overconfidence gives localized-but-wrong failure.) We analyze the transitions between the various phases numerically and with renormalization group arguments. We show that some of these have unusual critical behavior, which the conventional $ε$ expansion fails to describe. Recent rigorous results for directed polymers indicate an alternative scenario. Many of our results, including a scaling relation for exponents at pinning transitions and results for RG flows, are relevant to other phase transitions that involve surface growth or directed polymers in 2+1D or 3+1D.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Bayesian tracking of a diffusing target monitored by noisy distributed sensors to higher dimensions (d=2,3), using a mapping to KPZ growth with a moving defect / directed polymer pinning. It reveals a depinning phase transition in d=2 (Bayes-optimal tracking always succeeds; suboptimal overconfident inference can fail) and three phases in d=3 (success, delocalized failure/no-detection, and localized-wrong-position failure/false detection), meeting at a Nishimori-like multicritical point. Analysis combines renormalization group, numerics, and rigorous directed polymer results.
AI.motivation: To understand Bayesian tracking of diffusing targets in higher-dimensional sensor networks beyond the previously studied one-dimensional case, revealing the phase structure for both Bayes-optimal and suboptimal (misspecified) inference through a mapping to KPZ growth and directed polymer pinning.
AI.method: Mapping to KPZ growth with a moving defect (equivalent to directed polymer pinning); weak-coupling renormalization group; numerical simulations; comparison with rigorous directed polymer results and ε expansion.
AI.result: In d=2, a depinning transition separates successful tracking from failure; Bayes-optimal tracking always succeeds but overconfident suboptimal inference can fail. In d=3, three phases exist: success, delocalized posterior (no detection, Edwards-Wilkinson statistics), and wrongly positioned sharp localization (false detection, KPZ statistics), meeting at a Nishimori-like multicritical point. Underconfidence and overconfidence drive distinct unpinned failure phases. Some transitions show unusual critical behavior that standard ε expansion fails to describe.
AI.conclusion: The phase diagram for Bayesian tracking generalizes richly beyond 1D, with scaling relations and RG flow results that are relevant to other phase transitions involving surface growth or directed polymers in 2+1D and 3+1D.

title: AutoXRD: Autonomous LLM Agents and Comprehensive Evaluation for Powder Diffraction Analysis
summary: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) is central to materials characterization, yet reliable end-to-end automation remains challenging. An XRD agent must interpret diffraction evidence, operate refinement software, manage coupled parameters in a defensible order, and distinguish numerical improvement from physical validity. In this paper, we propose AutoXRD, an autonomous large language model (LLM) agent framework that organizes powder-XRD analysis as stepwise refinement, grounds actions in observed evidence, and applies deterministic crystallographic and physical checks before accepting results. We further introduce XRDBench with two complementary tracks. XRDBench-QA contains 100 bounded diagnostic tasks that isolate scientific reasoning and decision-making, whereas XRDBench-E2E contains 34 executable workflows that test whether agents can compose these capabilities into complete analyses requiring file inspection, crystallographic-software execution, iterative refinement, evidence preservation, and reporting. We evaluate ten recent LLMs across 1,340 model--task runs. Models average only 57.8 out of 100, falling from 61.9 on XRDBench-QA to 53.7 on XRDBench-E2E. They perform best on refinement-history assessment and result acceptance, but remain substantially weaker on refinement-action selection, phase quantification, indexing, and Rietveld refinement. GPT-5.6 Sol achieves the highest overall score of 81.1, GPT-5.6 Terra the highest XRDBench-E2E point estimate of 81.0, and GPT-5.6 Luna the best score--cost trade-off. Ablations show that all six AutoXRD components consistently improve performance, supporting the framework design. Finally, execution-trace analysis reveals recurring failures in coupled-parameter control, quantitative reasoning, evidence preservation, and workflow termination, motivating stronger scientific constraints, uncertainty-aware decisions, and more efficient planning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AutoXRD, an autonomous LLM agent framework for powder X-ray diffraction analysis that structures analysis as stepwise refinement with deterministic crystallographic and physical validation. It also presents XRDBench with two tracks (QA and E2E) for evaluating LLM agents. Evaluation of ten LLMs across 1,340 runs shows a mean score of only 57.8/100, with GPT-5.6 Sol best overall (81.1). Ablations confirm all six AutoXRD components contribute positively, while execution-trace analysis identifies recurring failure modes in coupled-parameter control, quantitative reasoning, and workflow termination.
AI.motivation: Powder XRD is central to materials characterization, but reliable end-to-end automation remains unsolved. An XRD agent must integrate multiple capabilities—interpreting diffraction evidence, operating refinement software, managing coupled parameters, and judging physical validity over mere numerical improvement—which no existing framework or benchmark adequately addresses.
AI.method: The authors propose AutoXRD, an LLM agent framework that organizes powder-XRD analysis as stepwise refinement, grounds actions in observed evidence, and applies deterministic crystallographic/physical checks before accepting results. They introduce XRDBench with two tracks: XRDBench-QA (100 bounded diagnostic tasks isolating reasoning) and XRDBench-E2E (34 executable workflows requiring file inspection, crystallographic-software execution, iterative refinement, evidence preservation, and reporting). Ten recent LLMs are evaluated across 1,340 model-task runs, supplemented by ablation studies and execution-trace analysis.
AI.result: Models average only 57.8/100 overall, dropping from 61.9 on XRDBench-QA to 53.7 on XRDBench-E2E. Models perform best on refinement-history assessment and result acceptance but are notably weaker on refinement-action selection, phase quantification, indexing, and Rietveld refinement. GPT-5.6 Sol achieves the highest overall score (81.1), GPT-5.6 Terra the highest E2E estimate (81.0), and GPT-5.6 Luna the best score-cost trade-off. All six AutoXRD components improve performance in ablations. Execution-trace analysis reveals recurring failures in coupled-parameter control, quantitative reasoning, evidence preservation, and workflow termination.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that while LLM agents show promise for XRD automation, current models are substantially limited, particularly in complex compositional tasks. The AutoXRD framework design is validated by consistent gains from each component. The observed failure modes motivate stronger scientific constraints, uncertainty-aware decisions, and more efficient planning in future systems.

title: Mixture of Polyconvex Neural Potentials for Parametric Hyperelasticity: Towards Foundation Material Models
summary: Hyperelastic constitutive models enable modeling large deformations in elastic solids. In common practice, a strain energy density function is prescribed in advance and model-specific parameters are calibrated from experiments. However, many applications require constitutive models for a family of related materials whose mechanical behavior varies with composition. A fixed constitutive model-form may not capture the full range of behavior across the family, while fitting separate forms does not provide a direct way to predict the response of new compositions. Recent work has developed data-driven constitutive models that learn flexible strain energy functions while incorporating key physical constraints. In this work, we propose using mixtures of convex neural potentials based on input convex neural networks as a modular and data efficient approach to modeling material families. Each potential is convex and monotonic with respect to polyconvex strain invariants, while a conditioning network maps material descriptors to mixture weights. We compare the approach with a monolithic partially input-convex neural network using experimental data from PolyJet 3D-printed materials and a synthetic Gent-type benchmark. Across both benchmarks, the mixture architecture generalized better to material descriptors not seen during training. In the PolyJet experimental benchmark, we showed that the mixture architecture is less sensitive to model hyperparameters, while in the Gent-type benchmark it generalized more reliably with sparse data in the material-descriptor space. These results suggest that representing a material family through a small set of shared convex neural potentials provides a useful structural prior for learning descriptor-dependent constitutive behavior from limited data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using mixtures of convex neural potentials (based on input convex neural networks) as a modular, data-efficient approach to model families of hyperelastic materials. Each potential is convex and monotonic with respect to polyconvex strain invariants, while a conditioning network maps material descriptors to mixture weights. The mixture architecture showed better generalization to unseen material descriptors than a monolithic partially input-convex neural network on both a PolyJet 3D-printed material dataset and a synthetic Gent-type benchmark.
AI.motivation: Many applications require constitutive models for families of materials whose behavior varies with composition. A fixed constitutive model-form may fail to capture the full range of behavior across the family, while fitting separate models does not provide a direct way to predict responses of new compositions. A method that learns flexible strain energy functions while generalizing across material descriptors is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose representing a material family as a mixture of shared convex neural potentials based on input convex neural networks (ICNNs). Each potential is convex and monotonic with respect to polyconvex strain invariants, enforcing physical constraints. A conditioning network takes material descriptors as input and outputs mixture weights that combine the convex potentials. This architecture is compared to a monolithic partially input-convex neural network on two benchmarks: experimental PolyJet 3D-printed materials and a synthetic Gent-type model.
AI.result: The mixture architecture generalized better to material descriptors not seen during training on both benchmarks. In the PolyJet benchmark, it was less sensitive to model hyperparameters. In the Gent-type benchmark, it generalized more reliably with sparse data in the material-descriptor space.
AI.conclusion: Representing a material family through a small set of shared convex neural potentials provides a useful structural prior for learning descriptor-dependent constitutive behavior from limited data. This modular mixture approach offers better generalization and robustness compared to monolithic neural network approaches.

title: How Landau caterpillars turn into Hofstadter butterflies by tuning the periodic potential strength
summary: It is well-known that the spectrum of two-dimensional electrons in a perpendicular magnetic field is given by discrete flat Landau levels. By contrast, electrons in a two-dimensional tight-binding model give rise to a fractal Hofstadter butterfly spectrum. In this paper, we connect these two opposite limits by showing how a butterfly spectrum emerges from broadened Landau `caterpillars', by continuously increasing the periodic potential strength. We identify a series of topological transitions that isolate a lowest trivial band, a necessary condition for the butterfly to emerge. The resulting butterfly is topologically distinct from the Hofstadter butterfly at fluxes $φ>1$, due to anomalous behavior of diagonal hopping. Moreover, the hopping parameters of an effective tight-binding model, obtained by a Wannierization procedure at large magnetic field, are highly dependent on the flux, revealing that Wannier orbitals themselves change under the applied magnetic field. Our methods and results are relevant for artificial materials, such as moiré systems, where a full quantum of flux per lattice unit cell is experimentally accessible. On a theoretical level, having Wannierization methods for each specific flux allows more accurate many-body calculations in large magnetic fields.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges the gap between the flat Landau levels of two-dimensional electrons in a magnetic field and the fractal Hofstadter butterfly spectrum in tight-binding models, showing how the butterfly emerges from broadened Landau levels as periodic potential strength increases. It identifies topological transitions isolating a lowest trivial band, reveals a butterfly topologically distinct from Hofstadter's at higher fluxes due to anomalous diagonal hopping, and shows that effective tight-binding hopping parameters from Wannierization are highly flux-dependent.
AI.motivation: To understand the connection between two opposite limits in condensed matter: continuous electrons in a magnetic field (Landau levels) versus lattice-bound electrons (Hofstadter butterfly), particularly relevant for artificial materials like moiré systems where full flux quanta per unit cell are experimentally accessible.
AI.method: The authors continuously increase the periodic potential strength to show the butterfly spectrum emerging from broadened Landau levels. They identify topological transitions that isolate a lowest trivial band, and apply a Wannierization procedure at large magnetic field to derive an effective tight-binding model, analyzing how hopping parameters depend on flux.
AI.result: A butterfly spectrum emerges from broadened Landau "caterpillars" as periodic potential increases. The resulting butterfly is topologically distinct from the Hofstadter butterfly for fluxes φ>1 due to anomalous diagonal hopping behavior. The effective tight-binding hopping parameters from Wannierization are highly flux-dependent, indicating Wannier orbitals themselves change under the applied magnetic field.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified theoretical framework connecting Landau levels and Hofstadter physics, with implications for moiré systems where flux quantization is experimentally feasible. The flux-specific Wannierization methods enable more accurate many-body calculations in large magnetic fields.

title: Smoothed truncated Coulomb potential for periodic Gaussian-basis Hartree--Fock exchange
summary: Truncated Coulomb (TC) potentials reduce finite-size errors and accelerate thermodynamic-limit convergence in periodic Hartree--Fock (HF) calculations, but their use with Gaussian basis sets is complicated by the evaluation of electron repulsion integrals (ERIs), particularly for nonspherical truncation domains and all-electron calculations. We introduce the smoothed truncated Coulomb (sTC) potential as a systematically improvable approximation to a parent TC potential. A real-space Gaussian convolution smooths the sharp truncation boundary, and a single dimensionless parameter, $η$, controls the width of the smoothing window, which can be tightened to systematically approach the TC reference. The smoothing by sTC enables a dual-space algorithm for evaluating periodic Gaussian-basis ERIs that requires neither a large plane-wave basis nor new molecular integral kernels and is applicable to both pseudopotential and all-electron calculations, including the important Wigner--Seitz-cell truncation boundaries. Benchmarks spanning insulating, semiconducting, layered, metallic, and molecular-crystal systems show that sTC-based HF closely reproduces TC results in pseudopotential calculations and extends TC-quality calculations to all-electron settings. Across these systems, sTC substantially improves thermodynamic-limit convergence relative to the probe-charge Ewald method while remaining practical for all-electron calculations in which direct TC-based calculations are computationally challenging.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a smoothed truncated Coulomb (sTC) potential that approximates truncated Coulomb potentials via a Gaussian convolution controlled by a single parameter η. This smoothing enables an efficient dual-space algorithm for evaluating periodic Gaussian-basis electron repulsion integrals applicable to both pseudopotential and all-electron calculations, without requiring large plane-wave bases or new molecular integral kernels. Benchmarks across various material classes show sTC reproduces TC results and substantially improves thermodynamic-limit convergence over the probe-charge Ewald method.
AI.motivation: Truncated Coulomb potentials accelerate thermodynamic-limit convergence in periodic Hartree-Fock calculations but are difficult to combine with Gaussian basis sets because evaluating electron repulsion integrals becomes complicated, especially for nonspherical truncation domains and all-electron calculations.
AI.method: The authors introduce the smoothed truncated Coulomb (sTC) potential, which applies a real-space Gaussian convolution to smooth the sharp truncation boundary of a TC potential. A single dimensionless parameter η controls the smoothing window width and can be tightened to systematically recover the TC reference. This smoothing permits a dual-space algorithm for evaluating periodic Gaussian-basis ERIs that avoids large plane-wave bases and new molecular integral kernels, supporting both pseudopotential and all-electron calculations including Wigner-Seitz-cell truncation boundaries.
AI.result: Benchmarks across insulating, semiconducting, layered, metallic, and molecular-crystal systems show sTC-based HF closely matches TC results in pseudopotential calculations and extends TC-quality results to all-electron settings. sTC substantially improves thermodynamic-limit convergence relative to the probe-charge Ewald method while remaining practical for all-electron calculations where direct TC is computationally prohibitive.
AI.conclusion: The sTC potential offers a systematically improvable, practical route to TC-quality Hartree-Fock calculations in periodic Gaussian-basis methods, bridging the gap between TC accuracy and computational feasibility, particularly for all-electron calculations.

title: Subgap Bound States from Dynamical Impurities
comment: Main document: 7 pages, 6 Figures. Supplement: 13 pages, 3 Figures
summary: We find that a single non-magnetic dynamical impurity (e.g., a low-frequency localized "vibron" mode) induces a subgap bound state in an s-wave superconductor. A closed-form solution for the bound state energy is found as a function of the vibron frequency in the elastic scattering limit, with the salient features of the bound state energies unaffected by inelastic scattering processes in the sub-THz regime. In addition to subgap features in the low-frequency local density of states, such impurities result in real space regions of reduced spectroscopic weight outside the gap peak.

AI.tldr: A single non-magnetic dynamical impurity (low-frequency vibron) creates a subgap bound state in an s-wave superconductor. The bound state energy has a closed-form solution in the elastic scattering limit, robust to inelastic scattering in the sub-THz regime, and manifests as reduced spectroscopic weight near the impurity.
AI.motivation: To understand how non-magnetic dynamical impurities—distinct from static or magnetic impurities—can generate subgap bound states in s-wave superconductors, potentially explaining experimental spectroscopic features that are not captured by conventional impurity models.
AI.method: The authors analyze a non-magnetic dynamical impurity modeled as a low-frequency localized vibron mode coupled to an s-wave superconductor. They derive a closed-form expression for the bound state energy in the elastic scattering limit and examine the effects of inelastic scattering, particularly in the sub-THz frequency regime. They also compute the spatial dependence of the local density of states.
AI.result: A closed-form bound state energy is obtained as a function of vibron frequency in the elastic limit. The bound state energies remain essentially unchanged even when inelastic scattering is included at sub-THz frequencies. The impurity also produces subgap features in the low-frequency local density of states and creates real-space regions of suppressed spectroscopic weight outside the gap peak.
AI.conclusion: Non-magnetic dynamical impurities can serve as a mechanism for generating subgap bound states in s-wave superconductors, offering a new way to interpret low-energy spectroscopic signatures beyond standard magnetic or static impurity paradigms.

title: A Constrained Kuramoto Gradient-Flow System Can Perform High-Accuracy Finite-Time Inference
summary: A central question in physical inference is whether strongly constrained dynamical systems can realize accurate input--output maps through their own finite-time evolution. We study this question in Kuramoto phase networks, whose deterministic dynamics form an input-conditioned gradient flow and whose predictions are read directly from output oscillators. As a constructive training approach, we develop a two-stage teacher--student procedure. A neural teacher is first converted into an explicit phase trajectory whose terminal oscillator activations reproduce the teacher outputs, and the Kuramoto parameters are trained by matching the student vector field along this prescribed path. Because accurate teacher-forced path matching does not ensure accurate autonomous inference, we then differentiate through the autonomous finite-time rollout and directly align its terminal output with the neural target. The resulting oscillator system, with $74$ oscillators, reaches mean test accuracies of $96.711\%$ on MNIST and $86.399\%$ on Fashion-MNIST. This capability persists across neural-teacher architectures, matched system sizes, thermal perturbations, and integration-grid refinement. Together, these results provide a constructive demonstration that a strongly constrained, small-sized Kuramoto gradient-flow system can be trained for high-accuracy finite-time inference through a direct oscillator readout.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that strongly constrained Kuramoto phase networks can perform accurate finite-time inference through their own deterministic dynamics. A two-stage teacher-student training procedure first matches a neural teacher's outputs via a prescribed phase trajectory, then directly differentiates through the autonomous rollout to align terminal outputs with the neural target. The resulting 74-oscillator system achieves 96.7% on MNIST and 86.4% on Fashion-MNIST, with robustness across architectures, system sizes, perturbations, and grid refinements.
AI.motivation: The central question is whether strongly constrained dynamical systems—whose dynamics form a gradient flow—can realize accurate input-output maps through their own finite-time evolution, rather than requiring external computation. This probes the fundamental limits of physical inference in low-dimensional, highly constrained systems.
AI.method: The approach is a two-stage teacher-student procedure. First, a neural teacher is converted into an explicit phase trajectory whose terminal oscillator activations match the teacher outputs. Second, Kuramoto parameters are trained by (1) matching the student vector field along the prescribed teacher-forced path, and (2) differentiating through the autonomous finite-time rollout to directly align the terminal readout with the neural target, since teacher-forced matching alone does not guarantee accurate autonomous inference.
AI.result: The trained Kuramoto system with 74 oscillators achieves mean test accuracies of 96.711% on MNIST and 86.399% on Fashion-MNIST. The capability persists across different neural-teacher architectures, matched system sizes, thermal perturbations, and integration-grid refinement.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a constructive demonstration that a strongly constrained, small-sized Kuramoto gradient-flow system can be trained to perform high-accuracy finite-time inference with a direct oscillator readout, suggesting that physical dynamics themselves can serve as viable computational substrates for classification tasks.

title: Higher-Winding Fractionalization
summary: Higher-winding skyrmion textures can generate emergent magnetic fields with multiple flux quanta per unit cell. This opens an intriguing route toward fractionalization, allowing fractionalized quantum anomalous Hall states to arise even at integer filling of the microscopic unit cell. We show that, in this setting, increasing lattice-scale inhomogeneity of the emergent magnetic field drives a Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless (BKT) transition between a fractionalized liquid and a crystalline dielectric state. This transition carries a topological signature: under flux insertion, the many-body polarization defines a quantized winding number that is nonzero in the fractionalized phase and vanishes in the dielectric crystal.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that higher-winding skyrmion textures generating multi-flux-quantum emergent magnetic fields can host fractionalized quantum anomalous Hall states at integer filling. Increasing lattice-scale inhomogeneity of the emergent field drives a BKT transition between a fractionalized liquid and a crystalline dielectric state, characterized by a quantized topological winding number in the many-body polarization under flux insertion.
AI.motivation: To explore a route toward fractionalization where emergent magnetic fields from higher-winding skyrmions with multiple flux quanta per unit cell enable fractionalized quantum anomalous Hall states even at integer filling, and to understand the phase transition out of such states driven by emergent-field inhomogeneity.
AI.method: The paper analyzes a system of higher-winding skyrmion textures with multi-flux-quantum emergent fields, studying the effect of lattice-scale inhomogeneity on emergent magnetic field. It identifies a BKT transition between fractionalized liquid and crystalline dielectric phases, using many-body polarization under flux insertion to define a quantized winding number as a topological order parameter.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that increasing lattice-scale inhomogeneity of the emergent magnetic field drives a BKT transition from a fractionalized liquid to a crystalline dielectric state. This transition exhibits a topological signature: under flux insertion, the many-body polarization shows a quantized winding number that is nonzero in the fractionalized phase and vanishes in the dielectric crystal.
AI.conclusion: Higher-winding skyrmion textures provide a platform for fractionalized quantum anomalous Hall states at integer filling, and the transition to a dielectric crystalline state via emergent-field inhomogeneity is characterized by a topological invariant (quantized polarization winding number), offering a robust diagnostic for the fractionalized phase.

title: Bound states, resonances, and their thermodynamic properties in pseudospin-1 systems with short-range impurities
summary: Bound states and resonances induced by short-range impurities modeled by circular potential wells are analyzed in the vicinity of flat and dispersive bands in gapped and gapless pseudospin-1 systems. We find that the bound and resonant states derived from the flat band show unusual characteristics originating from the multicomponent structure of pseudospin-1 fermions, which are distinct from those for pseudospin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ fermions. Contrary to gapped Dirac systems and unlike bound states in the vicinity of the upper dispersive band, the bound states derived from the flat band occur for any value of the total angular momentum. The energies of these bound states with higher angular momentum $j$ tend to decrease with $|j|$. In addition, it is found that their wave functions are localized at the potential well edge and the localization increases with $|j|$. The signatures of the impurity states in the local density of states are determined. Using the Anderson model for independent electrons in the disorder potential, the thermodynamic potential, entropy density, and heat capacity are obtained. In the regime dominated by bound states derived from the flat band, the entropy density monotonically increases with temperature and saturates, whereas the heat capacity exhibits a single maximum.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes bound states and resonances induced by short-range circular potential well impurities in pseudospin-1 systems near flat and dispersive bands. Unlike pseudospin-1/2 systems, flat-band-derived bound states exist for any total angular momentum, with energies decreasing and wave functions localizing more strongly at the impurity edge as |j| increases. The thermodynamic signatures (entropy and heat capacity) of these impurity states are also derived.
AI.motivation: To understand how short-range impurities modeled by circular potential wells affect the electronic properties of pseudospin-1 systems, particularly the unusual bound and resonant states derived from flat bands—which are expected to differ fundamentally from those in pseudospin-1/2 (Dirac) systems due to the multicomponent structure of pseudospin-1 fermions.
AI.method: Analytical analysis of circular potential wells as impurity models in gapped and gapless pseudospin-1 systems, near both flat and dispersive bands. Bound state energies and wave function characteristics are examined as a function of total angular momentum. The Anderson model for independent electrons in a disorder potential is employed to compute thermodynamic quantities (thermodynamic potential, entropy density, and heat capacity).
AI.result: (1) Flat-band-derived bound states occur for any total angular momentum value, unlike gapped Dirac systems and unlike those derived from the upper dispersive band. (2) Bound state energies with higher angular momentum j tend to decrease with |j|. (3) Wave functions of these states are localized at the potential well edge, with localization increasing with |j|. (4) Signatures of impurity states in the local density of states are determined. (5) In the flat-band-bound-state-dominated regime, entropy density monotonically increases with temperature and saturates, while heat capacity shows a single maximum.
AI.conclusion: Flat-band-induced impurity states in pseudospin-1 systems exhibit qualitatively distinct physics compared to pseudospin-1/2 Dirac systems, notably the existence of bound states for arbitrary angular momentum and enhanced edge localization for higher j. These states produce characteristic thermodynamic signatures—monotonic saturating entropy and single-peaked heat capacity—which can be used as observable fingerprints of such impurity effects.

title: Fermi-Level Metal-d Character of Group-6 Bis-Hexahapto Bilayer Graphene
comment: 20 pages, 7 figures. DFT study of bis-hexahapto group-6 bilayer graphene; electron-phonon coupling not computed
summary: Superconductivity in graphite intercalation compounds requires occupancy of a carbon-derived interlayer band filled by charge from an electropositive intercalant. Bis-hexahapto (eta6-eta6) coordination binds transition metals covalently to two graphene sheets with little charge transfer -- the mechanism that defines this chemistry removes the donation on which intercalated-graphite superconductivity rests. We ask, for group-6 Cr, Mo and W in bilayer graphene, whether Fermi-level states retain the interstitial, carbon-p character of ionic references, with bulk CaC6 and same-cell C12Ca/C12Li controls. Electron-phonon coupling is not computed. At one metal per gallery (C12M), the ionic controls retain 68 and 45 per cent, respectively, of gallery spectral weight in atom-masked interstitial regions at EF; the group-6 systems retain 15, 22 and 23 per cent. The contrast is compositional: group-6 galleries carry more absolute interstitial weight than C12Li, but projected density of states within +/-0.15 eV of EF is carbon p dominated in the ionic references and metal d dominated (~73 per cent) in all three group-6 bilayers. Every system studied is metallic; they differ in what carries the Fermi surface. Geometrically, eta6-eta6 coordination requires AA stacking and reverses the intrinsic Bernal preference by 400-600 meV wherever metal is present. Ordered phases are metastable against bulk metal (+2.9-5.0 eV per atom) but bound against isolated atoms (-1.6-4.1 eV); instability ordering (Cr least, W most) matches Cr > Mo > W reactivity. C12Cr is metallic; tungsten alone carries 0.65 muB. Bis-hexahapto intercalation delivers strong interlayer bonding and a definite AA registry, but not the interlayer-band character associated with superconducting graphite intercalation compounds.

AI.tldr: Bis-hexahapto group-6 metal intercalation (Cr, Mo, W) in bilayer graphene creates strong covalent metal-carbon bonds with minimal charge transfer, reversing Bernal stacking toward AA registry and providing interlayer bonding, but the Fermi-level states are metal d-dominated (~73%) rather than carbon-derived interlayer-band character, unlike ionic references (CaC6, C12Li), making these systems unsuitable for superconducting graphite intercalation compound behavior.
AI.motivation: To determine whether bis-hexahapto (η6-η6) coordinated group-6 transition metals in bilayer graphene retain the interstitial carbon-p interlayer-band character at the Fermi level that underlies superconductivity in graphite intercalation compounds, given that this covalent coordination mechanism removes charge donation.
AI.method: Density functional analysis comparing group-6 (Cr, Mo, W) bis-hexahapto bilayer graphene systems to ionic control references (bulk CaC6 and same-cell C12Ca/C12Li), using spectral weight analysis in atom-masked interstitial regions and projected density of states within ±0.15 eV of the Fermi level. Electron-phonon coupling was not computed.
AI.result: Group-6 galleries retain only 15, 22 and 23% of gallery spectral weight in interstitial regions at EF (vs. 68% and 45% for C12Ca and C12Li ionic controls), with metal d states dominating ~73% of the PDOS near EF. All systems are metallic but differ in Fermi-surface carrier character. η6-η6 coordination requires and enforces AA stacking, reversing Bernal preference by 400-600 meV. Ordered phases are metastable against bulk metal (+2.9-5.0 eV/atom) but bound vs. isolated atoms (-1.6-4.1 eV/atom); C12Cr is metallic, W carries 0.65 μB.
AI.conclusion: Bis-hexahapto transition-metal intercalation provides strong interlayer bonding and definite AA registry but does not deliver the carbon-derived interlayer-band character necessary for superconducting graphite intercalation behavior; the common architectural motif masks a fundamental electronic difference from ionic alkali/alkaline-earth intercalates.

title: Nonlinear Fluctuating Hydrodynamics from Interacting Noisy Quantum Matter
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures without end matter and supplementary material
summary: A universal characterization of non-equilibrium steady states in interacting quantum many-body systems remains one of the central challenges of statistical physics. Here, we address this problem for a paradigmatic model of diffusive interacting quantum matter---the boundary-driven XXZ spin chain with bulk dephasing---and derive, directly from its microscopic Lindblad dynamics, an emergent classical Macroscopic Fluctuation Theory (MFT) governing its large-scale fluctuations. Crucially, the resulting hydrodynamics carries a density-dependent diffusivity and mobility as the fingerprint of interactions. This effective description enables the exact computation of the stationary density profile, long-range correlations, and the full counting statistics of the current, in excellent agreement with tensor-network simulations. Our work demonstrates that noisy quantum many-body systems can realize the universality class of genuinely interacting diffusive matter, beyond the constant-diffusivity class of the symmetric simple exclusion process, and establishes MFT as a powerful universal framework for interacting diffusive quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a classical Macroscopic Fluctuation Theory (MFT) directly from the microscopic Lindblad dynamics of a boundary-driven XXZ spin chain with bulk dephasing, demonstrating that noisy interacting quantum systems belong to the universality class of genuinely interacting diffusive matter with density-dependent transport coefficients.
AI.motivation: A universal characterization of non-equilibrium steady states in interacting quantum many-body systems remains a central open challenge in statistical physics. This work aims to address this gap for a paradigmatic model of diffusive interacting quantum matter.
AI.method: Starting from the microscopic Lindblad dynamics of a boundary-driven XXZ spin chain with bulk dephasing, the authors derive an emergent classical Macroscopic Fluctuation Theory that describes the large-scale fluctuations. The resulting hydrodynamics features density-dependent diffusivity and mobility encoding interaction effects. Exact computations of the stationary density profile, long-range correlations, and full counting statistics of the current are validated against tensor-network simulations.
AI.result: The effective MFT description enables exact computation of the stationary density profile, long-range correlations, and current full counting statistics, all in excellent agreement with tensor-network simulations. The results show this noisy quantum many-body system realizes the universality class of genuinely interacting diffusive matter, beyond the constant-diffusivity class of the symmetric simple exclusion process.
AI.conclusion: Noisy quantum many-body systems can realize the universality class of genuinely interacting diffusive matter, and MFT is established as a powerful universal framework for interacting diffusive quantum systems.

title: A Non-Isothermal Viscoplastic Constitutive Model for Clay Slip Surfaces
summary: Clayey slip surfaces control the reactivation and long-term deformation of slow-moving landslides and may experience thermal fluctuations from climate, seasonal ground-temperature changes, or subsurface heat sources. Experiments show that residual shear strength depends on temperature and shearing rate, yet most numerical approaches use temperature-independent strength parameters. We present a non-isothermal viscoplastic constitutive model for clayey slip surfaces implemented with zero-thickness interface elements. It includes temperature-dependent normal and tangential stiffness, progressive degradation of cohesion and friction angle, and rate-dependent viscoplastic slip governed by a non-associated flow rule. Coupling with hydraulic and thermal balance equations allows the interface response to evolve with stress state, temperature, aperture, and accumulated irreversible displacement. Validation against temperature-controlled drained ring-shear tests on bentonite and smectite-rich soils covers heating--cooling, cooling--heating, and combined thermal paths. The simulations reproduce thermal strengthening at slow shearing rates and thermal weakening or limited sensitivity at higher rates. Application to the Congress Street cut benchmark shows that zero-thickness elements improve the representation of strain localization and progressive failure. Increasing temperature progressively degrades interface strength, increases displacement, joint aperture, and shear strain, and accelerates sliding. Temperature-dependent interface degradation can therefore reduce the apparent stability margin of clayey slopes and should be included in slope-stability assessments involving thermal fluctuations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a non-isothermal viscoplastic constitutive model for clayey slip surfaces implemented with zero-thickness interface elements, incorporating temperature-dependent stiffness, progressive cohesion/friction degradation, and rate-dependent viscoplastic slip. Validated against temperature-controlled ring-shear tests, the model captures thermal strengthening/weakening behaviors and demonstrates that temperature-induced interface degradation accelerates sliding and reduces slope stability margins.
AI.motivation: Clayey slip surfaces control landslide reactivation and long-term deformation, yet existing numerical approaches use temperature-independent strength parameters despite experimental evidence showing residual shear strength depends on temperature and shearing rate.
AI.method: A non-isothermal viscoplastic constitutive model is developed for clayey slip surfaces using zero-thickness interface elements. It features temperature-dependent normal and tangential stiffness, progressive degradation of cohesion and friction angle, and rate-dependent viscoplastic slip governed by a non-associated flow rule. Coupling with hydraulic and thermal balance equations enables interface response evolution with stress, temperature, aperture, and accumulated irreversible displacement. Validation uses temperature-controlled drained ring-shear tests on bentonite and smectite-rich soils, and application to the Congress Street cut benchmark.
AI.result: The model reproduces thermal strengthening at slow shearing rates and thermal weakening or limited sensitivity at higher rates. Zero-thickness elements improve strain localization and progressive failure representation in the Congress Street cut benchmark. Increasing temperature progressively degrades interface strength, increases displacement, joint aperture, and shear strain, and accelerates sliding.
AI.conclusion: Temperature-dependent interface degradation can reduce the apparent stability margin of clayey slopes and should be incorporated into slope-stability assessments involving thermal fluctuations.

title: Entanglement from particle number fluctuations in a second-order topological insulator
summary: Higher-order topological insulators are materials with a bulk energy gap featuring gapless modes at $(d-n)$-dimensional edges, where $n > 1$. Despite this modified bulk-boundary correspondence, their nontrivial topology can nevertheless be observed through the bipartite entanglement spectrum. Inspired by works suggesting fluctuations in conserved quantities could be used to study topology in one-dimensional systems, which likewise feature zero-dimensional edge modes, we extend this treatment to a two-dimensional second-order topological insulator where corner states play an analogous role. We show that the standard bipartite entanglement entropy and particle number fluctuation lack striking signals of topological phase transitions, both in the static case and in the time evolution after a quench, obscured by an area-law term from the subsystem edges. By introducing a quadripartite construction of the subsystem, we show that it is possible to isolate the topological contributions, producing sharp transition peaks in both quantities, observable by studying subsystems much smaller than the full system. As particle number fluctuations are accessible in existing experiments, these results establish a concrete and scalable path to experimental detection of the entanglement in higher-order topological insulators.

AI.tldr: The paper studies higher-order topological insulators (2D second-order with corner states) and shows that standard bipartite entanglement entropy and particle number fluctuations fail to reveal topological phase transitions due to area-law contributions from subsystem edges. By introducing a quadripartite subsystem construction, the authors isolate topological contributions, resulting in sharp transition peaks in both quantities measurable on small subsystems, offering a scalable experimental route to detect entanglement in higher-order topological insulators.
AI.motivation: Higher-order topological insulators exhibit modified bulk-boundary correspondence with gapless modes at (d-n)-dimensional edges, making their topology hard to observe in standard ways. Prior work suggested fluctuations of conserved quantities can probe topology in 1D systems with zero-dimensional edge modes; the authors extend this to 2D second-order topological insulators where corner states play an analogous role.
AI.method: The authors analyze bipartite entanglement entropy and particle number fluctuation in both static configurations and time evolution after a quench. They demonstrate that these standard measures are masked by an area-law term originating from subsystem edges. They propose a quadripartite construction of the subsystem that isolates topological contributions, yielding sharp peaks at topological phase transitions even when subsystems are much smaller than the full system.
AI.result: The quadripartite construction produces sharp transition peaks in both entanglement entropy and particle number fluctuations, observable using small subsystems far smaller than the whole system. These quantities are accessible in existing experiments, providing a concrete detection pathway for entanglement in higher-order topological insulators.
AI.conclusion: Particle number fluctuations measured with a suitable quadripartite subsystem geometry can serve as a scalable, experimentally accessible probe of topological entanglement in higher-order topological insulators, overcoming the obscuring effect of area-law contributions.

title: Use of Cholesky decomposition in the CFOUR program package
summary: An overview is given about our efforts to speed up high-level computations of molec- ular energies and properties using Cholesky decomposition (CD). We describe the cor- responding developments in the CFOUR quantum-chemical package with a focus on (a) the use of CD in complete-active space self-consistent-field (CASSCF) and coupled- cluster (CC) computations, (b) the implementation of analytic CC gradients using CD, (c) the efficient calculation of magnetic properties (NMR shieldings and magnetizabili- ties) using CD when carried out with explicit magnetic-field dependent basis functions, i.e., the so-called gauge-including atomic orbitals (GIAOs), (d) the efficient computa- tion of CASSCF response properties using CD, (e) the use of CD in relativistic two- and four-component computations, as well as (f) computations for molecules in finite magnetic fields using GIAOs together with CD. An outlook on future developments concerning the CFOUR package is given.

AI.tldr: This paper provides an overview of efforts to accelerate high-level molecular energy and property computations using Cholesky decomposition (CD) within the CFOUR quantum-chemical package, covering its applications to CASSCF, coupled-cluster, analytic CC gradients, magnetic properties (NMR shieldings and magnetizabilities), response properties, relativistic computations, and molecules in finite magnetic fields. The authors also present an outlook on future CFOUR developments.
AI.motivation: The goal is to speed up high-level quantum-chemical computations of molecular energies and properties by leveraging Cholesky decomposition to reduce computational cost associated with two-electron integrals.
AI.method: The paper describes the implementation of Cholesky decomposition within the CFOUR package across multiple domains: (a) CASSCF and coupled-cluster energy computations, (b) analytic CC gradients, (c) magnetic properties (NMR shieldings and magnetizabilities) with gauge-including atomic orbitals (GIAOs), (d) CASSCF response properties, (e) relativistic two- and four-component computations, and (f) computations for molecules in finite magnetic fields using GIAOs combined with CD.
AI.result: The paper presents an overview of completed CD-based developments across these computational domains in CFOUR, demonstrating significant acceleration in high-level molecular computations.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the broad applicability of Cholesky decomposition for accelerating high-level quantum-chemical computations, with future developments for the CFOUR package outlined.

title: Impurity-dependent quantum geometry in 2D flat band superconductors
summary: In flat band superconductors, quantum geometry, rather than kinetic energy, governs pairing and transport. However, how this geometry manifests in the response to a local, individually addressable impurity remains largely unexplored. Here, we study the Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) bound state induced by a magnetic adatom that hybridizes with every orbital of a two-dimensional flat band superconductor, and characterize its spatial profile using two quantities: the quadratic spread $Q_S$ and the localization length $ξ$. We show that $Q_S$ is not set by the quantum metric alone, as geometric corrections arising from inter-orbital interference and, more importantly, from the anisotropy of the adatom-lattice hybridization contribute on equal footing, making $Q_S$ strongly impurity dependent and tunable. On the other hand, $ξ$ emerges from the projection onto the flat band alone and is a universal property set by the overlap of compact localized states. All impurity dependence is instead isolated in the prefactor of the wavefunction whose magnitude correlates directly with $Q_S$. We, therefore, report a clean separation between universal and impurity-tunable physics from the induced YSR bound state in these systems, and confirm our results numerically via exact diagonalization.

AI.tldr: This paper studies Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) bound states induced by a magnetic adatom in two-dimensional flat band superconductors. It shows that the quadratic spread Q_S of the bound state is strongly impurity-dependent and tunable due to inter-orbital interference and adatom-lattice hybridization anisotropy, while the localization length ξ is universal, determined solely by the projection onto the flat band and the overlap of compact localized states.
AI.motivation: In flat band superconductors, quantum geometry governs pairing and transport, but how this geometry manifests in the response to a local, individually addressable impurity (magnetic adatom) has remained largely unexplored. This motivates investigating how the induced YSR state probes the system's quantum geometry.
AI.method: The authors study a YSR bound state induced by a magnetic adatom that hybridizes with every orbital of a two-dimensional flat band superconductor. They characterize its spatial profile using two quantities: the quadratic spread Q_S and the localization length ξ. They derive analytic expressions separating geometric corrections (inter-orbital interference and adatom-lattice hybridization anisotropy) from the pure flat-band projection contribution, and confirm results numerically via exact diagonalization.
AI.result: Q_S is not determined by quantum metric alone; geometric corrections from inter-orbital interference and adatom-lattice hybridization anisotropy contribute equally, making Q_S strongly impurity dependent and tunable. In contrast, ξ emerges purely from the flat band projection and is universal, set by the overlap of compact localized states. All impurity dependence is isolated in the wavefunction prefactor whose magnitude correlates directly with Q_S, giving a clean separation of universal and impurity-tunable physics.
AI.conclusion: The paper reports a clean separation between universal (ξ) and impurity-tunable (Q_S and prefactor) physics in the YSR bound state of flat band superconductors, confirmed by exact diagonalization.

title: Thickness-Dependent Orbital-to-Spin Torque Signatures in Cr/Gd/Co Thin Films
summary: We studied orbital-torque generation in Cr(10nm)/Gd($t_{\mathrm{Gd}}$)/Co(3nm)/TaO$_x$ and the inverted stack Co(3nm)/Gd($t_{\mathrm{Gd}}$)/Cr(10nm) with $t_{\mathrm{Gd}}$ from 0 to $5\,\mathrm{nm}$ by combining electrical harmonic Hall measurements with magnetometry. A detailed understanding of the magnetometric data is obtained by cross-sectional chemical composition mapping. The data show temperature-dependent magnetic compensation points, while elemental analysis provides evidence of pronounced intermixing, in particular of Gd and Co layers. From the harmonic Hall dataset we extract the damping-like (DL) and field-like (FL) torque efficiencies normalized to the applied electric field, $ξ_{\mathrm{DL}}^{E}$ and $ξ_{\mathrm{FL}}^{E}$, and interpret their dependence on the Gd interlayer thickness using two different descriptions: (i) a naive-layer model and (ii) an alloy model that accounts for interfacial mixing. Notably, upon reversing the stack order, the FL contribution changes sign, whereas the DL contribution does not change sign within the harmonic Hall measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates orbital-torque generation in Cr/Gd/Co/TaOx heterostructures with varying Gd thickness using harmonic Hall measurements and magnetometry, revealing temperature-dependent magnetic compensation points, pronounced Gd-Co intermixing, and asymmetric behavior of damping-like versus field-like torque efficiencies upon stack inversion.
AI.motivation: To understand orbital-torque generation mechanisms in heavy-metal/ferromagnet heterostructures, particularly the role of a Gd interlayer and stack ordering, which is relevant for spintronic device applications.
AI.method: Combining electrical harmonic Hall measurements with magnetometry, supported by cross-sectional chemical composition mapping. Two models were used to interpret torque efficiency dependence on Gd thickness: a naive-layer model and an alloy model accounting for interfacial mixing.
AI.result: Temperature-dependent magnetic compensation points were observed; pronounced intermixing of Gd and Co layers was found. Upon reversing the stack order, the field-like (FL) torque efficiency changes sign while the damping-like (DL) torque efficiency does not.
AI.conclusion: The orbital-torque contributions exhibit a distinct symmetry behavior under stack inversion, with FL torque being sensitive to layer ordering while DL torque is not, which is interpreted through the layered versus alloyed interface descriptions.
