title: Engineering tunable $p$-wave magnetism in antiferromagnetic bilayers
summary: We propose a symmetry-guided route to engineer tunable $p$-wave magnetism in a bilayer system composed of two AB-stacked antiferromagnetic square lattices with their collinear moments nonparallel to each other. We show that an in-plane relative shift between the two layers selectively breaks the symmetries protecting spin degeneracy while preserving time-reversal-related constraints, thereby generating odd-parity spin splitting in a fully compensated magnetic state without spin-orbit coupling. The direction and the magnitude of the resulting $p$-wave spin-splitting, together with the associated spin responses, can be continuously tuned by the in-plane displacement, providing a potential knob for control. We further map the bilayer system onto an effective bond-modulated square lattice and investigate the corresponding Hubbard model within a mean-field framework. The calculated phase diagram reveals extended regions where $p$-wave magnetism with coplanar or chiral spin textures emerges spontaneously. Our results establish a minimal equilibrium platform for realizing and manipulating $p$-wave magnetism in two-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a symmetry-guided approach to create tunable p-wave magnetism in a bilayer of two AB-stacked antiferromagnetic square lattices with nonparallel moments. An in-plane relative shift selectively breaks spin-degeneracy-protecting symmetries while preserving time-reversal constraints, generating odd-parity spin splitting in a fully compensated magnetic state without spin-orbit coupling. The spin-splitting direction, magnitude, and spin responses can be continuously tuned by displacement. The system is mapped to a bond-modulated square lattice and studied via mean-field Hubbard model, revealing extended phase regions with spontaneous coplanar or chiral p-wave magnetism. This establishes a minimal equilibrium platform for p-wave magnetism in 2D systems.
AI.motivation: To establish a minimal equilibrium platform for realizing and manipulating p-wave magnetism in two-dimensional systems without relying on spin-orbit coupling.
AI.method: Symmetry-guided design of a bilayer system of two AB-stacked antiferromagnetic square lattices with noncollinear moments; in-plane relative layer shift to selectively break spin-degeneracy symmetries; mapping onto an effective bond-modulated square lattice; mean-field Hubbard model analysis.
AI.result: Generation of odd-parity (p-wave) spin splitting in a fully compensated magnetic state without spin-orbit coupling; continuous tunability of splitting direction and magnitude via in-plane displacement; phase diagram showing extended regions with spontaneous coplanar or chiral p-wave magnetism.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a minimal equilibrium platform for realizing and manipulating p-wave magnetism in two-dimensional systems, controlled by in-plane layer displacement.

title: Accelerating dynamic simulations of photoexcited materials and their evolution by electron-informed machine learning
summary: Nonadiabatic coupled electron-nuclear dynamics upon electronic excitation underpin the microscopic mechanism and rational modulation of diverse photoinduced functional phenomena in materials, yet their direct first-principles simulations remain computationally demanding. Here we develop a framework for nonadiabatic excited-state machine-learning molecular dynamics (EMLMD) simulations, where the nonequilibrium electronic information upon photoexcitation such as electron temperature is rigorously calibrated from high-precision real-time time-dependent density functional theory (rt-TDDFT) benchmark simulations, enabling accurate reconstruction of excited-state potential energy surfaces (PES). This framework natively incorporates the excited-state electron-phonon couplings and intrinsically captures photoinduced phonon anharmonicity, both of which are missing in standard machine learning molecular dynamics, thus delivering first-principles-level accuracy for excited-state atomic evolutions. Large-scale EMLMD simulations resolve time- and momentum-resolved phonon dynamics in photoexcited materials, directly uncovering the competition between photogenerated coherent phonons and thermal phonons during photoinduced phase transition of bismuth. It also simultaneously resolves elusive atomic-scale microscopic dynamics and global structural rearrangement for selenium photoamorphization. Balancing high accuracy and efficiency, EMLMD offers a versatile paradigm to tackle key challenges in the study of complex excited-state molecular dynamics.

AI.tldr: The authors develop an excited-state machine-learning molecular dynamics (EMLMD) framework that calibrates nonequilibrium electronic information (electron temperature) from rt-TDDFT benchmarks to reconstruct excited-state potential energy surfaces, natively incorporating excited-state electron-phonon couplings and photoinduced phonon anharmonicity. Large-scale EMLMD simulations reveal the competition between photogenerated coherent phonons and thermal phonons during bismuth's photoinduced phase transition, and resolve both atomic-scale and global dynamics in selenium photoamorphization.
AI.motivation: Direct first-principles simulations of nonadiabatic coupled electron-nuclear dynamics in photoexcited materials remain computationally prohibitive, motivating the need for an efficient yet accurate framework that captures excited-state behavior including electron-phonon coupling and phonon anharmonicity—features absent in standard ML molecular dynamics.
AI.method: The framework (EMLMD) calibrates nonequilibrium electronic information such as electron temperature from high-precision real-time time-dependent density functional theory (rt-TDDFT) benchmark simulations, enabling accurate reconstruction of excited-state potential energy surfaces via machine learning. It natively incorporates excited-state electron-phonon couplings and captures photoinduced phonon anharmonicity, enabling large-scale simulations of excited-state atomic evolution.
AI.result: Large-scale EMLMD simulations resolve time- and momentum-resolved phonon dynamics in photoexcited materials. The method directly uncovered competition between photogenerated coherent phonons and thermal phonons during the photoinduced phase transition of bismuth, and simultaneously resolved atomic-scale microscopic dynamics and global structural rearrangement in selenium photoamorphization.
AI.conclusion: Balancing high accuracy and efficiency, EMLMD provides a versatile computational paradigm to address key challenges in complex excited-state molecular dynamics, offering a pathway to study nonadiabatic photoinduced phenomena at first-principles accuracy with scalable simulation capability.

title: Magnetic frustration and non-collinear textures in layered Gd magnets
summary: Using scale-bridging simulations based on electronic structure theory and atomistic spin dynamics, we investigate the magnetic properties of skyrmionic GdRu$_2$Si$_2$ and GdRu$_2$Ge$_2$ layered rare-earth magnets and similar Gd-based compounds (GdAu$_2$Si$_2$, GdAu$_2$Ge$_2$, GdAg$_2$Si$_2$ and GdAg$_2$Ge$_2$). By studying the trends across this structural family, we confirm the importance of magnetic frustration and dipolar interactions for the stability of non-collinear and skyrmion phases. Furthermore, our calculations predict promising opportunities for chemical tuning of these magnets in terms of the balance between various exchange interactions and the character of the magnetic anisotropy. These changes lead to the formation of new types of skyrmions that are stable in a wide range of applied external magnetic field. In particular, we propose partial alkali-metal substitution of Gd in GdRu$_2$Si$_2$ leading to GdKRu$_4$Si$_4$, GdRbRu$_4$Si$_4$, GdCsRu$_4$Si$_4$ as well as GdYRu$_4$Si$_4$ compounds, and suggest that it is likely to result in an ordered layered structure, similarly to previously reported iron pnictides like CaKFe$_4$As$_4$.

AI.tldr: The paper uses scale-bridging simulations (electronic structure theory + atomistic spin dynamics) to study skyrmionic magnetic properties across a family of Gd-based layered rare-earth magnets (Ru, Au, Ag silicides/germanides), confirms the roles of magnetic frustration and dipolar interactions in non-collinear/skyrmion stability, and predicts new stable skyrmion phases via chemical tuning—including alkali-metal substitution to form GdKRu4Si4, GdRbRu4Si4, GdCsRu4Si4, and GdYRu4Si4.
AI.motivation: To understand the underlying mechanisms stabilizing skyrmion phases in Gd-based layered magnets and to identify chemical tuning strategies that could yield new materials with stable skyrmions over wide magnetic field ranges.
AI.method: Scale-bridging approach combining electronic structure theory (DFT-based) with atomistic spin dynamics simulations, applied systematically across the GdRu2Si2, GdRu2Ge2 and structurally similar Gd compounds (Au, Ag analogues). This includes analyzing exchange interactions, magnetic anisotropy, frustration, and dipolar effects, as well as proposing and testing alkali-metal substituted variants.
AI.result: The work confirms that magnetic frustration and dipolar interactions are key for stabilizing non-collinear and skyrmion phases; chemical substitution alters exchange balances and magnetic anisotropy character, yielding new skyrmion types stable over broad magnetic field ranges; partial alkali substitution in GdRu2Si2 is predicted to produce ordered layered GdKRu4Si4, GdRbRu4Si4, GdCsRu4Si4, GdYRu4Si4 structures.
AI.conclusion: Chemical tuning across the Gd-based layered magnet family offers promising routes to engineer new skyrmion phases, and specific alkali-metal substitutions are proposed as experimentally viable candidates for ordered layered skyrmionic materials.

title: Duality between the level statistics of Hermitian and non-Hermitian random matrices
summary: Random matrix theory describes complex quantum systems statistically, with symmetry as its organizing principle. We uncover an exact duality between the level statistics of Hermitian and non-Hermitian random matrices in the large-$N$ (matrix size) limit. It acts class by class: the two replica partition functions, given by fermionic nonlinear $σ$ models, are related by analytic continuation. Applied to the three Wigner--Dyson classes, the duality yields the universal bulk eigenvalue pair-correlation functions of non-Hermitian random matrices. This establishes a non-Hermitian counterpart of Dyson's threefold way, organized by transposition symmetry: generic complex, complex symmetric, and complex self-dual matrices. The dissipative spectral form factors of these classes follow in closed form as well. Applied to the seven nonstandard Altland--Zirnbauer classes, the duality yields the exact spectral densities near the origin, the non-Hermitian hard-edge statistics. Most of these statistics were previously known only numerically. Exact diagonalization confirms the analytical predictions, and physical models demonstrate their universality. We expect these results to be the tip of a deeper correspondence between Hermitian and non-Hermitian random matrix theory.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes an exact duality between Hermitian and non-Hermitian random matrix level statistics in the large-N limit, acting class by class via analytic continuation of replica partition functions. This yields universal bulk eigenvalue pair-correlation functions for the three Wigner-Dyson classes (organized by transposition symmetry as a non-Hermitian Dyson threefold way), closed-form dissipative spectral form factors, and exact hard-edge spectral densities for the seven nonstandard Altland-Zirnbauer classes—many previously only known numerically. Exact diagonalization and physical models confirm universality.
AI.motivation: To uncover an exact analytic correspondence between Hermitian and non-Hermitian random matrix ensembles, providing a rigorous framework to compute non-Hermitian spectral statistics—many of which (especially hard-edge statistics of Altland-Zirnbauer classes) were previously accessible only numerically.
AI.method: The authors derive a class-by-class duality between level statistics of Hermitian and non-Hermitian random matrices in the large-N limit. The proof connects the two replica partition functions, expressed as fermionic nonlinear σ models, via analytic continuation. Applied to Wigner-Dyson classes, this yields bulk eigenvalue pair correlations; for Altland-Zirnbauer classes it produces hard-edge spectral densities.
AI.result: Universal bulk eigenvalue pair-correlation functions for non-Hermitian matrices across three symmetry classes (generic complex, complex symmetric, complex self-dual), closed-form dissipative spectral form factors, and exact non-Hermitian hard-edge statistics for the seven nonstandard Altland-Zirnbauer classes. Analytical predictions are confirmed by exact diagonalization and physical model universality tests.
AI.conclusion: A non-Hermitian counterpart of Dyson's threefold way exists, organized by transposition symmetry. The results suggest a deeper correspondence between Hermitian and non-Hermitian random matrix theory, likely extending beyond the statistics derived here.

title: GW and Bethe-Salpeter Theory for Molecular Polaritons, Quasiparticles, and Excitons
summary: The electron self-energy is central to quasiparticle theory, yet how an optical cavity enters it remains unclear. We address this question for a molecule in a single-mode cavity using the dipole-gauge Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian and a coherent-state QED Hartree-Fock reference. The cavity enters through three channels: the static dipole self-energy (DSE) shift of reference orbital energies, direct DSE augmentation of the screened interaction, and the polariton pole carrying the bilinear electron-photon coupling. We benchmark QED-$GW$ ionization potentials (IPs) and electron affinities (EAs) against a cavity $Δ$-method ladder from QED-HF to correlated wave-function methods, whose cavity-induced shifts agree within 1 meV where directly comparable. For closed-shell molecules with unbound anions, $GW$ systematically overestimates cavity-induced IP redshifts, whereas EA shifts are reproduced nearly quantitatively, although this does not imply comparable accuracy for absolute EAs. For ionic molecules with bound anions, this ordering reverses, consistent with published QED coupled-cluster results. Coupling and detuning scans show that the error is predominantly quadratic in $λ$ and DSE-driven rather than resonant. The spectral function develops a polariton-replica photoemission sideband with weight scaling as $λ^2$. In the static screened interaction used in the Bethe-Salpeter equation, bare-photon exchange cancels the matching DSE contribution to the direct interaction, while exchange and polariton-screening corrections remain. Their net effect on the lowest excitation is appreciable only for ammonia in the molecules studied. Exciton-binding energies involving unbound anions are strongly basis-dependent and should therefore be viewed as diagnostics of electron-hole interactions rather than basis-converged molecular quantities.

AI.tldr: The paper clarifies how an optical cavity enters the electron self-energy in QED-GW theory for molecules coupled to a single-mode cavity, identifying three channels (static dipole self-energy shifts, DSE augmentation of screening, and polariton-pole bilinear coupling), and benchmarks cavity-induced IP/EA shifts against correlated wave-function methods, finding systematic over/underestimation patterns depending on anion binding character plus purely DSE-driven quadratic-in-λ errors and polariton sidebands.
AI.motivation: To clarify the mechanism by which an optical cavity modifies the electron self-energy in quasiparticle theory, a question that remains unanswered despite the centrality of self-energy to QED-GW approaches.
AI.method: Uses the dipole-gauge Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian with a coherent-state QED-Hartree-Fock reference; derives three channels for cavity entry into the self-energy; benchmarks QED-GW ionization potentials and electron affinities against a cavity Δ-method ladder from QED-HF to correlated wavefunction methods; performs coupling and detuning scans; analyzes the spectral function and Bethe-Salpeter static screening with exchange and polariton contributions.
AI.result: Cavity-induced shifts from QED-GW agree within 1 meV with correlated wavefunction methods where directly comparable. GW systematically overestimates cavity-induced IP redshifts for closed-shell molecules with unbound anions while reproducing EA shifts nearly quantitatively, with the ordering reversing for ionic molecules with bound anions consistent with published QED-CC. Error is predominantly quadratic in λ and DSE-driven rather than resonant. Spectral function shows a λ²-weighted polariton-replica sideband. In BSE static screening, bare-photon exchange cancels matching DSE direct-interaction contributions while exchange and polariton screening corrections remain, appreciably affecting only ammonia among studied molecules. Exciton-binding energies with unbound anions are strongly basis-dependent.
AI.conclusion: The cavity enters the self-energy via three distinct channels, and QED-GW accuracy for cavity-induced property shifts depends systematically on whether the molecule has a bound or unbound anion; errors are dominated by DSE quadratic-in-λ effects rather than resonance, and exciton-binding-energy quantities for unbound anions should be treated as diagnostics rather than converged molecular observables.

title: Chiral phonons driven by chiral cavities
summary: Lattice vibrations carrying angular momentum give rise to fundamental phenomena such as the phonon Hall effect and the Einstein-de Haas effect, offering new opportunities for manipulating angular momentum in condensed-matter systems. Generating such circularly polarized phonons requires either the use of an external magnetic field, or of polarized light pulses. The latter approach does not require the use of any magnetic response of the material, but it has limitations, in particular regarding the duration of the pulse. Consequently, any effect stemming from phonons generated by light pulses is transient. In this paper, we propose the use of a driven electromagnetic cavity as a route to generate a steady-state population of chiral phonons. We derive a general description of cavity-chiral phonon interaction, with a particular focus on modes of chiral cavities. We show that, under optimized conditions, a significant effective phonon-induced magnetic field can be generated by means of an external drive with realistic power. Our approach is specially tailored for Gamma point phonons with THz frequencies, and opens a new route for investigating chiral phonons with electromagnetic cavities.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using a driven electromagnetic cavity to generate a steady-state population of chiral phonons (lattice vibrations carrying angular momentum), overcoming the transient limitation of light-pulse-based generation. The authors derive a general framework for cavity-chiral phonon interaction and show that a significant effective phonon-induced magnetic field can be generated under realistic drive conditions.
AI.motivation: Chiral phonons enable phenomena like the phonon Hall effect and Einstein-de Haas effect, offering new ways to manipulate angular momentum in condensed matter. Existing generation methods—external magnetic fields or polarized light pulses—have limitations: light pulses produce only transient effects, while magnetic-field-based approaches require material magnetic response.
AI.method: The authors derive a general theoretical description of cavity-chiral phonon interaction, focusing on modes of chiral cavities. They analyze how a driven electromagnetic cavity can sustain a steady-state chiral phonon population and quantify the resulting effective phonon-induced magnetic field under optimized conditions.
AI.result: Under optimized conditions, a significant effective phonon-induced magnetic field can be generated using an external drive with realistic power. The approach is specifically tailored for Gamma-point phonons with THz frequencies.
AI.conclusion: Driven electromagnetic cavities offer a new, practical route for generating steady-state chiral phonons in condensed-matter systems, circumventing the transient nature of laser-pulse excitation and enabling persistent investigation of chiral-phonon phenomena.

title: Diagnosing Latent Energy Decomposition in Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials via Interacting Quantum Atoms
summary: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can reproduce potential energies and forces accurately, but their internal energy allocation is often difficult to interpret. E3D-IQA is introduced as a diagnostic framework connecting the latent edge-energy representation of an Allegro-type MLIP with Interacting Quantum Atoms (IQA) energy decomposition. The Allegro edge-energy path is retained as a latent pair contribution, while a node-energy path is trained against the IQA intra-atomic energy. IQA interatomic energies are not direct training targets; instead, the learned edge energies are evaluated after training against the IQA pair terms. Tests on H/C/N/O organic reaction structures show that intra-atomic supervision is essential: energy and force training alone does not recover an IQA-like one-body/two-body allocation. With intra-atomic supervision, node energies reproduce IQA intra-atomic terms, and latent edge energies show meaningful correspondence with IQA interatomic terms. Residual errors are concentrated in positive or weak pair interactions, exposing internal allocation failures that remain hidden in total-energy and force metrics. Adding structures labeled only with energies and forces improves transfer to larger molecules and reduces decomposition errors. E3D-IQA therefore provides a route for diagnosing and guiding latent scientific representations using partially labeled quantum-chemical datasets.

AI.tldr: E3D-IQA is a diagnostic framework that connects the latent edge-energy representation of Allegro-type machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to Interacting Quantum Atoms (IQA) energy decomposition, enabling interpretable internal energy allocation by training node energies against IQA intra-atomic terms and evaluating latent edge energies against IQA interatomic terms.
AI.motivation: MLIPs accurately reproduce energies and forces but have opaque internal energy allocations, making it difficult to understand how energy is distributed across atomic interactions. A diagnostic framework is needed to link latent representations to physically meaningful quantum-chemical energy decomposition.
AI.method: The Allegro edge-energy path is retained as a latent pair contribution, while a separate node-energy path is trained against IQA intra-atomic energies. IQA interatomic energies are not direct training targets; instead, learned edge energies are post-hoc evaluated against IQA pair terms. Tests are performed on H/C/N/O organic reaction structures, varying supervision by adding intra-atomic labels and unlabeled structures with only energies/forces.
AI.result: Intra-atomic supervision is essential: energy and force training alone does not recover an IQA-like one-body/two-body allocation. With intra-atomic supervision, node energies reproduce IQA intra-atomic terms and latent edge energies show meaningful correspondence with IQA interatomic terms. Residual errors concentrate in positive or weak pair interactions. Adding energy/force-labeled structures improves transfer to larger molecules and reduces decomposition errors.
AI.conclusion: E3D-IQA provides a route for diagnosing and guiding latent scientific representations using partially labeled quantum-chemical datasets, exposing internal allocation failures hidden in total-energy and force metrics.

title: Comment on "Distinct Behaviors of Inner and Outer CuO$_2$ Planes in Quadruple-Layer Cuprate (Cu,C)Ba$_2$Ca$_3$Cu$_4$O$_{11 + δ}$"
summary: In a recent Letter, Sun et al. report photoemission spectroscopy measurements on the four-layer cuprate (Cu,C)Ba2Ca3Cu4O11 (CuC-1234) in which they resolve two superconducting gaps associated with the inner (IP) and outer (OP) CuO2 planes. CuC-1234 has a Tc as 117 K in a sample previously structurally characterized using neutron powder diffraction. From the Luttinger sum, the beta-band of the IP was found to be heavily underdoped (p~0.07) while the OP alpha2 bonding band was strongly overdoped (p~0.25). Each revealed a gap with very different momentum and temperature dependences. A large gap on the beta band was found to close at the bulk Tc, while a smaller gap on the alpha2 band closed at 70 K. Such two-gap behavior would indicate weak-coupling between the IP and OP, resulting in a second gap-opening temperature, Tc2, and implying a two-step development of the superfluid density on cooling, first on the IPs then on the OPs. Here, we point out that the observed values of Tc and Tc2 are fully consistent with a long-standing correlation of Tc with a bond-valence sum parameter, V+, calculated from the crystallographic bond lengths. This suggests that Tc2 in the OP is entirely consistent with the local structure of the OP where the value of V+(OP) is reduced by the presence of the apical oxygens and Tc2 reduced accordingly. It is as though two largely decoupled superconductors are present in the single 1234 compound and their individual pairing temperatures are determined by their local nearest-neighbour structure, reflecting the very short-range physics.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes two superconducting gaps observed in the four-layer cuprate CuC-1234 and explains them through bond-valence sum calculations, showing that the two gap-closing temperatures (Tc=117K and Tc2=70K) correspond to the local structural environments of the inner and outer CuO2 planes, suggesting two largely decoupled superconductors within one compound governed by very short-range physics.
AI.motivation: To explain the origin of the two distinct superconducting gaps observed in CuC-1234 photoemission measurements, and to demonstrate that the two gap-opening temperatures arise naturally from the local crystallographic structures of the inner and outer CuO2 planes rather than requiring unconventional coupling mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors compare the observed Tc and Tc2 values from the photoemission experiments with a known empirical correlation relating Tc to the bond-valence sum parameter V+, computed from crystallographic bond lengths of the respective CuO2 planes.
AI.result: The observed Tc (117 K) and Tc2 (70 K) values are fully consistent with the bond-valence sum correlation. The reduced Tc of the outer planes is explained by the presence of apical oxygens which lower V+(OP), thereby lowering its pairing temperature relative to the inner planes.
AI.conclusion: The two-gap behavior in CuC-1234 reflects two largely decoupled superconducting subsystems whose individual pairing temperatures are dictated by their local nearest-neighbor structure, emphasizing the very short-range nature of the pairing physics in these cuprates.

title: Size-Dependent Growth Rates Amplify Infinitesimal Asymmetry in Nanocrystals
summary: The kinetic Wulff construction predicts symmetric nonequilibrium shapes when crystallographically equivalent facets share a fixed growth rate. However, nanocrystals grow through finite facets whose nucleation barriers and ligand coverages depend on facet size. Here we develop a size-dependent kinetic construction and show that as a consequence infinitesimal seed asymmetries can be amplified into strongly asymmetric nanocrystal morphologies even when all symmetry-related facets obey the same microscopic growth law. Spatially heterogeneous nucleation rates and boundary limited growth generate facet growth velocities that depend on size, and deterministic shape evolution translates these local rates into global shape symmetry breaking. We illustrate the mechanism of persistent anisotropic growth on square and triangular lattices in two dimensions and on FCC seeds in three dimensions, where cuboctahedra can evolve toward rods or tetrahedra depending on which facet-area perturbations are amplified.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a size-dependent kinetic Wulff construction showing that nanocrystal facet growth velocities depend on facet size due to heterogeneous nucleation rates and boundary-limited growth. This causes infinitesimal seed asymmetries to be amplified into strongly asymmetric morphologies (e.g., cuboctahedra evolving into rods or tetrahedra) even when all symmetry-related facets obey the same microscopic growth law.
AI.motivation: The classical kinetic Wulff construction assumes crystallographically equivalent facets share a fixed growth rate and thereby predicts symmetric nonequilibrium shapes. However, real nanocrystals grow through finite facets whose nucleation barriers and ligand coverages depend on facet size, undermining this symmetry assumption. The authors seek to explain how asymmetric nanocrystal morphologies can arise despite symmetric growth laws.
AI.method: The authors develop a size-dependent kinetic construction where facet growth velocities depend on facet size. They incorporate spatially heterogeneous nucleation rates and boundary-limited growth, then model deterministic shape evolution that translates local size-dependent rates into global morphology. They illustrate the mechanism on square and triangular lattices in 2D and on FCC seeds in 3D.
AI.result: The construction demonstrates that infinitesimal seed asymmetries can be amplified into strongly asymmetric nanocrystal morphologies even under symmetry-conserving microscopic growth laws. On FCC seeds, cuboctahedra evolve toward rods or tetrahedra depending on which facet-area perturbations are amplified.
AI.conclusion: Size-dependent facet growth, arising from finite-size nucleation effects and boundary-limited kinetics, is a viable mechanism for persistent anisotropic growth and symmetry-breaking in nanocrystal morphology, offering an explanation beyond fixed-rate kinetic Wulff constructions.

title: Exact joint eigenvalue densities of non-Hermitian random matrices are Calogero scattering states
summary: Determining exact joint eigenvalue densities is central to random matrix theory. We solve this long-standing problem for non-Hermitian matrices with transposition symmetry (complex symmetric and complex self-dual) at arbitrary matrix size. Up to a Vandermonde factor, they are scattering-state wave functions of the Calogero model, a line of particles interacting through an inverse-square potential, with the coupling strength set by the symmetry. In contrast to many previously known joint densities, the densities cannot be written as a gas of eigenvalues with pairwise interactions. We further compute the complex level spacing distributions and two-point spectral correlation functions, which carry power-law tails, absent in a Coulomb gas. Our results shed light on the interplay among random matrices, integrability, and symmetry.

AI.tldr: The authors solve the long-standing problem of determining exact joint eigenvalue densities for non-Hermitian random matrices with transposition symmetry (complex symmetric and complex self-dual) at arbitrary matrix size. They show these densities are scattering-state wave functions of the Calogero model and compute complex level spacing distributions and two-point spectral correlation functions, revealing power-law tails absent in Coulomb gas descriptions.
AI.motivation: Determining exact joint eigenvalue densities is a central and long-standing open problem in random matrix theory, particularly for non-Hermitian matrices with transposition symmetry, which had resisted solution.
AI.method: The authors establish an exact mapping between the joint eigenvalue densities of non-Hermitian matrices with transposition symmetry (complex symmetric and complex self-dual ensembles) and scattering-state wave functions of the Calogero model—a one-dimensional system of particles interacting via an inverse-square potential—with coupling strength determined by the symmetry type.
AI.result: The joint densities (up to a Vandermonde factor) are identified with Calogero scattering states. The authors compute the complex level spacing distributions and two-point spectral correlation functions, which exhibit power-law tails. They demonstrate these densities cannot be represented as a pairwise-interacting eigenvalue gas (Coulomb gas), in contrast to many previously known joint densities.
AI.conclusion: The work provides exact solutions for joint eigenvalue densities of symmetric non-Hermitian ensembles at arbitrary size, revealing novel connections among random matrix theory, integrability (Calogero model), and symmetry, and highlighting qualitative differences from Coulomb gas behavior.

title: Floquet scattering and Fano resonances in nodal-ring and multi-Weyl semimetals: Role of propagating and evanescent modes
summary: We develop a comprehensive Floquet scattering theory for quantum transport in periodically driven nodal-ring semimetals (NRSs) and multi-Weyl semimetals (mWSMs), extending our earlier study reported in Annalen der Physik 535, 2200460 (2023), in which evanescent modes were neglected, to a complete formalism that includes both propagating and evanescent channels. By solving the full boundary-value problem, we obtain the complete set of scattering states and show that, although evanescent modes are indispensable for satisfying the matching conditions at the potential interfaces, they carry zero net probability current and do not contribute to any observable transport quantity. We identify a previously unexplored transport regime in NRSs in which two propagating channels coexist and participate in coherent scattering, producing multi-channel quantum interference and Floquet-induced Fano resonances. The transmission, reflection, pumped shot noise, and the associated Fano resonance features are determined entirely by the propagating channels, and the resonance energies coincide with those of the corresponding quasi-bound states of the static potential well. Our results establish a unified framework for Floquet transport in anisotropic topological semimetals, and confirm that the approximation of neglecting evanescent modes in our earlier work is justified for all measurable transport properties.

AI.tldr: The paper extends a previous study of Floquet quantum transport in driven nodal-ring semimetals (NRSs) and multi-Weyl semimetals (mWSMs) by adding evanescent channels to the previously propagating-only formalism. Solving the full boundary-value problem reveals evanescent modes carry zero net current and do not affect observables, while a new two-propagating-channel regime in NRSs produces multi-channel interference and Floquet-induced Fano resonances. The authors establish a unified framework confirming the earlier evanescent-neglecting approximation is valid for all measurable transport quantities.
AI.motivation: To develop a complete Floquet scattering formalism for quantum transport in periodically driven NRSs and mWSMs by including both propagating and evanescent channels, generalizing an earlier work that neglected evanescent modes, and to verify whether that approximation was justified.
AI.method: Construction of a full Floquet scattering theory that solves the complete boundary-value problem, including both propagating and evanescent scattering states at potential interfaces, and analysis of transport observables such as transmission, reflection, pumped shot noise, and Fano resonances in the multi-channel regime.
AI.result: Evanescent modes are necessary to satisfy matching conditions at potential interfaces but carry zero net probability current and contribute nothing to observable transport. A previously unexplored regime in NRSs with two coexisting propagating channels exhibits multi-channel quantum interference and Floquet-induced Fano resonances whose energies coincide with quasi-bound states of the static potential well. All transport quantities are fully determined by propagating channels alone.
AI.conclusion: The complete formalism establishes a unified framework for Floquet transport in anisotropic topological semimetals and confirms that neglecting evanescent modes in the earlier work (Ann. Phys. 535, 2200460, 2023) is justified for all measurable transport properties.

title: Heavily Sr-Doped La$_{2}$SrNi$_{2}$O$_{7-δ}$ as a Tetragonal Ruddlesden-Popper Phase at Ambient Pressure
summary: High-temperature superconductivity has been found in bilayer Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) nickelates in bulk samples under high pressure, or in thin films via compressive strain. In the superconducting state, a tetragonal structure with a straight Ni-O-Ni bond along c-axis has been commonly observed, together with the suppression or diminishing of the density-wave orders. Therefore, it remains an open question whether these factors are sufficient for achieving superconductivity at ambient pressure. Here we report the first successful synthesis of heavily Sr-doped La$_{2}$SrNi$_{2}$O$_{7-δ}$ under high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) conditions with a flux method. X-ray diffraction and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) confirm that the material adopts a tetragonal (I4/mmm) structure with an 180$^{\circ}$ Ni-O-Ni bond angle along c-axis. Resistance measurements reveal metallic behavior with a low-temperature upturn and no density-wave features are observed. However, neither pressure nor oxygen variation induces superconductivity. Density functional theory calculations indicate that the holes introduced by Sr doping are predominantly doped into the Ni-3d$_{z^2}$ orbital, leading to the appearance of a very large $γ$ pocket on the Fermi surface at ambient pressure and significantly reducing the occupation of the Ni-3d$_{z^2 }$ orbital. Combining the experimental observations with theoretical calculations, we attribute the absence of superconductivity to the serious deviation from the half-filling state of the Ni-3d$_{z^2 }$ band, which is crucial for the interlayer antiferromagnetic interaction and thus for pairing. Our work unravels important issues for achieving superconductivity in bilayer nickelate system.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first synthesis of heavily Sr-doped La2SrNi2O7-δ under high-pressure and high-temperature conditions, resulting in a tetragonal (I4/mmm) structure with straight 180° Ni-O-Ni bonds along the c-axis and suppressed density-wave orders. Despite these favorable structural features, no superconductivity is observed under pressure or oxygen variation. DFT calculations reveal that Sr doping predominantly dopes holes into the Ni-3dz² orbital, deviating the system from half-filling of this orbital, which is proposed to be essential for interlayer antiferromagnetic interactions and pairing.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the structural factors commonly associated with superconductivity in bilayer Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates—specifically a tetragonal structure with straight Ni-O-Ni bonds and suppression of density-wave orders—are sufficient for achieving superconductivity at ambient pressure, by testing a heavily Sr-doped system.
AI.method: Sr-doped La2SrNi2O7-δ samples were synthesized under high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) conditions using a flux method. The crystal structure was characterized by X-ray diffraction and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). Electrical transport measurements were performed under varying pressure and oxygen conditions. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were used to analyze the orbital character of doped holes and the resulting Fermi surface topology.
AI.result: The synthesized material adopts a tetragonal (I4/mmm) structure with 180° Ni-O-Ni bond angles along the c-axis and exhibits metallic behavior with a low-temperature upturn in resistance, without density-wave features. No superconductivity was induced by pressure or oxygen variation. DFT calculations show that Sr doping mainly dopes holes into the Ni-3dz² orbital, generating a large γ Fermi surface pocket and significantly reducing the Ni-3dz² orbital occupation.
AI.conclusion: The absence of superconductivity in this structurally favorable compound is attributed to the serious deviation from half-filling of the Ni-3dz² band, which is crucial for interlayer antiferromagnetic interactions and pairing. This work clarifies important conditions required for achieving superconductivity in bilayer nickelates.

title: Correlation-Driven Nonlinear Magnetoelectric Response in an Altermagnet: A Dynamical Mean-Field Study
summary: We investigate the optical nonlinear magnetoelectric effect (NMEE) in a strongly correlated altermagnet using dynamical mean-field theory. Unlike effective band descriptions with an imposed spin splitting, our approach determines the altermagnetic order, electronic spectrum, and optical nonlinear response self-consistently. We find that the NMEE is finite in the altermagnetic phase and vanishes in the paramagnetic phase. Its frequency dependence reflects the spin-resolved spectral structure and provides an estimate of the characteristic altermagnetic spin-splitting scale. Interaction and temperature tuning produce qualitatively different behavior: at low temperature, reducing the interaction strength toward the interaction-driven magnetic phase boundary enhances the response, whereas increasing the temperature suppresses it and drives it to zero above the critical temperature. These results establish the optical NMEE as a probe of correlated altermagnetic order and suggest that tuning parameters such as pressure, strain, or chemical substitution toward an interaction-driven phase boundary may provide a promising route to maximizing the response.

AI.tldr: Using dynamical mean-field theory, the authors investigate the optical nonlinear magnetoelectric effect (NMEE) in a strongly correlated altermagnet. They find the NMEE is finite only in the altermagnetic phase, its frequency dependence reveals the spin-splitting scale, and it can be enhanced by tuning interactions toward the magnetic phase boundary at low temperature but suppressed by temperature.
AI.motivation: To understand the optical nonlinear magnetoelectric effect in strongly correlated altermagnets using a self-consistent approach that goes beyond effective band models with imposed spin splitting, and to assess whether the NMEE can serve as a probe of correlated altermagnetic order.
AI.method: Dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) is employed to self-consistently determine the altermagnetic order, electronic spectrum, and optical nonlinear response, rather than relying on a priori spin-split band structures.
AI.result: The NMEE is finite in the altermagnetic phase and vanishes in the paramagnetic phase. Its frequency dependence reflects the spin-resolved spectral structure and estimates the altermagnetic spin-splitting scale. Reducing interaction strength toward the magnetic phase boundary at low temperature enhances the response, while increasing temperature suppresses it to zero above the critical temperature.
AI.conclusion: The optical NMEE is established as a probe of correlated altermagnetic order, and tuning parameters such as pressure, strain, or chemical substitution toward an interaction-driven phase boundary is proposed as a promising route to maximize the response.

title: Cryogenic Enhancement of Electron Spin Polarization from a Strained GaAs/GaAsP Superlattice Photocathode
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures; Supplemental Material contains 8 pages, 3 figures, and 1 table. Ancillary files contain the measured spectra and a Jupyter notebook that reproduces figures and values, also archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22212862
summary: We report electron spin polarization of 95.0 +/- 0.8 (stat) +/- 2.4 (sys)% from a strained GaAs/GaAsP superlattice photocathode grown by metalorganic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) and cooled to dry-ice temperature (195 K). We achieved this polarization with 97.8% circularly polarized excitation light and a quantum efficiency of 0.7% at the peak polarization wavelength. This measurement exceeds the values of previously reported GaAs-based photocathode polarizations, which have clustered near 92% for two decades. We vary the temperature of the cathode and measure the polarization and quantum-efficiency spectra at 295 K, 273 K, 195 K, and 77 K. The polarization rises from 91.2(1)% at 295 K to its maximum at 195 K, while the spectral peak shifts from 775 nm to 739 nm (78 meV) over the full temperature range, tracking the widening band gap. The spectra probe two depolarization mechanisms: a thermalized transport channel that is suppressed on cooling, and energy-dependent hot-electron relaxation that persists and sets the low-temperature saturation. The polarization recovers after a full cooling and warmup cycle and is stable while the quantum efficiency decays, which disfavors surface energy filtering as the origin of the gain. These results indicate that modest cooling to 195 K, for which dry ice suffices, is a practical route to higher-polarization GaAs-based electron sources.

AI.tldr: A strained GaAs/GaAsP superlattice photocathode grown by MOCVD achieves a record electron spin polarization of 95.0% when cooled to dry-ice temperature (195 K), surpassing the ~92% plateau that GaAs-based photocathodes have been stuck at for two decades. Temperature-dependent measurements (295 K to 77 K) reveal two distinct depolarization mechanisms and indicate modest cooling is a practical route to higher-polarization electron sources.
AI.motivation: GaAs-based photocathodes have had their electron spin polarization clustered near 92% for two decades, and the field seeks to exceed this plateau to enable higher-performance applications in spin-resolved electron beams, photoemission-based accelerators, and spin-polarized electron microscopy.
AI.method: The authors used a strained GaAs/GaAsP superlattice photocathode grown by MOCVD, excited it with 97.8% circularly polarized light, and measured spin polarization and quantum efficiency spectra at 295 K, 273 K, 195 K, and 77 K. They also tested recovery after a full cooling/warmup cycle and examined how quantum efficiency decayed over time.
AI.result: Electron spin polarization of 95.0% was achieved at 195 K with 0.7% quantum efficiency at the peak polarization wavelength. Polarization rose from 91.2% at 295 K to a maximum at 195 K, while the spectral peak shifted from 775 nm to 739 nm (78 meV) over the full temperature range. Two depolarization mechanisms were identified, and the polarization was stable during quantum efficiency decay and recovered after thermal cycling.
AI.conclusion: Modest cooling to 195 K, achievable with dry ice, is a practical route to higher-polarization GaAs-based electron sources. The results disfavor surface energy filtering as the origin of the polarization gain and instead point to thermalized transport channel suppression as the key mechanism.

title: A Human-AI Theorem Connecting Spontaneous and Field-Induced Mechanisms of Collective Behavior in One Dimension
summary: Can an artificial intelligence (AI) generate a scientific hypothesis outside a human collaborator's active hypothesis space (AHS), and can human-AI research be organized to make such breakthroughs more likely? We document such a case while proving a theorem that connects two basic organizing mechanisms of statistical physics: collective behavior arising in zero field from competing interactions and that induced or controlled by an external field. A zero-field $O(n)$-vector open chain with arbitrary inhomogeneous nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor interaction functions $U_i(S_i\cdot{S}_{i+1})$ and $V_i(S_i\cdot{S}_{i+2})$ is microscopically, via a temperature-independent mapping at the Hamiltonian level, equivalent to a simpler $O(n)$ open chain with nearest-neighbor interaction $V_i( σ_i\cdot σ_{i+1})$ and axial single-spin potential $U_i(σ_i^z)$ for every integer $n\ge1$ and every system size $L\ge1$. The homogeneous linear specialization maps the foundational frustrated $J_1$-$J_2$ model onto the canonical $J$-$h$ field model---with $n=1,2,3$ being the Ising, XY, and Heisenberg classical spin models, respectively. An analogous theorem holds when the continuous $O(n)$ spins are replaced by the $q$-state Potts spins with the standard Potts interaction, implying a closed-form exact solution of the $J_1$-$J_2$ Potts open chain for every $q\ge2$ and every $L\ge1$. The emergence of the theorems from sustained human-AI collaboration suggests that involving AI throughout a systematic research program may incubate autonomous scientific breakthroughs.

AI.tldr: This paper documents a case where AI generated a scientific hypothesis outside the human collaborator's active hypothesis space, proving a theorem connecting zero-field collective behavior from competing interactions to field-induced/controlled behavior in statistical physics. The theorem shows that a zero-field O(n)-vector open chain with inhomogeneous nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor interactions is microscopically equivalent (via a temperature-independent Hamiltonian-level mapping) to a simpler O(n) open chain with nearest-neighbor interactions and an axial single-spin potential, for all n≥1 and system sizes L≥1. The homogeneous linear specialization maps the frustrated J1-J2 model onto the canonical J-h field model for Ising (n=1), XY (n=2), and Heisenberg (n=3) classical spin models. An analogous theorem holds for q-state Potts spins, yielding a closed-form exact solution of the J1-J2 Potts open chain for all q≥2 and L≥1. The authors argue that sustained human-AI collaboration throughout a systematic research program may incubate autonomous scientific breakthroughs.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates two intertwined questions: (1) whether AI can generate scientific hypotheses outside a human collaborator's active hypothesis space, and (2) whether organizing human-AI research in a particular way makes such breakthroughs more likely. The authors document a concrete mathematical/physics breakthrough achieved through sustained human-AI collaboration, providing evidence for AI's capacity to produce genuinely novel scientific insight.
AI.method: The authors proved a theorem establishing a temperature-independent, Hamiltonian-level mapping between a zero-field O(n)-vector open chain with arbitrary inhomogeneous nearest-neighbor (Ui) and next-nearest-neighbor (Vi) interactions, and a simpler O(n) open chain with nearest-neighbor interaction Vi(σi·σi+1) plus an axial single-spin potential Ui(σi^z). The mapping covers all integers n≥1 and system sizes L≥1, and specializes to relate the frustrated J1-J2 model to the canonical J-h field model for Ising, XY, and Heisenberg spins. An analogous theorem was proved for the q-state Potts model, enabling closed-form exact solutions of the J1-J2 Potts open chain.
AI.result: The theorem connects two fundamental organizing mechanisms of statistical physics: zero-field collective behavior from competing interactions (frustration) and behavior induced by an external field. It provides exact solutions for frustrated spin chains including the J1-J2 model across Ising, XY, Heisenberg, and Potts cases. Critically, the theorem was discovered through sustained human-AI collaboration, demonstrating that AI can contribute hypotheses beyond the human's active hypothesis space.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that AI is capable of generating hypotheses outside a human collaborator's active hypothesis space, and that structured, sustained human-AI collaboration throughout a research program can incubate autonomous scientific breakthroughs. This suggests a model for organizing research—with AI integrated from start to finish—that may systematically accelerate the discovery of novel scientific results.

title: Fourier Neural Operators for Composition-Driven Crystal Structure Discovery
summary: Crystalline materials discovery is essential for energy, electronics, and catalysis, but the vast chemical and structural space makes exhaustive screening infeasible. Existing voxel-based methods are limited by the local receptive fields of three-dimensional convolutional neural networks and the posterior collapse of high-dimensional variational autoencoders. Here, we develop a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO)-based crystal-field solver that maps a prescribed chemical formula and lattice parameters to periodic number-density and electron-density fields. By operating on global Fourier modes, the solver captures long-range correlations in periodic crystal fields beyond conventional local convolutions. Building on this solver, we construct a coupled generation-solving framework in which a conditional variational autoencoder generates diverse candidate lattice parameters in a low-dimensional basis-coefficient space, followed by density-field prediction and atomic reconstruction through peak detection, position optimization, and weight optimization. The reconstructed structures are further screened using voxel-level filtering, machine-learning interatomic-potential relaxation, and first-principle calculations. The framework generates novel structures across 104 chemical formulas with competitive reconstruction accuracy, demonstrating high generative diversity and structural validity. By extending Fourier neural operators to periodic crystal fields and coupling them with composition-conditioned lattice generation, our approach provides a scalable route to crystal structure discovery from prescribed chemical compositions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO)-based crystal-field solver coupled with a conditional variational autoencoder to generate novel crystal structures from prescribed chemical compositions. The framework maps chemical formulas and lattice parameters to periodic number/electron-density fields via global Fourier modes, overcoming local receptive field and posterior collapse limitations of voxel-based methods. Structures are reconstructed via peak detection and optimization, then screened through ML-potential relaxation and first-principles calculations, demonstrating high generative diversity and structural validity across 104 chemical formulas.
AI.motivation: Crystalline materials discovery is critical for energy, electronics, and catalysis, yet exhaustive screening across the vast chemical and structural space is infeasible. Existing voxel-based methods suffer from limited local receptive fields of 3D CNNs and posterior collapse in high-dimensional VAEs, motivating a scalable generative approach for crystal structure discovery from prescribed compositions.
AI.method: The method introduces an FNO-based crystal-field solver operating on global Fourier modes to capture long-range periodic correlations, mapping chemical formulas and lattice parameters to periodic density fields. This is coupled with a conditional VAE that generates lattice parameters in a low-dimensional basis-coefficient space. Structures are reconstructed via peak detection, position optimization, and weight optimization from predicted density fields, then screened through voxel-level filtering, machine-learning interatomic-potential relaxation, and first-principles calculations.
AI.result: The framework successfully generates novel structures across 104 chemical formulas with competitive reconstruction accuracy, demonstrating high generative diversity and structural validity according to screening criteria.
AI.conclusion: By extending Fourier neural operators to periodic crystal fields and coupling them with composition-conditioned lattice generation, the approach provides a scalable route to crystal structure discovery from prescribed chemical compositions, addressing key limitations of prior voxel-based generative methods.

title: Narrow-Sense Type-III Dirac Cones and Additional Flat Lines on a Honeycomb Lattice with Anisotropic Next-Nearest-Neighbor Hoppings
comment: 12 pages, 23 figures, The Supplemental Material is included as an Appendix
summary:
Critically tilted Dirac cones have attracted considerable attention because of their unconventional electronic properties in two-dimensional massless Dirac-fermion systems. Among them, the narrow-sense type-III Dirac cone is characterized by a flat dispersion along the direction connecting the two Dirac points.
  Using a tight-binding model on a single-orbital honeycomb lattice, we demonstrate that narrow-sense type-III Dirac cones can be realized by tuning anisotropic next-nearest-neighbor hoppings. Type-I and type-II Dirac cones emerge on either side of the critical point, enabling a systematic investigation of the electronic properties across the type-I, narrow-sense type-III, and type-II regimes.
  We further find that the present model exhibits additional flat lines in momentum space whose energy coincides with the Dirac-point energy at the narrow-sense type-III critical point. This band structure produces a pronounced enhancement of the density of states at the Fermi energy and, consequently, a substantial enhancement of the electronic specific heat compared with that expected for an ideal narrow-sense type-III Dirac cone. Our results show that the honeycomb lattice with anisotropic next-nearest-neighbor hoppings provides a simple platform for exploring unconventional thermodynamic properties arising from the energy coincidence of narrow-sense type-III Dirac cones and additional flat lines at the Fermi energy.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that narrow-sense type-III Dirac cones can be realized in a single-orbital honeycomb lattice by tuning anisotropic next-nearest-neighbor hoppings. The model exhibits additional flat lines whose energy coincides with the Dirac-point energy at the critical point, producing an enhanced density of states and substantially increased electronic specific heat compared to an ideal narrow-sense type-III Dirac cone. This provides a simple platform for exploring unconventional thermodynamic properties at the Fermi energy.
AI.motivation: Critically tilted Dirac cones, particularly the narrow-sense type-III Dirac cone characterized by flat dispersion along the direction connecting two Dirac points, have attracted attention due to their unconventional electronic properties. The authors aim to provide a simple model system to realize and systematically study such cones.
AI.method: The authors use a tight-binding model on a single-orbital honeycomb lattice and tune anisotropic next-nearest-neighbor hoppings. They analyze how the band structure transitions across type-I, narrow-sense type-III, and type-II Dirac regimes, and compute the density of states and electronic specific heat.
AI.result: Narrow-sense type-III Dirac cones are realized at a critical point in the hopping parameters, with type-I and type-II Dirac cones on either side. Additional flat lines in momentum space appear whose energy coincides with the Dirac-point energy at the critical point, leading to an enhanced density of states and substantially enhanced electronic specific heat relative to an ideal narrow-sense type-III Dirac cone.
AI.conclusion: The honeycomb lattice with anisotropic next-nearest-neighbor hoppings is a simple and effective platform for exploring unconventional thermodynamic properties arising from the energy coincidence of narrow-sense type-III Dirac cones and additional flat lines at the Fermi energy.

title: Expanding the trilayer Ruddlesden-Popper nickelate family: Synthesis and characterization of Sm$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10-δ}$ single crystals
summary: The discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) nickelates has attracted significant attention. Bulk superconductivity emerges under pressure in trilayer nickelates La$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10-δ}$ (T$_c$ $\approx$ 30 K) and Pr$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10-δ}$ (T$_c$ $\approx$ 40.5 K), where the reduced ionic radius of Pr$^{3+}$ may generate internal chemical pressure and enhance T$_c$. However, synthesizing trilayer RP phases with smaller rare-earth elements (Ln) is extremely challenging. So far, only the La, Pr, and Nd analogues have been synthesized with stable phases in the single rare-earth form. Here we report the first successful high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) synthesis of samarium-based compound Sm$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10-δ}$. Magnetization and transport measurements consistently confirm a density wave (DW) transition at ~180 K at ambient pressure. Through a careful fitting to the structural data of Sm$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10-δ}$, it is found that the bond angle of (Ni-O-Ni) associating with the interlayer apical oxygen is much smaller than 180$^{\circ}$, which was assumed to be the key factor for the occurrence of superconductivity. By applying pressures up to 80 GPa, despite partial suppression of insulating behavior and the DW order, but superconductivity is not observed in our present study. Density functional theory calculations suggest that the 3d$_{z^2}$ and 3d$_{x^2-y^2}$ are separated from other t$_{2g}$ orbitals and make a primary contribution to the Fermi surface. The newly synthesized trilayer nickelate Sm$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10-δ}$ offers a unique platform for probing the fundamental physics of RP nickelates.

AI.tldr: The authors report the first successful high-pressure high-temperature synthesis of Sm₄Ni₃O₁₀₋δ, a trilayer Ruddlesden-Popper nickelate with a smaller rare-earth ion (Sm³⁺) than previously synthesized analogues. This compound exhibits a density wave transition at ~180 K at ambient pressure. Despite applying pressures up to 80 GPa, superconductivity was not observed, likely due to an unfavorable (Ni-O-Ni) bond angle along the interlayer apical oxygen that deviates significantly from 180°. DFT calculations reveal that the 3d_z² and 3d_x²-y² orbitals dominate the Fermi surface.
AI.motivation: The discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in trilayer RP nickelates La₄Ni₃O₁₀₋δ (T_c ≈ 30 K) and Pr₄Ni₃O₁₀₋δ (T_c ≈ 40.5 K) has generated interest, with the smaller ionic radius of Pr³⁺ possibly providing internal chemical pressure that enhances T_c. This motivates exploring even smaller rare-earth analogues such as Sm³⁺, but synthesizing trilayer RP phases with smaller lanthanides is extremely challenging, and no Sm-based compound had been synthesized prior to this work.
AI.method: High-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) synthesis was used to prepare Sm₄Ni₃O₁₀₋δ for the first time. Magnetization and transport measurements characterized its electronic behavior. Structural data were analyzed via careful fitting, particularly the (Ni-O-Ni) bond angle involving interlayer apical oxygen. High-pressure electrical transport experiments up to 80 GPa were performed. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were conducted to probe the electronic band structure and orbital contributions to the Fermi surface.
AI.result: Sm₄Ni₃O₁₀₋δ was successfully synthesized and exhibits a density wave (DW) transition at ~180 K at ambient pressure. The (Ni-O-Ni) bond angle linking the interlayer apical oxygen is significantly smaller than 180°, which is proposed to be detrimental for superconductivity. Under applied pressures up to 80 GPa, the insulating behavior and DW order were partially suppressed, but superconductivity was not observed. DFT reveals that the 3d_z² and 3d_x²-y² orbitals are well separated from t₂g states and dominate the Fermi surface.
AI.conclusion: The newly synthesized Sm₄Ni₃O₁₀₋δ constitutes the first trilayer RP nickelate with Sm as the rare-earth element, providing a unique platform for studying the fundamental physics of RP nickelates. The absence of superconductivity up to 80 GPa, attributed to the distorted apical (Ni-O-Ni) bond angle, offers important insight into the structural prerequisites for superconductivity in this family of materials.

title: Self-Healing Diffusion Monte Carlo applied to a simple fermionic model: A critical assessment of the method
summary: We investigate the Self-Healing Diffusion Monte Carlo (SHDMC) method using a one-dimensional model with periodic boundary conditions. An inversion symmetry is introduced to mimic the antisymmetry property of fermionic wavefunctions, with the bosonic and fermionic sectors being modeled by the even and odd eigenstates, respectively. As in realistic fermionic systems, the nodal structure is only partially constrained by symmetry, making this model a non-trivial testbed for nodal optimization algorithms such as SHDMC. We show that the nodal evolution under SHDMC iterations can be cast into a dynamical system exhibiting both attractive and repulsive fixed points. In the standard formulation of SHDMC applied to this model, the fixed-node energy is found to increase upon iteration, and the node converges to a wrong value, indicating that SHDMC does not always converge to the correct solution. We further show that this problem is partially cured by modifying the nodal update criterion to give more importance to the nodal region. Achieving convergence in the general case very likely requires the use of a localized basis set, as is the case for this model.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates Self-Healing Diffusion Monte Carlo (SHDMC) using a one-dimensional periodic model with inversion symmetry mimicking fermionic antisymmetry. The authors find that standard SHDMC iterations form a dynamical system with attractive and repulsive fixed points, and in this model the algorithm fails to converge to the correct node, even causing the fixed-node energy to increase upon iteration. The problem is partially mitigated by modifying the nodal update criterion to emphasize the nodal region, but general convergence likely requires a localized basis set.
AI.motivation: To test whether SHDMC, a nodal optimization algorithm for fermionic quantum Monte Carlo, reliably converges to the correct nodal structure when symmetry only partially constrains the nodes—an essential requirement for accurate fixed-node calculations in realistic fermionic systems.
AI.method: A one-dimensional model with periodic boundary conditions and inversion symmetry is constructed. Even and odd eigenstates mimic bosonic and fermionic sectors respectively, with nodes partially unconstrained by symmetry. SHDMC iterations are analyzed as a dynamical system, examining fixed-point stability and testing modifications to the nodal update criterion and basis set choices.
AI.result: SHDMC iterations form a dynamical system with both attractive and repulsive fixed points. In the standard formulation, the node converges to a wrong value and the fixed-node energy increases with iteration, demonstrating that SHDMC does not always converge to the correct solution. Modifying the nodal update to weight the nodal region more heavily partially fixes the problem, though full convergence likely requires a localized basis set.
AI.conclusion: SHDMC is not unconditionally convergent and can be attracted to incorrect nodal fixed points; algorithmic modifications and appropriate basis-set choices are needed to ensure reliable nodal optimization in realistic fermionic systems.

title: Multi-image Overlap Stitching and Automatic Image Construction for Coherent X-ray Imaging
summary: Direct-space and real-time coherent X-ray imaging (direct-CXI) enables visualization of magnetic-domain structures and dynamics over length scales exceeding the field of view of a single image. However, large-area measurements typically require raster scanning, producing hundreds of partially overlapping images that must be accurately aligned and combined before quantitative analysis can be performed. Here, we present Multi-image Overlap Stitching and Automatic Image Construction for coherent X-ray imaging (MOSAICX), an automated stitching workflow for large-area direct-space coherent X-ray imaging. The workflow consists of image centering, masking, trimming, binarization, hierarchical stitching, and post-processing. To demonstrate the method, we apply it to a dataset comprising 434 direct-CXI images of the antiferromagnetic topological insulator MnBi$_2$Te$_4$. The images are first combined into column reconstructions and subsequently stitched into a single large-area composite image. The resulting reconstruction reveals the complete magnetic-domain and domain-wall landscape over the scanned region while suppressing imaging artifacts and detector defects. The presented workflow provides an efficient approach for processing large direct-CXI datasets and enables visualization and analysis of magnetic-domain structures beyond the field of view of individual measurements.

AI.tldr: MOSAICX is an automated stitching workflow for large-area direct-space coherent X-ray imaging (direct-CXI) that combines hundreds of overlapping images into a single composite image. Demonstrated on 434 images of MnBi2Te4, it reveals the complete magnetic-domain landscape while suppressing artifacts.
AI.motivation: Large-area direct-CXI measurements require raster scanning that generates hundreds of partially overlapping images needing accurate alignment and combination before quantitative analysis. No automated workflow exists to efficiently process such large datasets.
AI.method: The MOSAICX workflow consists of six steps: image centering, masking, trimming, binarization, hierarchical stitching, and post-processing. Images are first combined into column reconstructions, then stitched into a single large-area composite image.
AI.result: Applied to 434 direct-CXI images of the antiferromagnetic topological insulator MnBi2Te4, the workflow produced a composite reconstruction revealing the complete magnetic-domain and domain-wall landscape over the scanned region while suppressing imaging artifacts and detector defects.
AI.conclusion: MOSAICX provides an efficient, automated approach for processing large direct-CXI datasets, enabling visualization and analysis of magnetic-domain structures beyond the field of view of individual measurements.

title: Parafermions in plain sight
summary: We show that for any potential with a discrete energy spectrum, the well-known interpolation between ideal boson and fermion partition functions at discrete values of $ξ=-1/m$ yielded zero temperature ground state energies corresponding to $m$ fermions occupying a single quantum state. The grand canonical partition function in this case can be a result from genuine parastatistics.

AI.tldr: For any potential with a discrete energy spectrum, interpolating between ideal boson and fermion partition functions at discrete values ξ = -1/m yields zero-temperature ground state energies equivalent to m fermions occupying a single quantum state, where the grand canonical partition function arises from genuine parastatistics.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical meaning of the well-known interpolation between bosonic and fermionic partition functions at discrete values ξ = -1/m, specifically by analyzing the resulting ground state energies at zero temperature.
AI.method: The authors examine the interpolation between ideal boson and fermion partition functions at discrete values ξ = -1/m for arbitrary potentials with discrete energy spectra, then analyze the resulting zero-temperature ground state energies and identify the statistical interpretation of the grand canonical partition function.
AI.result: At ξ = -1/m, the zero-temperature ground state energy corresponds to m fermions occupying a single quantum state. The resulting grand canonical partition function is found to be consistent with genuine parastatistics.
AI.conclusion: The interpolation between bosonic and fermionic partition functions at discrete values ξ = -1/m has a well-defined physical interpretation in terms of m-fermion systems confined to a single quantum state, and the emergent partition function can be attributed to genuine parastatistics for any discrete-spectrum potential.

authors: César Javier Lockhart de la Rosa
title: Process-Technology Co-optimization for 2D-FETs
summary: We present the first experimental machine learning (ML)-enabled Process-Technology Co-Optimization (PTCO) framework for optimizing 2D transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) FET fabrication directly from statistically meaningful experimental data rather than pure simulation data. We first introduce a transition voltage metric, VTrans, to quantify the gate voltage required for off-to-on switching and reveal its direct correlation with subthreshold swing (SS), highlighting an overlooked switching characteristic that governs both off-state and on-state performance. By integrating automated metric extraction, multi-objective recipe ranking, and predictive modeling, our framework uncovers hidden process-performance correlations and predicts the performance of unexplored fabrication recipes from limited experimental data. Experimental validation shows close agreement with ML predictions, thus demonstrating the framework's ability to efficiently guide gate stack optimization through iterative experimental feedback.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first experimental ML-enabled Process-Technology Co-Optimization (PTCO) framework for 2D TMD FET fabrication, using a new transition voltage metric (VTrans) correlated with subthreshold swing to uncover process-performance correlations and predict fabrication recipe outcomes from limited experimental data, with experimental validation confirming ML prediction accuracy.
AI.motivation: Traditional PTCO frameworks rely on pure simulation data, lacking statistically meaningful experimental grounding. Additionally, conventional performance metrics overlook an important switching characteristic that governs both off-state and on-state performance in 2D TMD FETs.
AI.method: The framework introduces a transition voltage metric (VTrans) to quantify off-to-on switching gate voltage and reveal its correlation with subthreshold swing (SS). It integrates automated metric extraction, multi-objective recipe ranking, and predictive modeling to identify hidden process-performance correlations and forecast performance of unexplored fabrication recipes from limited experimental data.
AI.result: Experimental validation closely matched ML predictions, demonstrating the framework's ability to efficiently guide gate stack optimization through iterative experimental feedback using ML-enabled PTCO built on real experimental data.
AI.conclusion: The ML-enabled PTCO framework effectively bridges the gap between simulation-based design and experimental reality for 2D TMD FET fabrication, providing a data-driven pathway for gate stack optimization and process tuning.

title: Microscopic Origin of Pressure-Enhanced and Robust Superconductivity in Infinite-Layer La$_{0.8}$Sr$_{0.2}$NiO$_2$
summary: Recent transport measurements on freestanding La$_{0.8}$Sr$_{0.2}$NiO$_2$ membranes revealed a broad superconducting dome extending from ambient pressure to 210 GPa, with an onset transition temperature reaching 74.5 K near 146 GPa. Using first-principles calculations, a pressure-dependent two-orbital model, and self-consistent FLEX calculations combined with the linearized Eliashberg equation, we determine how compression modifies the pairing tendency. Pressure increases the kinetic-energy scale, reduces $U_x/t_1$, strengthens interlayer hybridization, and transfers holes from the La/Sr-derived charge reservoir to the correlated Ni sector. Within the present low-energy description, the increasing kinetic scale and the approach to optimal intermediate coupling account for the initial enhancement of pairing, whereas pressure-induced self-doping into the overdoped regime is primarily responsible for its high-pressure suppression. Despite a pronounced three-dimensionalization of the Fermi surface, the pairing-relevant spin susceptibility remains weakly dependent on $q_z$ and peaked near $(π,π)$. Consequently, the Ni-$d_{x^2-y^2}$-dominated $d$-wave pairing state remains stable over the calculated pressure range. These results provide a unified microscopic interpretation of both the superconducting dome and its unusual robustness under megabar compression.

AI.tldr: A unified microscopic theory explaining the superconducting dome in freestanding La0.8Sr0.2NiO2 membranes under pressure, where initial pairing enhancement arises from increased kinetic energy and optimal intermediate coupling, while high-pressure suppression is driven by pressure-induced self-doping into the overdoped regime. The d-wave pairing state remains robust to 210 GPa despite Fermi surface three-dimensionalization.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments revealed an unusual superconducting dome in freestanding La0.8Sr0.2NiO2 membranes extending from ambient pressure to 210 GPa (Tc up to 74.5 K near 146 GPa), which lacks a microscopic theoretical explanation. Understanding how megabar compression tunes the pairing mechanism is essential for explaining both the dome shape and the remarkable stability of superconductivity under extreme pressure.
AI.method: First-principles calculations combined with a pressure-dependent two-orbital model, self-consistent FLEX (fluctuation exchange) calculations, and the linearized Eliashberg equation to determine how compression modifies pairing propensity.
AI.result: Pressure increases the kinetic-energy scale, reduces Ux/t1, strengthens interlayer hybridization, and transfers holes from the La/Sr charge reservoir to the correlated Ni sector. The increasing kinetic scale and approach to optimal intermediate coupling drive initial enhancement of pairing, while pressure-induced self-doping into the overdoped regime causes high-pressure suppression. The pairing-relevant spin susceptibility remains peaked near (π,π) with weak qz dependence despite Fermi-surface three-dimensionalization, keeping Ni-d(x2-y2)-dominated d-wave pairing stable across the entire pressure range.
AI.conclusion: The calculations provide a unified microscopic interpretation of both the superconducting dome and its unusual robustness under megabar compression, reconciling the roles of kinetic-energy enhancement, coupling strength, self-doping, and interlayer hybridization in the nickelate system.

title: XUV Transmission Spectroscopy Using a Tabletop High-Harmonic Source
summary: High-harmonic generation (HHG) provides a coherent ultrashort-pulse light source in the extreme- ultraviolet (XUV) region and has potential applications in time-resolved spectroscopy and materials characterization. In this study, we constructed an HHG system using a Yb:KGW laser system (PHAROS, Light Conversion) as the driving source and Ar gas as the nonlinear medium. High-order harmonics were observed up to a photon energy of 70.6 eV, corresponding to the 59th harmonic order. As an application of the developed XUV source, we measured the transmission of a Mg thin film and a Si3N4 membrane. In addition, the surface chemical state of the Mg thin film was characterized by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and the results were compared with the transmission measured using the HHG source. This comparison was used to examine the relationship between the surface condition, including surface oxidation, and the XUV transmission of the Mg thin film. These results demonstrate the applicability of the developed Ar-based HHG source to the characterization of thin-film transmission in the XUV spectral region.
