They applied it to measure the XUV transmission of Mg thin films and Si3N4 membranes, and correlated Mg film surface chemical state (via XPS) with measured transmission to investigate the effect of surface oxidation on XUV transmission.

AI.method: An HHG system was built using a Yb:KGW laser (PHAROS) as the driving source and Ar gas as the nonlinear medium. XUV transmission measurements were performed on a Mg thin film and a Si3N4 membrane. AI.conclusion: The developed Ar-based HHG source is applicable to thin-film transmission characterization in the XUV spectral region, and the combined HHG transmission and XPS approach enables investigation of the relationship between surface conditions and XUV optical properties.

title: Feedback-Enhanced Quantum Metrology and Clock Precision under Thermodynamic Uncertainty
summary: Feedback can convert continuously monitored quantum jumps into a thermodynamic resource. We formulate full counting statistics for open quantum systems under unital jump feedback by incorporating the feedback maps into the tilted generator. The resulting trajectory ensemble determines both current fluctuations and the Fisher information of the measurement record. We show that feedback can enhance reservoir-parameter estimation and clock precision without necessarily changing average thermodynamic currents. This enhanced precision is not bounded by reservoir entropy production alone. By embedding the reduced dynamics in an enlarged measurement-feedback process, we derive a feedback-modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation in which the information entropy production of the feedback apparatus supplies the missing cost. A charge-monitored double quantum dot illustrates the framework: jump-conditioned feedback improves thermometry and chemical-potential sensing, and stabilizes a quantum clock defined by output-current ticks.

Feedback can enhance reservoir-parameter estimation and clock precision without changing average thermodynamic currents, challenging entropy-production bounds. A feedback-modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation is derived by embedding the dynamics in an enlarged measurement-feedback process, where information entropy production of the feedback apparatus supplies the missing cost. The framework is illustrated with a charge-monitored double quantum dot where jump-conditioned feedback improves thermometry, chemical-potential sensing, and stabilizes a quantum clock.

AI.method: The authors incorporate feedback maps directly into the tilted generator of an open quantum system's full counting statistics, constructing trajectory ensembles that capture both current fluctuations and Fisher information. They embed the reduced feedback-controlled dynamics into an enlarged measurement-feedback process to derive a modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation, identifying information entropy production of the feedback apparatus as the compensating cost term.

The feedback-modified thermodynamic uncertainty relation demonstrates that information entropy production supplies the missing cost. The double quantum dot example demonstrates improved sensing and clock stabilization via jump-conditioned feedback.

title: Classifying coherent peaks in nanoelectronic devices by the presence or absence of spin exchange
summary: Coherent peaks appearing in the differential conductance of quantum-dot single-electron transistors (QDSETs) and quantum point contact (QPC) devices are classified into two categories according to the scaling function onto which the temperature-scaled differential-conductance maxima collapse and the underlying spin dynamics. The zero-bias peaks (ZBPs) observed in QPCs and in the triplet state of the even-particle sector of QDSETs belong to the same category, whereas the ZBP in the odd-particle sector of a QDSET belongs to a different category together with all finite-bias coherent peaks observed in QPCs and in the even-particle sector of QDSETs. The spin dynamics of the former category involve spin exchange, a hallmark of Kondo dynamics, whereas those of the latter category involve only cotunneling of an up--down spin pair. Furthermore, for the former type of ZBP, the scaling temperature coincides with one-half of the full width at half maximum (FWHM), which corresponds to the Kondo temperature. In contrast, for the latter type, the scaling temperature does not coincide with the (1/2)FWHM-derived energy scale. To support these findings, the gate-voltage-dependent differential-conductance line shapes measured in the odd-particle sector of a QDSET are theoretically reproduced. The results demonstrate that the observed ZBP is a merging of two coherent side peaks generated solely by the cotunneling of up--down spin pairs.

AI.tldr: Coherent conductance peaks in QDSETs and QPCs are classified into two categories based on their scaling function and underlying spin dynamics. The first category (including QPC ZBPs and the triplet-state ZBP in even-particle QDSETs) involves Kondo spin exchange, with scaling temperature equal to half the FWHM (Kondo temperature). The second category (odd-particle QDSET ZBPs and all finite-bias coherent peaks) involves only cotunneling of up-down spin pairs. Theoretical reproduction of odd-sector QDSET data shows the observed ZBP results from merging two coherent side peaks from such cotunneling.
AI.motivation: To establish a systematic classification of coherent conductance peaks (including zero-bias peaks) observed in QDSET and QPC devices, and to clarify the physical origin of these peaks in terms of spin dynamics.
AI.method: The authors classify peaks by comparing the scaling function onto which temperature-scaled differential-conductance maxima collapse, and by relating the scaling temperature to FWHM-derived energy scales. They distinguish spin-exchange (Kondo) dynamics from up-down spin-pair cotunneling, and provide theoretical reproduction of gate-voltage-dependent line shapes in the odd-particle sector of a QDSET.

Category 1 (QPC ZBPs and triplet-state even-sector QDSET ZBPs) exhibits Kondo spin exchange with scaling temperature = (1/2)FWHM = Kondo temperature. Category 2 (odd-sector QDSET ZBPs and all finite-bias coherent peaks) arises from cotunneling of up-down spin pairs and has scaling temperature not matching the (1/2)FWHM scale. The odd-sector QDSET ZBP is shown to be a merging of two coherent side peaks from spin-pair cotunneling.
AI.conclusion: Coherent conductance peaks have two distinct physical origins: Kondo-like spin-exchange dynamics (scaling temperature = (1/2)FWHM = Kondo temperature) versus cotunneling of up-down spin pairs. The classification unifies QPC and QDSET behavior and provides a microscopic explanation for the odd-particle-sector ZBP in QDSETs.

title: Beyond Panchromatic Absorption: Deciphering the Excited-State Maze from Light Absorption to Photocatalysis in Dye-Sensitized MOFs
comment: Main manuscript + Supporting Information appended at the end
summary: Metal--organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising photocatalysts whose visible-light absorption can be extended through linker functionalization; however, a red-shifted absorption edge does not guarantee enhanced efficiency. Here, we establish a multi-spectroscopic framework to decipher the photophysical fate of photoexcited states in diazo-sensitized UiO-66 using 2D photoluminescence (PL/PLE) mapping and wavelength-resolved continuous-wave X-band photo-EPR. By correlating visible absorption with photo-EPR and PLE action spectra, we distinguish a \textit{productive red shift} from a \textit{non-productive emissive red shift}. In highly active UiO-66-Anisole (97\% activity relative to \ch{TiO2}), photo-EPR tracks the new absorption band, confirming that excitation populates a charge-transfer pathway yielding persistent, spin-separated states. Conversely, poorly active UiO-66-$β$-naphthol (4\%) exhibits an extended visible absorption tracked by PLE but not photo-EPR. This reflects excitation trapping in a localized state caused by an \textit{ortho}-$\mathrm{OH}$ group forming a rigid intramolecular hydrogen bond, which locks the keto-hydrazone tautomer and disrupts the conjugated azo bridge. A new optical overlap descriptor ($S_{\mathrm{Exc}}$) quantitatively captures this trade-off across the series. We demonstrate that photosensitizer design must suppress rigid tautomeric traps and target specific charge-transfer manifolds ($λ\le 500$~nm) rather than merely maximizing apparent panchromatic absorption breadth.

title: Resolving unconventional gap structure in kagome superconductors with hybrid microwave circuits
summary: Unconventional superconductivity is a hallmark of exotic quantum matter, where determining the pairing symmetry is essential for uncovering its microscopic origin. Kagome superconductors provide a fertile landscape for emergent phenomena arising from strong electronic correlations and nontrivial band topology, yet their superconducting pairing symmetry remains elusive. The superconducting gap structure is commonly probed via electrodynamic response, but such measurements are inapplicable to thin flakes due to their small volume and delicate nature. Superconducting microwave resonators offer a coherent and highly sensitive platform for probing electrodynamic responses, with versatile designs that enable incorporation of diverse materials and geometries. Here, we integrate flakes into microwave circuits, enabling noninvasive access to the superfluid response through contactless coupling that preserves structural integrity. By engineering the device geometry to suppress parasitic two-level-system losses that dominate dissipation in microwave circuits, we isolate the intrinsic material response. Remarkably, the temperature-dependent superfluid density exhibits linear behavior at low temperatures, consistent with a nodal gap structure. Our approach establishes a noninvasive platform for probing electrodynamic response of fragile superconducting flakes while advancing hybrid microwave architectures for quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates a noninvasive microwave resonator platform that integrates superconducting flakes via contactless coupling to probe their superfluid response, revealing a linear temperature-dependent superfluid density at low temperatures indicative of nodal gap structure in kagome superconductors.
AI.motivation: Kagome superconductors host exotic quantum phenomena from strong correlations and nontrivial band topology, but their superconducting pairing symmetry remains unresolved. Conventional electrodynamic probes of gap structure fail on thin flakes due to their small volume and fragility.
AI.method: Superconducting microwave resonators are used as a coherent, highly sensitive platform. Flakes are integrated into microwave circuits via contactless coupling, avoiding physical contact and preserving structural integrity. Device geometry is engineered to suppress parasitic two-level-system losses that dominate dissipation, isolating the intrinsic material response.
AI.result: The temperature-dependent superfluid density shows linear behavior at low temperatures, consistent with a nodal superconducting gap structure.
AI.conclusion: This approach establishes a noninvasive platform for probing the electrodynamic response of fragile superconducting flakes, and advances hybrid microwave architectures relevant for quantum technologies.

title: Optical-Phonon-Enabled Large Lattice Thermal Conductivity Anisotropy in Hexagonal Perovskites Cs$BX_3$ ($B$ = Mg, Cd; $X$ = Cl, Br, I)
summary: Materials exhibiting strongly anisotropic lattice thermal conductivity are desirable for thermal-management applications, yet such behavior is commonly associated with layered or quasi-one-dimensional van der Waals crystals and highly anisotropic elastic properties. Here, we investigate lattice thermal transport in the hexagonal perovskites Cs$BX_3$ ($B=$ Mg, Cd; $X=$ Cl, Br, I) using first-principles calculations. At 300~K, the calculated in-plane and out-of-plane lattice thermal conductivities range from 0.13--0.83 and 0.34--6.26~Wm$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, respectively, corresponding to anisotropy ratios of 2.6--7.5. This pronounced anisotropy is remarkable given the relatively modest elastic anisotropy, characterized by $C_{33}/C_{11}$ = 0.994--1.842. Our analysis reveals that medium-frequency optical phonons provide an efficient out-of-plane heat-transport channel, contrary to the conventional picture in which heat transport is dominated by acoustic phonons. These findings identify face-sharing octahedral frameworks as a promising platform for engineering strong thermal-conductivity anisotropy in mechanically near-isotropic, non--van der Waals crystals.

This work seeks anisotropic thermal transport in mechanically isotropic, non-van der Waals crystals.

title: Strengthened second law for periodic processes
summary: Many physical systems evolve under periodic driving: the same control protocol is applied again and again, even though the state of the system itself need not return to where it started after each cycle. We derive a physics-independent lower bound on the entropy production of \emph{any} periodic process modeled by the evolution of an initial distribution $p_0$ by a repeated application of the same map $G$. This is a strict strengthening of the second law of thermodynamics for periodic processes. It does not require that the single-period dynamics arise from a CTMC, satisfy (local) detailed balance, or be subject to other typical restrictions. We discuss its application to spins in the Curie-Weiss model and Deterministic Finite Automata, with possible extensions to other uniform computers.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a physics-independent lower bound on entropy production for any periodic process described by repeated application of a fixed map G to an initial distribution, strengthening the second law of thermodynamics without requiring typical assumptions such as continuous-time Markov chain dynamics or detailed balance.
AI.motivation: Many physical systems evolve under periodic driving where the same control protocol is applied repeatedly. Existing bounds on entropy production typically rely on restrictions like CTMC dynamics or detailed balance; the authors seek a universal, physics-independent lower bound applicable to any periodic process.
AI.method: The authors derive a strict lower bound on entropy production that strengthens the second law for periodic processes. The bound applies to any evolution formed by repeatedly applying a fixed map G to an initial distribution p0, and requires no assumptions about the single-period dynamics being a CTMC, satisfying detailed balance, or other typical constraints. Applications are discussed for spins in the Curie-Weiss model and Deterministic Finite Automata.

AI.conclusion: The authors provide a universal, physics-independent lower bound on entropy production for periodic processes, which is a strict strengthening of the second law and holds under minimal assumptions on the underlying dynamics.

title: Anti-higher-order topological insulators
summary: Duality is a fundamental concept in physics that connects complementary opposites like particles and holes. Similarly, while topological states in topological insulators localize at boundaries, the existence and nature of their dual counterparts remain unexplored. Here, we introduce anti-topological states as the dual of topological states, exemplified by anti-higher-order topological insulators. Unlike higher-order topological insulators, where states localize at corners, anti-higher-order topological insulators host states along edges but absent at corners, realizing an inverted distribution of states. We demonstrate this phenomenon in a bilayer Chern insulator with opposite Chern numbers, where the band inversion surfaces enclose distinct high-symmetry points. The topological invariant distinguishing these phases is given by the topological charges enclosed by band inversion surfaces. This work establishes anti-topology as a new paradigm, opening a chapter in topological research.

This is demonstrated in a bilayer Chern insulator with opposite Chern numbers, where the distinguishing topological invariant is the topological charges enclosed by band inversion surfaces.

This gap motivates the introduction of anti-topological states.
AI.method: The authors define anti-topological states as duals of topological states, concretely realized as anti-higher-order topological insulators where states localize along edges but are absent at corners. They demonstrate this in a bilayer Chern insulator with opposite Chern numbers, where band inversion surfaces enclose distinct high-symmetry points. The topological invariant is defined via the topological charges enclosed by band inversion surfaces.

AI.conclusion: This work establishes anti-topology as a new paradigm in topological research, introducing a previously unexplored class of topological phases and opening a new chapter in the field.

title: First-principles optical response of shock-compressed LiF: Quasiparticle, excitonic, and ionic-temperature effects
comment: Submitted to the Journal of Applied Physics; presented at XLI Fortov International Conference on Equations of State for Matter, 2026; 19 pages, 12 figures
summary: We investigate the refractive index $n$ of LiF using DFT+G$_0$W$_0$+BSE, with ionic-temperature effects included through QMD. We calculate photon-energy dispersions $n(ω)$ and $k(ω)$ at ambient pressure and $n(ρ,T)$ at 532 and 1550 nm under shock compression, where $ρ$ and $T$ vary together. Quasiparticle band structures at ambient and compressed conditions and the ambient-pressure orbital-projected density of states connect the optical response to the electronic structure. At ambient pressure, G$_0$W$_0$ yields a quasiparticle gap of 14.25 eV, close to the experimental 14.2 eV, while BSE reproduces the main excitonic feature at 12.5 eV, close to the observed 12.6 eV. Quasiparticle and excitonic effects are thus essential for accurate optical dispersion; the hybrid HSE functional does not reproduce the optical spectra. Along the principal Hugoniot up to 140 GPa, $n(ρ)$ agrees closely with shock data at 1550 nm and acceptably at 532 nm, and agrees better overall than earlier first-principles calculations. Above approximately 110-120 GPa, QMD produces a downturn relative to cold $n(ρ)$ curves, suggesting that ionic dynamics may contribute to deviations from the linear $n$-$ρ$ Gladstone-Dale relation. QMD-sampling and finite-k-grid uncertainties are estimated, and transition-peak broadening is assessed using a recently proposed criterion. The gap increases under pressure, with a transition to a $Γ\to\mathrm L$ indirect gap near 50 GPa. An exploratory calculation at approximately 1400 GPa finds a gap of about 24 eV, disfavoring gap-closure metallization. Structural and elastic benchmarks of the underlying models are also provided.

title: Robust thermodynamics constrain disorder and pairing in far-overdoped Tl$_2$Ba$_2$CuO$_6$
summary: The physical origin of the suppression of superconductivity with hole doping in overdoped cuprates remains unclear. We measure the electronic specific heat of microgram-scale Tl$_2$Ba$_2$CuO$_6$ crystals and find sharp superconducting anomalies persisting far into the overdoped regime, with $Δγ(T_{\rm c})/γ_n\approx0.6$ for $T_{\rm c}=14$-$25$K. A weak-coupling BCS-like framework incorporating the known Fermi surface and cation disorder quantitatively reproduces the observed anomaly and its weak doping dependence. We conclude that the observed $T_{\rm c}(p)$ cannot be driven predominantly by increasing disorder and is instead consistent with a smoothly decreasing pairing strength.

A weak-coupling BCS-like framework incorporating known Fermi surface and cation disorder quantitatively reproduces the observed anomaly and its weak doping dependence. The results show Tc(p) cannot be driven predominantly by increasing disorder but is consistent with smoothly decreasing pairing strength.

title: Magnetic quantum defects in a uniaxial antiferromagnetic insulator
summary: Point defects have been successfully utilized in various quantum technologies, serving as quantum qubits for quantum computation, single-photon emitters for quantum communication, and nanoscale sensors for quantum metrology. However, their further development faces key challenges, particularly in discovering and exploring suitable defect-host systems that meet the necessary criteria for quantum applications. Here, using polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy and terahertz absorption spectroscopy, we discover three distinct chromium-vacancy-induced excitations in the uniaxial antiferromagnetic insulator, Cr$_2$O$_3$. These vacancy-induced excitations have an energy scale of a few tens of millielectronvolts and are twofold degenerate, and the lowest one at 64 $cm^{-1}$ is sharp and sensitive to the external magnetic field along the easy-axis direction, particularly close to the spin-flop regime around 6T, where the mode softens from 64 to 27$cm^{-1}$. Based on the defect supercell first-principles calculations, we interpret the mode at 64 $cm^{-1}$ as a local magnetic excitation of the local moment within the chromium vacancy state. Our results establish that the magnetic defect states in Cr$_2$O$_3$ have potential for quantum applications.

The lowest mode at 64 cm⁻¹ is sharp, twofold degenerate, magnetic-field-sensitive, and softens to 27 cm⁻¹ near the spin-flop transition at ~6 T. First-principles calculations identify this mode as a local magnetic excitation of the chromium vacancy moment, suggesting potential for quantum applications.

This work aims to explore magnetic defect states in antiferromagnetic insulators as candidate systems.
AI.method: Polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy and terahertz absorption spectroscopy were used to detect vacancy-induced excitations in uniaxial antiferromagnetic Cr₂O₃. Defect supercell first-principles calculations were performed to interpret the origin of the observed modes.

The lowest mode at 64 cm⁻¹ is sharp and magnetic-field-sensitive along the easy axis, softening from 64 to 27 cm⁻¹ near the spin-flop regime (~6 T). AI.conclusion: The magnetic defect states in Cr₂O₃ exhibit properties (sharpness, degeneracy, magnetic tunability) making them promising candidates for quantum applications such as spin-based qubits or quantum sensors.

title: Lead-free piezoelectric perovskites for arterial-pulse e-skin: from configurational complexity to equivariant machine-learning potentials
summary: Continuous, non-invasive monitoring of the arterial pulse is a clinical priority for cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of global mortality. Flexible piezoelectric electronic skins can transduce the 1-10 kPa pressure wave into a self-powered voltage, but the best-performing piezoceramics are lead-based, and their toxicity is incompatible with skin contact and with tightening RoHS/REACH regulation. Among lead-free alternatives, the BaTiO$3$-based solid solution BZT-BCT reaches $d{33} \approx 620$ pC/N near its tricritical morphotropic phase boundary, rivalling soft PZT while remaining biocompatible. Exploiting this in a wearable confronts a sensitivity-flexibility paradox and three computational walls: the combinatorial explosion of atomic configurations in a disordered solid solution, the band-gap error of affordable density-functional approximations, which corrupts leakage and insulation estimates, and the 0 K nature of standard calculations against a 310 K operating temperature. We review lead-free piezoelectrics, morphotropic-boundary physics and fabricated flexible devices, then argue that equivariant machine-learning interatomic potentials --- coupled to a tiered functional hierarchy and finite-temperature lattice dynamics --- can survey the full configurational ensemble at body temperature and close the gap to a clinically viable lead-free pulse sensor.

AI.tldr: This review argues that equivariant machine-learning interatomic potentials, combined with a tiered functional hierarchy and finite-temperature lattice dynamics, can overcome the computational and physical barriers—configurational combinatorial explosion, band-gap errors, and 0 K limitations—to computationally design a clinically viable, lead-free, biocompatible BZT-BCT piezoelectric skin for continuous arterial pulse monitoring.
AI.motivation: Continuous non-invasive arterial pulse monitoring is critical for cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of global death. Current best piezoelectric materials are lead-based and toxic, conflicting with skin contact and RoHS/REACH regulations. Lead-free BZT-BCT rivals soft PZT (d33≈620 pC/N) but exploiting it in a wearable poses a sensitivity-flexibility paradox and three computational walls: combinatorial explosion of atomic configurations, band-gap errors of DFT approximations, and the 0 K nature of standard calculations versus 310 K body temperature.
AI.method: The paper reviews lead-free piezoelectrics, morphotropic-phase-boundary physics, and fabricated flexible devices, then proposes a computational strategy combining equivariant machine-learning interatomic potentials with a tiered density-functional hierarchy and finite-temperature lattice dynamics to survey the full configurational ensemble at body temperature.
AI.result: The paper presents a review and forward-looking computational framework rather than new experimental results, arguing that the proposed MLIP-based multi-tiered approach can close the gap toward a clinically viable lead-free pulse sensor by accurately modeling the disordered BZT-BCT configurational ensemble at finite temperature.
AI.conclusion: A clinically viable lead-free pulse sensor is within reach if equivariant machine-learning potentials and finite-temperature methods are applied to survey the configurational space of BZT-BCT at 310 K, resolving the sensitivity-flexibility paradox and overcoming the three computational barriers that currently impede lead-free piezoelectric e-skin development.

title: BKT-like Correlation Scaling and Twist Responses in a One-Dimensional Fractional $U(1)$ Ginzburg--Landau Model
summary: We study a one-dimensional fractional $U(1)$ Ginzburg--Landau model whose quadratic part has Fourier multiplier $|k|^σ$, focusing on the marginal case $σ=1$. This dispersion yields logarithmic spin-wave fluctuations, suggesting BKT-like behavior despite the one-dimensional setting. We sample the equilibrium Gibbs measure using stochastic Gross--Pitaevskii dynamics and analyze correlation functions, dimensionless ratios, effective exponents, and twist responses. The correlation function shows a low-temperature algebraic branch with a temperature-dependent exponent, while the high-temperature regime exhibits a nonlocal-kernel-induced tail consistent with $C(r)\sim r^{-2}$. The correlation and Binder ratios are nearly size independent at low temperature and collapse with the BKT-type variable $(T-T_{\rm BKT})(\log L)^2$; finite-size effects set in around $T\simeq0.35\text{--}0.4$, consistent with $T_{\rm BKT}\simeq0.35$. Unlike the two-dimensional XY model, twist responses do not yield a finite helicity modulus: the ordinary linear-response quantity grows with system size, whereas the cusp twist response scales as $L^{-η(T)}$, like the squared zero-mode order parameter. Thus, the transition is BKT-like in correlation scaling, but lacks a universal helicity-modulus jump.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a one-dimensional fractional U(1) Ginzburg-Landau model with quadratic dispersion |k|^σ at the marginal case σ=1. Despite being 1D, the logarithmic spin-wave fluctuations induce BKT-like behavior. Sampling the equilibrium Gibbs measure via stochastic Gross-Pitaevskii dynamics, the authors find algebraic low-temperature correlations with temperature-dependent exponents and a high-temperature r^{-2} tail. Binder and correlation ratios collapse with BKT scaling variable (T-T_BKT)(log L)^2, locating T_BKT≈0.35. However, unlike the 2D XY model, twist responses do not produce a finite helicity modulus—the linear-response quantity grows with system size while the cusp response scales as L^{-η(T)}—so the transition is BKT-like in correlations but lacks a universal helicity-modulus jump.
AI.motivation: To understand whether a one-dimensional system with logarithmic spin-wave fluctuations (from σ=1 fractional dispersion) can exhibit BKT-like physics, and to characterize the nature of its phase transition—particularly whether it possesses a universal helicity modulus feature as in the 2D XY model.
AI.method: The study employs stochastic Gross-Pitaevskii dynamics to sample the equilibrium Gibbs measure of the 1D fractional U(1) Ginzburg-Landau model with Fourier multiplier |k|^σ at σ=1. Analysis tools include correlation functions, dimensionless ratios (Binder), effective critical exponents, and two types of twist responses (linear-response and cusp), compared against BKT-type finite-size scalings.
AI.result: Correlations display a low-temperature algebraic branch with temperature-dependent exponents, and a high-temperature nonlocal-kernel tail C(r)∼r^{-2}. Binder and correlation ratios are nearly size-independent at low T and collapse under (T-T_BKT)(log L)^2 with finite-size effects around T≈0.35-0.4, giving T_BKT≈0.35. The twist responses differ from 2D XY: the linear-response helicity modulus grows with system size, while the cusp twist response scales as L^{-η(T)} like the squared zero-mode order parameter, indicating no universal helicity-modulus jump.
AI.conclusion: The σ=1 marginal case of the 1D fractional Ginzburg-Landau model exhibits BKT-like correlation scaling and a BKT-type transition at T_BKT≈0.35, but unlike the 2D XY model, it lacks a universal helicity-modulus jump. This reveals that BKT-like correlation behavior can occur without the standard stiffness-jump signature, suggesting the transition is BKT-like in correlation scaling only.

title: Anti-higher-order Weyl semimetal
summary: Higher-order topology extends the bulk-boundary correspondence by enabling corner or hinge localized states. Here we identify an anti-higher-order Weyl semimetal, a three dimensional topological phase in which the conventional boundary hierarchy is reversed. Unlike conventional higher-order Weyl semimetals where bulk topology enforces hinge Fermi arcs, this phase hosts anti-hinge states, meaning the bulk topology forces states to vanish at specific hinge orientations. Using a minimal two-band model, we show how Weyl points separate the Brillouin zone into quantum anomalous Hall and anti-higher-order topological insulating regions, with the latter characterized by a band-inversion surface enclosing two distinct high-symmetry points carrying opposite topological charges. Analytical solutions for Weyl points, Berry curvature monopoles, and slice Chern numbers are derived, with numerical simulations confirming the resulting anti-hinge behavior. Our work establishes anti-higher-order topology as a dual counterpart to conventional higher-order phenomena, further extending the exploration of topological phases.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a new topological phase called an anti-higher-order Weyl semimetal, a 3D topological phase where the conventional bulk-boundary correspondence hierarchy is reversed—bulk topology forces states to vanish at specific hinge orientations (anti-hinge states) rather than localizing there.
AI.motivation: To extend the understanding of higher-order topology by discovering and characterizing its dual counterpart, where the boundary hierarchy is reversed compared to conventional higher-order Weyl semimetals.
AI.method: A minimal two-band model is used to demonstrate how Weyl points separate the Brillouin zone into quantum anomalous Hall and anti-higher-order topological insulating regions. The latter is characterized by a band-inversion surface enclosing two distinct high-symmetry points carrying opposite topological charges. Analytical solutions are derived for Weyl points, Berry curvature monopoles, and slice Chern numbers, with numerical simulations confirming the anti-hinge behavior.
AI.result: The paper establishes the existence of anti-higher-order Weyl semimetals, derives exact analytical expressions for key topological quantities (Weyl point positions, Berry curvature monopoles, slice Chern numbers), and confirms anti-hinge state behavior via numerical simulation—demonstrating that bulk topology can enforce the vanishing of states at specific hinges.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes anti-higher-order topology as a dual counterpart to conventional higher-order topological phenomena, thereby extending the exploration of topological phases in three dimensions.

title: Superconducting diode effect from field-induced $s+if$ pairing in Ising superconductors
summary: The in-plane critical field of Ising superconductors exceeds the Pauli limit by an order of magnitude because the Ising spin-orbit coupling locks the electron spins out of the basal plane. The same locking converts an in-plane Zeeman field into a source of equal-spin triplet Cooper pairs, so that the field-driven condensate acquires an $s+if$ character. We show that this conversion channel also generates Lifshitz invariants, the odd-in-momentum terms of the Ginzburg-Landau expansion responsible for the superconducting diode effect. When the basal mirror symmetry of the monolayer is lifted by a substrate or a gate, the field-induced triplets couple linearly to the Cooper-pair momentum, and an intrinsic diode response develops whose strength is set by the ratio of the Zeeman and spin-orbit energies rather than by the small ratio of the spin-orbit and Fermi energies familiar from parity-mixing mechanisms. We construct the symmetry-constrained two-component Ginzburg-Landau theory of the coupled singlet and triplet order parameters and derive all of its coefficients from the microscopic model of an Ising superconductor; the complete functional, including all gradient and quartic terms, is generated by a single pair-breaking function of temperature, field, and Cooper-pair momentum. An attractive triplet channel reshapes the diode response: at weak fields it suppresses the efficiency through destructive interference between the direct and the collective-mode conversion paths, while at strong fields it extends the diode regime well beyond the singlet-only critical field, with the maximal efficiency reached along the triplet-enhanced phase boundary. The diode effect thereby serves as a transport probe of a hidden triplet pairing channel and of the field-induced $s+if$ state.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a two-component Ginzburg-Landau theory for Ising superconductors where the Ising spin-orbit coupling converts an in-plane magnetic field into equal-spin triplet Cooper pairs, producing an s+if state. This conversion generates Lifshitz invariants that give rise to an intrinsic superconducting diode effect whose magnitude scales with the Zeeman-to-spin-orbit energy ratio, and the diode response can probe hidden triplet pairing channels.
AI.motivation: To understand and characterize the superconducting diode effect in Ising superconductors, where in-plane fields significantly exceed the Pauli limit, and to determine how the field-driven s+if state and triplet pairing channels influence this effect—thereby providing a transport probe of hidden triplet pairing.
AI.method: The authors construct a symmetry-constrained two-component Ginzburg-Landau (GL) theory coupling singlet and triplet order parameters. All coefficients are derived from a microscopic model of an Ising superconductor, with the complete functional (including gradient and quartic terms) generated from a single pair-breaking function of temperature, magnetic field, and Cooper-pair momentum. They analyze the effect of an attractive triplet channel on the diode response.
AI.result: The field-induced triplet conversion generates Lifshitz invariants when basal mirror symmetry is lifted, producing an intrinsic diode effect whose strength is controlled by the Zeeman/spin-orbit ratio rather than the small spin-orbit/Fermi ratio. An attractive triplet channel suppresses diode efficiency at weak fields via destructive interference but extends the diode regime beyond the singlet-only critical field at strong fields, with maximal efficiency along the triplet-enhanced phase boundary.
AI.conclusion: The superconducting diode effect in Ising superconductors serves as a transport probe of hidden triplet pairing channels and of the field-induced s+if state, with the diode efficiency magnitude set by the ratio of Zeeman to spin-orbit energies.

title: Kibble--Zurek Mechanism and Defect Freezing in Imbalanced-Pairing Kitaev Models
summary: We investigate driven dynamics across critical and exceptional points in the one- and two-dimensional imbalanced-pairing Kitaev models using both the wave-function normalization approach and the biorthogonal framework. For a positive pairing imbalance parameter, the quasiparticle spectrum remains real, and a pairing imbalance neither shifts the equilibrium phase boundaries nor generates imaginary eigenenergies. In this regime, the defect density follows the conventional Kibble--Zurek scaling in one dimension and the extended Kibble--Zurek scaling, arising from a gapless manifold, in two dimensions within both frameworks. The corresponding scaling exponents are therefore governed by those of the Hermitian transition. For a negative pairing imbalance parameter, time-reversal symmetry is broken, the quasiparticle spectrum develops complex eigenvalues, and the gap closes at exceptional points. For ramps ending at an exceptional point, the defect density follows the modified Kibble--Zurek scaling in the wave-function normalization approach, whereas it obeys the conventional Kibble--Zurek scaling in the biorthogonal framework. When the ramp traverses the time-reversal-symmetry-broken region, a finite density of defects remains even in the adiabatic limit, leading to defect freezing in both frameworks. Although this frozen background indicates a breakdown of adiabaticity, the excess defects generated on top of this background continue to obey the conventional Kibble--Zurek scaling in one dimension and the extended Kibble--Zurek scaling in two dimensions.

AI.tldr: This paper studies driven dynamics across critical and exceptional points in one- and two-dimensional imbalanced-pairing Kitaev models, comparing wave-function normalization and biorthogonal frameworks. For positive pairing imbalance (Hermitian-like regime), standard Kibble-Zurek scaling holds. For negative pairing imbalance (non-Hermitian regime with exceptional points), the defect dynamics depend on the framework and ramp path, with defect freezing occurring when traversing the time-reversal-symmetry-broken region, although excess defects on top of the frozen background still follow conventional Kibble-Zurek scaling.
AI.motivation: To understand how non-Hermitian features such as exceptional points and symmetry-broken regions affect non-equilibrium dynamics and topological defect generation in imbalanced-pairing Kitaev models, and to clarify how results depend on the choice of framework (wave-function normalization versus biorthogonal), since non-Hermitian systems lack a unique quantum-state normalization.
AI.method: The authors perform driven dynamics studies across critical and exceptional points in 1D and 2D imbalanced-pairing Kitaev models. They employ two complementary theoretical frameworks: the wave-function (state) normalization approach and the biorthogonal quantum framework. They compute defect densities after ramps through phase boundaries and exceptional points, and analyze the resulting scaling exponents against Kibble-Zurek predictions.
AI.result: (1) For positive pairing imbalance: the spectrum remains real, equilibrium phase boundaries are unchanged, no imaginary eigenenergies appear, and standard/extended Kibble-Zurek scaling is recovered. (2) For negative pairing imbalance: time-reversal symmetry breaks, the spectrum becomes complex with exceptional point gap closures. For ramps ending at an exceptional point, the wave-function normalization approach yields modified Kibble-Zurek scaling while the biorthogonal framework yields conventional scaling. When traversing the symmetry-broken region, a finite frozen defect background remains even in the adiabatic limit in both frameworks; however, excess defects on top follow conventional Kibble-Zurek scaling in 1D and extended Kibble-Zurek scaling in 2D.
AI.conclusion: The scaling behavior of defect production in non-Hermitian Kitaev models depends sensitively on the framework used and on whether the ramp traverses or merely ends at exceptional points. The frozen defect background signals a breakdown of adiabaticity, yet the universal Kibble-Zurek scaling structure for excess defects is preserved, indicating that hallmark non-equilibrium scaling laws partially survive non-Hermitian physics.

title: Cavity-control of Majorana bound states in superconductor-semiconductor heterostructures
summary: We theoretically study a hybrid superconductor-semiconductor platform hosting Majorana bound states coupled to a single mode photonic cavity. Starting with a one-dimensional wire coupled to a bulk $s$-wave superconductor embedded in a photonic cavity, we derive an effective light-matter Hamiltonian for such a platform. Assuming that the photonic vector potential is aligned along the tunneling between a wire and a superconductor, we find that the cavity coupling enters only in the effective superconducting pairing term. By solving the coupled electron-photon Hamiltonian using different approaches, such as exact diagonalization in case of zero or large number of photons, high-frequency expansion, and mean-field decoupling, we find that the phase boundary between the topological trivial phases is shifted to smaller values of the Zeeman energy compared to the uncoupled case. Cavity embedding has the strongest effect on the phase diagram in the semiclassical regime, corresponding to a large number of photons. In all cases, we find that at large values of the light-matter coupling strength the effective superconducting pairing is suppressed, driving the system into the gapless phase. We demonstrate that even small light-matter coupling strength allows for entering the topological phase at values of the Zeeman energy compared to the uncoupled platform.

AI.tldr: A theoretical study of a Majorana bound state platform where a 1D superconductor-semiconductor wire is embedded in a photonic cavity. The cavity coupling enters only the effective superconducting pairing term when the photonic vector potential aligns with tunneling. Cavity embedding shifts the topological phase boundary to smaller Zeeman energies, with the strongest effect in the semiclassical (large photon number) regime, and strong light-matter coupling suppresses superconducting pairing driving the system gapless.
AI.motivation: To understand how cavity quantum electrodynamics (light-matter coupling) can be used to control and tune topological superconducting phases hosting Majorana bound states, potentially enabling access to topological phases at lower Zeeman fields than required in conventional uncoupled platforms.
AI.method: Derives an effective light-matter Hamiltonian for a 1D wire coupled to a bulk s-wave superconductor in a photonic cavity. Multiple solution approaches are employed: exact diagonalization (for zero or large photon number limits), high-frequency expansion, and mean-field decoupling.
AI.result: The phase boundary between topological and trivial phases shifts to smaller Zeeman energies compared to the uncoupled case. The semiclassical (large photon number) regime shows the strongest cavity effect on the phase diagram. Large light-matter coupling suppresses the effective superconducting pairing, inducing a gapless phase. Even small coupling allows topological phase entry at reduced Zeeman energies.
AI.conclusion: Photonic cavity embedding provides a controllable knob to tune the topological phase transition of Majorana platforms, enabling topological superconducting phases at reduced Zeeman energies even with weak coupling, which has practical implications for realizing and manipulating Majorana bound states.

title: Understanding the superconducting proximity effect in semiconductors through quantum oscillations
summary: Superconductor-semiconductor hybrids host emergent states of matter and offer a platform for new qubits, but the superconducting metal shunts electrical transport, which rules out conventional semiconductor characterization and leaves the hybrid parameters to speculation. Here we determine density, mass, $g$-factor, mobility and subband occupation beneath the superconductor, from Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations of a buried InAs quantum well under Al, Sn, V, Nb, Ta and Re films, with a Dingle analysis that accounts for the shunt. Every metal adds an interface subband whose occupation falls into one of two classes, whereas the mass and $g$-factor of the buried well are unchanged to within 10\%. Within the uncertainty set by the transport mobility, no film shortens the quantum lifetime of the buried well, and Al and Sn lengthen it. Quantum lifetimes bound the hybridization of the interface subband to 2-4~meV. These measurements supply the normal-state parameters that tunnelling spectroscopy renormalizes but cannot measure.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a method to extract key normal-state parameters (density, mass, g-factor, mobility, and subband occupation) from a buried InAs quantum well beneath superconducting films (Al, Sn, V, Nb, Ta, Re) using Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations with a Dingle analysis that accounts for the superconducting shunt. The results show that while interface subbands form in two distinct classes, the buried well's mass and g-factor remain unchanged, and no superconductor degrades the quantum lifetime—Al and Sn even improve it—yielding quantum lifetime bounds on interface subband hybridization of 2–4 meV.
AI.motivation: Superconductor-semiconductor hybrids are promising platforms for topological states and qubits, but the superconducting metal shunts electrical transport, preventing conventional semiconductor characterization and leaving crucial hybrid parameters unknown.
AI.method: Shubnikov-de Haas oscillation measurements on a buried InAs quantum well under six different superconducting films (Al, Sn, V, Nb, Ta, Re), analyzed using a Dingle analysis that accounts for the current shunt through the superconductor.
AI.result: Each metal induces an interface subband falling into one of two occupation classes; the buried well's effective mass and g-factor are unchanged within 10%; no film shortens the quantum lifetime of the buried well, while Al and Sn lengthen it; quantum lifetimes bound interface subband hybridization to 2–4 meV.
AI.conclusion: The measurements supply the normal-state parameters that tunnelling spectroscopy renormalizes but cannot directly measure, providing essential grounding for understanding superconductor-semiconductor hybrid devices.

title: Overcoming the Efficiency-Stability Trade-off in Spin-Orbit Torque Devices with Thermally Robust BCC NiW Alloys
comment: 45 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to Nature Communications
summary: The development of high-performance spin-orbit torque (SOT) magnetic memories is fundamentally constrained by a persistent trade-off between spin Hall efficiency, thermal structural stability, and perpendicular magnetic anisotropy in conventional heavy metals. Here, we overcome this limitation by engineering body-centered-cubic (BCC) Ni-doped W alloys as highly efficient and thermally robust spin-current sources. Ni$_{30}$W$_{70}$/CoFeB heterostructures achieve deterministic out-of-plane magnetization switching at an ultra-low critical current density of 1.78 MA/cm$^2$, nearly threefold lower than that of $β$-W, while maintaining a high anisotropy field of 8,500 Oe and a thermal stability factor of 57.9. The BCC Ni$_{30}$W$_{70}$ alloy preserves its structural integrity and the perpendicular magnetic anisotropy of the adjacent CoFeB layer after annealing at 450 $^\circ$C, demonstrating robustness under the stringent thermal processing conditions relevant to back-end-of-line integration. Harmonic Hall and ferromagnetic resonance measurements reveal a large spin Hall angle of -0.39 and a high interfacial spin transparency of 0.75, demonstrating efficient spin-current generation and interfacial transmission. First-principles calculations further reveal enhanced intrinsic spin Hall conductivity in W-rich BCC NiW alloys, associated with the Fermi level lying within a spin-orbit-coupling-induced band gap. These findings establish BCC NiW alloys as a scalable and thermally resilient material platform for energy-efficient SOT-MRAM.

AI.tldr: Ni30W70/CoFeB heterostructures achieve ultra-low critical current density (1.78 MA/cm²) for deterministic magnetization switching, with a large spin Hall angle of -0.39, high interfacial spin transparency of 0.75, and thermal stability up to 450°C, establishing BCC NiW alloys as scalable spin-current sources for energy-efficient SOT-MRAM.
AI.motivation: Conventional heavy metals face a fundamental trade-off between spin Hall efficiency, thermal structural stability, and perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, limiting high-performance SOT magnetic memory development.
AI.method: Engineered BCC Ni-doped W alloys (Ni30W70) as spin-current sources; experimental characterization via harmonic Hall, ferromagnetic resonance, and annealing tests; complemented by first-principles calculations of intrinsic spin Hall conductivity.
AI.result: Ni30W70/CoFeB heterostructures show deterministic switching at 1.78 MA/cm² (threefold lower than β-W), anisotropy field of 8,500 Oe, thermal stability factor of 57.9, structural/PMA stability after 450°C annealing, spin Hall angle of -0.39, and interfacial spin transparency of 0.75.
AI.conclusion: BCC NiW alloys provide a scalable and thermally resilient material platform that simultaneously resolves the efficiency-stability-anisotropy trade-off, enabling energy-efficient SOT-MRAM relevant to back-end-of-line integration.

title: Statistical Language Competition Model with Dynamic Edge Weighting on a Random Network
summary: This paper presents a computational study of language competition dynamics on Erdős--Rényi random networks, extending the foundational Abrams--Strogatz model through two novel contributions: (i) a dynamic edge-weighting mechanism that reinforces social ties between co-minority speakers by an additive increment $Δ$, and (ii) a probabilistic agent-based framework governing language switching via a weighted majority rule. Phase boundaries separating the dominance and coexistence regimes are identified across a two-dimensional parameter space $(p, Δ)$, where $p$ denotes the network connectivity probability. We further characterise anomalous persistence zones within predicted dominance regions, attributing them to the formation of isolated minority speaker clusters. Scaling study across network sizes $N \in \{50, 100, 250, 500, 1000\}$ reveal that average cluster size decreases with $N$ and that phase boundaries diffuse with increasing stochastic noise. Finally, we discuss extensions to a tripartite bilingual model and heterogeneous prestige/volatility to more faithfully capture real sociolinguistic contact scenarios.

AI.tldr: A computational study of language competition on Erdős–Rényi random networks, extending the Abrams–Strogatz model with a dynamic edge-weighting mechanism reinforcing co-minority speaker ties and a probabilistic agent-based switching rule governed by weighted majority. Phase boundaries separating dominance and coexistence regimes are mapped in (p, Δ) parameter space, with anomalous persistence zones linked to isolated minority clusters. Scaling analysis over network sizes N ∈ {50–1000} shows cluster size decreases with N and phase boundaries diffuse under stochastic noise. Extensions to bilingual and heterogeneous prestige models are discussed.
AI.motivation: To better capture real sociolinguistic contact dynamics by extending the foundational Abrams–Strogatz model beyond mean-field assumptions, incorporating network structure (Erdős–Rényi random graphs) and dynamic social reinforcement mechanisms between minority speakers.
AI.method: Two novel extensions to the Abrams–Strogatz model: (i) a dynamic edge-weighting mechanism that adds an increment Δ to edges connecting co-minority speakers, reinforcing in-group social ties, and (ii) a probabilistic agent-based framework where language switching follows a weighted majority rule. Phase boundaries are studied across a two-dimensional (p, Δ) parameter space, complemented by a scaling analysis over network sizes N ∈ {50, 100, 250, 500, 1000}.
AI.result: Identification of phase boundaries separating dominance and coexistence regimes in (p, Δ) space; characterisation of anomalous persistence zones within predicted dominance regions attributed to isolated minority speaker clusters; scaling results showing average cluster size decreases with N and phase boundaries diffuse with increasing stochastic noise.
AI.conclusion: The extended model reveals richer phase structure than the classical Abrams–Strogatz framework and highlights the role of network topology and minority-cluster formation in sustaining language persistence. Extensions to tripartite bilingual models and heterogeneous prestige/volatility are proposed to better approximate real sociolinguistic scenarios.

title: Topological charges and parity selection at Floquet quasienergy degeneracies
summary: The quasienergy spectrum of a strongly driven two-level system as a function of the driving parameters exhibits conical intersections, which are enabled by hidden time-nonlocal symmetries. We show that each such crossing carries a quantized topological charge: the Floquet--Berry phase acquired along an adiabatic loop around a cone is equal to a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-valued charge. We further identify a second family of degeneracies that occurs at vanishing driving amplitude, when the level splitting matches $m$ energy quanta of the field. Along the Stark-shifted resonance line, the minimum quasienergy gap opens as $|A|^m$, and the charge is nontrivial only for odd $m$. We analytically derive both results from a perturbative reduction to a spin-$1/2$ in an effective two-dimensional magnetic field and confirm them numerically through the Bargmann invariant. Moreover, we propose a chirality-based protocol that cancels the dynamical phase to isolate the geometric one, and an ancilla-based Ramsey readout that renders the topological charge directly observable.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes conical intersections in the quasienergy spectrum of a strongly driven two-level system, showing they carry Z2-valued Floquet-Berry topological charges. A second family of degeneracies at vanishing driving amplitude is identified, with charge nontrivial only for odd resonance orders. Both results are derived via perturbation theory to an effective spin-1/2 in a 2D magnetic field, and experimental protocols are proposed to observe the topological charge.
AI.motivation: To understand the topological structure of degeneracies in driven quantum systems and to establish that conical intersections enabled by hidden time-nonlocal symmetries carry quantized topological charges, potentially enabling direct experimental observability of these charges.
AI.method: Analytical perturbative reduction of the strongly driven two-level system to an effective spin-1/2 experiencing a two-dimensional effective magnetic field, combined with numerical confirmation using the Bargmann invariant. A chirality-based protocol cancels the dynamical phase to isolate the geometric phase, and an ancilla-based Ramsey readout makes the topological charge observable.
AI.result: Each conical intersection carries a Z2-valued quantized topological charge equal to the Floquet-Berry phase around the cone. Along the Stark-shifted resonance line at vanishing amplitude, the minimum quasienergy gap scales as |A|^m, and the charge is nontrivial only for odd m. Both results are confirmed via the Bargmann invariant.
AI.conclusion: Strongly driven two-level systems exhibit two families of topologically nontrivial degeneracies with Z2-valued charges, arising from distinct symmetry mechanisms. These charges are theoretically accessible and experimentally measurable through proposed interferometric and Ramsey-type protocols.

title: Singular Weak-Field Thermodynamics of 2D Superconductors
summary: In a bulk 3D type-II superconductor, the lower critical field at which an isolated vortex becomes thermodynamically favorable is a size-independent material property. We show that the situation is different in 2D superconductors: the larger the superconductor, the weaker the field needed to create its first vortex. The lower critical field in 2D is always size-dependent. For a disk of area $\mathcal A$, the lower critical field $B_v(\mathcal A)$ scales as $\mathcal A^{-1}\ln(\mathcal A/\mathcal A_0)$ in the weak-screening regime and as $\mathcal A^{-1/2}$ in the strong-screening regime. We derive these results from an analytically tractable microscopic model that admits many-body wavefunctions for both the uniform and singly quantized vortex states in a magnetic field, and incorporate screening by coupling their long-distance 2D supercurrents to 3D Maxwell equations. These results motivate organizing the weak-field ground-state of a 2D superconductor in the $(1/\mathcal A,B)$ plane. The origin represents the zero-field thermodynamic limit and it is singular. Approaching the origin along the $B$ axis leads to an increasingly dilute vortex lattice, whereas approaching along the $1/\mathcal A$ axis yields the uniform vortex-free state. Our theory shows that every trajectory carrying fixed finite flux ultimately approaches the vortex-free state in the thermodynamic limit and provides a firm microscopic foundation for the weak-field thermodynamics of 2D superconductors.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the lower critical field for vortex entry in 2D superconductors is size-dependent, unlike in 3D where it is a material constant. For a disk of area A, it scales as A^-1 ln(A/A0) in weak screening and A^-1/2 in strong screening, derived from an exactly solvable microscopic model coupled to 3D Maxwell supercurrent screening.
AI.motivation: In bulk 3D type-II superconductors, the lower critical field is a size-independent material property. This paper investigates whether this holds in 2D and reveals a fundamentally different, size-dependent behavior that had not been previously established within a firm microscopic theoretical framework.
AI.method: The authors construct an analytically tractable microscopic model admitting many-body wavefunctions for both uniform and singly quantized vortex states in a magnetic field. Screening is incorporated by coupling the long-distance 2D supercurrents to 3D Maxwell equations. They analyze two regimes: weak screening (scaling as A^-1 ln(A/A0)) and strong screening (scaling as A^-1/2).
AI.result: The lower critical field in 2D superconductors is always size-dependent. For a disk of area A, it scales as A^-1 ln(A/A0) in the weak-screening regime and as A^-1/2 in the strong-screening regime. Mapping the weak-field ground state onto the (1/A, B) plane reveals a singular origin representing the zero-field thermodynamic limit, with trajectories along B giving dilute vortex lattices and along 1/A giving the vortex-free uniform state.
AI.conclusion: Every trajectory carrying fixed finite flux approaches the vortex-free state in the thermodynamic limit. The work provides a firm microscopic foundation for the weak-field thermodynamics of 2D superconductors and motivates a new organizational scheme for their ground states.

title: Phase Switchable Photocatalytic Water Splitting via a Paraelectric-Ferroelectric Transition in Zr2Ge2S6 Monolayer: A Comprehensive Theoretical Insights
summary: Photocatalytic water splitting (PWS) is a promising technology for addressing the global energy crisis and producing renewable and clean hydrogen fuel. Although numerous 2D materials have recently been proposed as potential photocatalysts, effective strategies for regulating photocatalytic reactions and improving energy conversion efficiency remain limited due to performance regulation challenges. Here, using first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that the photocatalytic activity and energy conversion efficiency of a Zr2Ge2S6 monolayer can be effectively tuned through a paraelectric-ferroelectric phase transition. The Zr2Ge2S6 monolayer exhibits excellent structural stability, favorable mechanical properties, a suitable band gap, optimal band edge positions, and broad-spectrum light absorption. Moreover, the Zr2Ge2S6 monolayer exhibits a higher oxidation potential and a stronger driving force for photogenerated holes to promote oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in the ferroelectric phase. In contrast, the paraelectric phase provides photogenerated electrons with a greater reduction potential and driving force for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). The solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency is also strongly influenced by the phase transition, increasing from 7.71% in the paraelectric phase to 15.31% in the ferroelectric phase because of the improved carrier utilization. Our theoretical investigation not only highlights the crucial role of ferroelectric polarization in photocatalytic water splitting but also provides an effective strategy for tuning the photocatalytic properties of 2D ferroelectric materials through ferroelectric switching.

AI.tldr: First-principles calculations demonstrate that a Zr2Ge2S6 monolayer's photocatalytic activity and solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency can be tuned via a paraelectric-ferroelectric phase transition, with conversion efficiency increasing from 7.71% to 15.31%.
AI.motivation: While numerous 2D materials have been proposed as photocatalysts for water splitting, effective strategies for regulating photocatalytic reactions and improving energy conversion efficiency remain limited due to performance regulation challenges.
AI.method: First-principles calculations were used to investigate the Zr2Ge2S6 monolayer, analyzing structural stability, mechanical properties, band gap, band edge positions, light absorption, and the effects of a paraelectric-ferroelectric phase transition on photocatalytic performance.
AI.result: The ferroelectric phase exhibits higher oxidation potential and stronger driving force for OER, while the paraelectric phase provides greater reduction potential and driving force for HER. The solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency increases from 7.71% (paraelectric) to 15.31% (ferroelectric).
AI.conclusion: Ferroelectric polarization plays a crucial role in photocatalytic water splitting, and ferroelectric switching provides an effective strategy for tuning the photocatalytic properties of 2D ferroelectric materials.

title: Nonmonotonic control of pattern formation by chemotaxis
summary: We investigate pattern formation in generic two-species reaction--diffusion systems with chemotaxis. We show that chemotaxis can give rise to a striking nonmonotonic dependence of pattern formation on its strength, opening the possibility of re-entrant transitions between patterned and homogeneous states controlled by chemotaxis. In certain regimes, chemotaxis also induces additional heretofore unexplored instabilities. Furthermore, varying the strength of chemotaxis can drive morphological transitions between spot and stripe patterns.

AI.tldr: The paper studies pattern formation in two-species reaction-diffusion systems with chemotaxis, revealing that chemotaxis strength can produce nonmonotonic effects on pattern formation, enabling re-entrant transitions between patterned and homogeneous states, inducing novel instabilities, and driving morphological transitions between spot and stripe patterns.
AI.motivation: To understand how chemotaxis influences pattern formation in generic two-species reaction-diffusion systems, particularly exploring its role in creating non-trivial dependencies and transitions in pattern behavior.
AI.method: Analytical and theoretical investigation of generic two-species reaction-diffusion systems with chemotaxis, analyzing instabilities and pattern formation as a function of chemotactic strength.
AI.result: Chemotaxis produces a nonmonotonic dependence of pattern formation on its strength, leading to re-entrant transitions between patterned and homogeneous states. It also induces previously unexplored instabilities and can drive morphological transitions between spot and stripe patterns.
AI.conclusion: Chemotaxis is a versatile control parameter in reaction-diffusion systems that can qualitatively alter pattern formation behavior, including enabling re-entrant transitions and morphological pattern shifts.

title: Interfacial orbital torques excite nanoscale terahertz magnons
summary: Exchange-dominated magnons in nanometer-thick ferromagnets extend to the terahertz regime through thickness quantization of perpendicular standing spin-wave (PSSW) modes. While interfacial spin-orbit torques (SOTs) have been shown to enable the excitation of such modes, the microscopic origin of the interfacial driving torque remains unclear. In particular, the coexistence of spin and orbital currents complicates the understanding. Here, we develop and use an atomistic framework that explicitly resolves interfacial symmetries and separates spin and orbital torque contributions. Exploiting a trilayer geometry for a thin ferromagnet sandwiched between non-magnetic layers, where the symmetry-controlled polarity of the interfacial torque produces mode-selective magnon excitation as observed in the recent experiment of Salikhov et al. Nature Phys. 19, 529 (2023), we disentangle the different interfacial torque contributions. By decomposing the torque into magnetization-even (field-like) and magnetization-odd components, we identify the field-like torque as the dominant contribution responsible for the excitation. Crucially, isolating orbital and spin contributions reveals that the interfacial orbital torque provides the primary channel for the efficient excitation of exchange-dominated THz magnons in thin ferromagnets. Our results establish a microscopic basis for symmetry-engineered control of confined terahertz spin dynamics in magnetic multilayers.

Through decomposition into field-like and magnetization-odd components, they identify the field-like torque as dominant, and crucially find that the interfacial orbital torque is the primary channel for efficient excitation of exchange-dominated terahertz magnons.

AI.method: They develop and use an atomistic framework that explicitly resolves interfacial symmetries and separates spin and orbital torque contributions. They exploit a trilayer geometry (thin ferromagnet sandwiched between non-magnetic layers), where symmetry-controlled polarity of the interfacial torque produces mode-selective magnon excitation (as in Salikhov et al.), and decompose the torque into magnetization-even (field-like) and magnetization-odd components.

title: Agentic programs: an emerging form of scientific software in computational materials science
summary: Computational materials science has traditionally delegated algorithmic tasks to computers while leaving scientific judgments to humans. We argue that recent LLM-based agent harnesses enable an emerging form of scientific software, agentic programs, that combine deterministic algorithms with bounded LLM-based judgment, task-specific verification, episodic maturation, and complete delegation in production. We illustrate this concept with DeMARS, an agentic program for constructing atomistic models from experimentally measured disordered crystal structures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "agentic programs"—a new class of scientific software combining deterministic algorithms with bounded LLM-based judgment, task-specific verification, episodic maturation, and complete delegation. This concept is illustrated with DeMARS, an agentic program that constructs atomistic models from experimentally measured disordered crystal structures.
AI.motivation: Computational materials science traditionally separates algorithmic computation (done by computers) from scientific judgment (done by humans). The authors argue that recent LLM-based agent harnesses enable a new paradigm where this boundary can be shifted, allowing machines to take on scientific judgment tasks in a bounded and verifiable manner.
AI.method: The paper conceptualizes "agentic programs" as scientific software that combines deterministic algorithms with bounded LLM-based judgment, incorporates task-specific verification, supports episodic maturation (learning/improving over episodes), and allows complete delegation in production. The concept is instantiated as DeMARS, an agentic program designed for constructing atomistic models from experimentally measured disordered crystal structures.
AI.result: DeMARS serves as a working demonstration of the agentic program paradigm, showing that this approach can handle the complex task of building atomistic models from experimentally derived data on disordered crystals—a task that traditionally requires significant human scientific expertise.
AI.conclusion: Agentic programs represent an emerging form of scientific software enabled by recent LLM-based agent harnesses, offering a fundamentally new division of labor between deterministic computation and LLM-mediated scientific judgment in materials science and potentially other scientific domains.

title: Dynamical phase transitions for single particles in the semiclassical and weak noise limits
summary: We present a unifying description of dynamical phase transitions in the unitary evolution of an isolated quantum particle and the dissipative relaxation of a classical Brownian particle, based on a dynamical generat- ing function. In the semiclassical and weak-noise limits, Fisher zeros of this function condense in the complex- time plane and reach the corresponding physical axes, producing dynamical phase transitions through a competition between return trajectories. This establishes a direct connection between quantum and classical (finite-time) dynamical phase transitions, where the semiclassical limit plays the role of the thermodynamic limit. In particular, the established link naturally provides a classical version of the Loschmidt amplitude and shows how dynamical quantum phase transitions, typically associated with isolated many-body systems, can arise in a single-particle quantum system. The dynamical phases are distinguished by a unifying, trajectory- based order parameter, realized as a classical correlation function and a sequential quantum weak value.

AI.tldr: The paper unifies dynamical phase transitions in isolated quantum particles and dissipative classical Brownian particles through a dynamical generating function, showing that Fisher zeros condense in the complex-time plane in semiclassical/weak-noise limits, linking quantum and classical phase transitions.
AI.motivation: To establish a direct connection between quantum and classical finite-time dynamical phase transitions, demonstrating that effects typically associated with isolated many-body quantum systems can emerge even in single-particle systems.
AI.method: Uses a dynamical generating function formalism; in semiclassical (quantum) and weak-noise (classical) limits, Fisher zeros of this function condense in the complex-time plane and reach physical axes, driven by competition between return trajectories. A unifying trajectory-based order parameter is defined via a classical correlation function and a sequential quantum weak value.
AI.result: Establishes that the semiclassical limit plays the role of the thermodynamic limit, providing a classical version of the Loschmidt amplitude and showing dynamical quantum phase transitions can occur in single-particle quantum systems.
AI.conclusion: Quantum and classical finite-time dynamical phase transitions share a common mathematical framework, with dynamical phases distinguished by a unified trajectory-based order parameter realized both classically and quantum mechanically.

title: Probing Nonlinear Interactions of Dipolar Interlayer Excitons in MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ Heterobilayers
summary: Interlayer excitons in transition-metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers possess intrinsic out-of-plane dipole moments, providing a platform for investigating exciton-exciton interactions at high densities. Here, we use excitation-energy-dependent photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy to probe the nonlinear response of dipolar interlayer excitons in chemical vapor deposition-grown MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ heterobilayers. By tuning the excitation energy across intralayer exciton resonances at fixed excitation power, we selectively vary the population injected into the interlayer exciton states. Resonant excitation drives the system into a nonlinear regime, leading to saturation of the interlayer exciton photoluminescence and an apparent broadening of the intralayer $1s$ resonances in the PLE spectra. At the same time, the interlayer exciton emission exhibits a pronounced blueshift, reaching approximately 2.5 meV at 4 K and 1 meV at 75 K. The blueshift increases systematically with the interlayer exciton population and is consistent with a net repulsive exciton-exciton interaction, with contributions from dipole-dipole repulsion in the density regime investigated. Our results establish PLE as a sensitive approach for accessing the nonlinear, high-density regime of interlayer excitons and probing their interactions in van der Waals heterostructures.

AI.motivation: Interlayer excitons in transition-metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers have intrinsic out-of-plane dipoles, providing a platform to study exciton-exciton interactions at high densities. The authors seek a sensitive probing method for this nonlinear high-density regime.
AI.method: Excitation-energy-dependent photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy on CVD-grown MoSe2/WSe2 heterobilayers. Excitation energy was tuned across intralayer exciton resonances at fixed power to selectively control the population injected into interlayer exciton states, enabling access to the nonlinear regime.
