The blueshift scales with interlayer exciton population and is consistent with net repulsive exciton-exciton interactions dominated by dipole-dipole repulsion.
AI.conclusion: PLE spectroscopy is established as a sensitive tool for accessing the nonlinear, high-density regime of interlayer excitons and probing their interactions in van der Waals heterostructures.

title: An exact and fast solution of the inverse Regularized Optimal Transport problem
summary: Optimal transport describes the most efficient way to move mass between two distributions, given a cost matrix for moving mass between each pair of locations. Entropic optimal transport, solved via the Sinkhorn algorithm, is a widely used regularized version of this problem. Its inverse problem asks the opposite question: given an observed transport plan, what cost matrix produced it? This is difficult because the cost is identifiable only up to an additive gauge freedom. Here we show that this freedom can be fixed exactly by a single double-centering operation applied to the observed plan, yielding the true cost matrix in closed form, with no iterative optimization required. When a modest number of true cost entries are known, the same approach lets us jointly estimate the temperature parameter controlling the entropic regularization, together with a diagnostic for the reliability of this estimate. We further show that the method is not specific to the entropic optimal transport, but extends to a broader class of transport models defined by an invertible relation between cost and plan.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the inverse entropic optimal transport problem—recovering the cost matrix from an observed transport plan—can be solved exactly via a single double-centering operation on the plan matrix, yielding the true cost in closed form without iterative optimization. The approach also enables joint estimation of the temperature parameter when partial cost entries are known, and extends to general invertible cost-plan mappings.
AI.motivation: The inverse problem of entropic optimal transport—recovering the cost matrix from an observed transport plan—is fundamentally difficult because costs are identifiable only up to an additive gauge freedom. Prior approaches required iterative optimization, and no exact closed-form solution existed.
AI.method: The paper demonstrates that the gauge freedom in the inverse entropic OT problem can be resolved exactly by applying a single double-centering operation to the observed transport plan matrix, producing the true cost matrix in closed form. When a subset of true cost entries is known, the same framework jointly estimates the entropic regularization temperature parameter and provides a reliability diagnostic. The method generalizes to any transport model where the cost-to-plan relation is invertible.
AI.result: The true cost matrix is recovered exactly with no iterative optimization. Additionally, the temperature parameter can be jointly estimated alongside a diagnostic for estimation reliability when partial ground-truth cost entries are available. The approach is shown to extend beyond entropic OT to broader invertible transport model classes.
AI.conclusion: The gauge ambiguity of the inverse entropic optimal transport problem can be eliminated non-iteratively via double-centering, providing an exact closed-form recovery of the cost. This framework further enables parameter estimation and generalizes to a wider family of transport models with invertible cost-plan relations.

title: Layer-selective and magnetic-field-enhanced transport of topological kink states in rhombohedral multilayer graphene
summary: Topological valley kink states (VKSs), which are quantum valley Hall states emerging at the interfaces between adjacent domains with opposite valley Chern numbers, have attracted considerable interest in graphene-based systems. In this work, we investigate the quantum transport of VKSs in ABC-stacked rhombohedral multilayer graphene in the presence of Anderson disorder and a perpendicular magnetic field. Two prominent transport characteristics are revealed. First, in the absence of a magnetic field, the kink states exhibit strong layer polarization, with their wave functions predominantly localized and equally distributed on the outermost top and bottom layers. As a result, their transport properties are highly sensitive to the layer-selective disorder distribution. Second, under a perpendicular magnetic field, the layer-symmetric spatial distribution of VKSs is broken, leading to a significant reduction in the wave-function overlap between counter-propagating VKSs from opposite valleys. Consequently, intervalley scattering is suppressed, and the transmission of VKSs through disordered regions is substantially enhanced. Our results provide new insights into multichannel topological valley transport in rhombohedral multilayer graphene and demonstrates disorder-engineering and magnetic fields as effective approaches for manipulating the propagation of VKSs.

Two key findings: (1) VKSs exhibit strong layer polarization without a magnetic field, making transport highly sensitive to layer-selective disorder; (2) a perpendicular magnetic field breaks the layer-symmetric distribution, reducing intervalley scattering and significantly enhancing VKS transmission through disordered regions.
AI.motivation: To understand how disorder and magnetic fields influence the quantum transport of topological valley kink states in rhombohedral multilayer graphene, which could enable disorder-engineering and magnetic-field-based manipulation of VKS propagation.
AI.method: The authors perform quantum transport calculations of VKSs in ABC-stacked rhombohedral multilayer graphene, incorporating Anderson disorder and a perpendicular magnetic field, and analyze wave-function localization, layer polarization, and transmission properties.
AI.result: Without a magnetic field, VKSs show strong layer polarization with wave functions concentrated equally on outermost layers, making transport sensitive to layer-selective disorder. Under a perpendicular magnetic field, the layer-symmetric distribution is broken, reducing wave-function overlap between counter-propagating VKSs from opposite valleys, which suppresses intervalley scattering and substantially enhances transmission through disordered regions.

title: Metastable defects in III-Nitrides
summary: Metastable states in III-nitrides (AlN, GaN, InN and their alloys) are an important topic across materials science, device physics, and epitaxial growth because these compounds exhibit multiple competing crystal structures, defect configurations, and phase behaviors that strongly affect optical, electrical, and mechanical properties. The paper is a concise, structured review-style summary covering the main concepts, mechanisms, experimental signatures, theoretical approaches, and device implications. Actions that should be proposed to avoid effect of metastable defects in III-Nitride based devices are discussed. Avoiding metastable defect effects in III nitride devices requires preventing their formation (through growth and doping control), stabilizing their electronic configuration (by annealing or optical activation), and designing device architectures that minimize field- or temperature induced transitions. These combined actions ensure consistent carrier density, higher mobility, and superior optical and electrical reliability in GaN , AlGaN , and InGaN based devices.

AI.tldr: A structured review of metastable states in III-nitrides (AlN, GaN, InN and alloys), covering competing crystal structures, defect configurations, and phase behaviors, with emphasis on experimental signatures, theoretical approaches, device implications, and mitigation strategies for metastable defects in device fabrication.
AI.motivation: Metastable states in III-nitrides strongly affect optical, electrical, and mechanical properties across materials science, device physics, and epitaxial growth. Understanding and controlling these states is essential for reliable device performance.
AI.method: A concise review-style synthesis covering main concepts, mechanisms, experimental signatures, theoretical approaches, and device implications of metastable states in III-nitride materials, with proposed mitigation actions.
AI.result: Proposes three actions to avoid metastable defect effects: (1) preventing defect formation via growth and doping control, (2) stabilizing electronic configurations through annealing or optical activation, and (3) designing device architectures that minimize field- or temperature-induced transitions. These ensure consistent carrier density, higher mobility, and improved optical/electrical reliability in GaN, AlGaN, and InGaN devices.
AI.conclusion: Combined growth, stabilization, and device design strategies are necessary to mitigate metastable defect effects and achieve reliable performance in III-nitride-based devices.

title: Pole-Zero Geometry, Model Reduction, and Identifiability in Sensory Adaptation
summary: Sensory adaptation provides a concrete setting in which low-order system identification can fail qualitatively. We show that one fixed higher-order adaptive system composed entirely of real first-order relaxation modes can be reduced to opposite sides of the second-order pole boundary: low-frequency moment matching gives $ρ_{\rm moment}=4.50$, whereas finite-window fitting gives $ρ_{\rm window}=3.31$, and the inferred pole class changes further with sampling protocol. Thus the real-versus-complex classification of a reduced model is not itself reduction invariant. We then use the general two-state spectrum to connect stochastic identifiability to adaptation: for nontrivial coupling and one-state observation, cross diffusion drops out of the scalar spectrum when the hidden state has no self-relaxation. In the adaptive model, this condition is precisely the integral-memory limit that produces exact adaptation, while leaky memory restores spectral sensitivity. For the exact-adaptation model, the Gaussian path-space irreversibility nevertheless depends on the hidden cross-diffusion channel. Hence $\{H,S_x\}$ does not determine the irreversibility rate. Independently, for a specified all-even reduced two-state drift with $ρ<4$, the drift-only lower bound is $σ\ge τ_x^{-1}(4/ρ-1)$. Published \textit{E.~coli} and \textit{C.~elegans} responses provide biological examples of these limits. The distinction established here between transfer-function invariants, reduction-dependent properties, and hidden-state quantities provides a concrete framework for evaluating the limitations of low-dimensional models of adaptive biological dynamics.

Using the general two-state spectrum, the authors connect stochastic identifiability to adaptation: cross diffusion becomes unobservable when the hidden state lacks self-relaxation, which corresponds to the integral-memory limit of exact adaptation; leaky memory restores spectral sensitivity. However, Gaussian path-space irreversibility of exact-adaptation models still depends on the hidden cross-diffusion channel, so {H,S_x} does not determine irreversibility. A drift-only lower bound σ≥τ_x^{-1}(4/ρ−1) is derived for specified all-even reduced two-state drift with ρ<4, with published E. coli and C. elegans data as biological examples.

They use the general two-state spectrum to connect stochastic identifiability to adaptation, examining cross diffusion, self-relaxation, integral-memory vs. leaky-memory limits, and path-space irreversibility. title: Interferometry reveals spin-singlet fractional quantum Hall edges in graphene
summary: The edge modes of spin-singlet fractional quantum Hall (FQH) phases are manifestations of multicomponent topological order and SU(2) spin symmetry. An archetype is the spin-unpolarized state at $ν$=2/3, whose edge is expected to host spatially coexisting yet counter-propagating charge and neutral spin modes. Despite efforts, its edge properties, including spin coherence and spin-charge separation, have remained elusive owing to the difficulty of resolving spins in FQH edge transport. Here, we develop a spin-sensitive probe of graphene FQH edges by using a p-n junction to interface a target FQH state with a probe integer quantum Hall (QH) state of opposite polarity. An Aharonov-Bohm (AB) interferometer forms along the interface, when the target and probe edge channels carry the same spin. We identify the spin-unpolarized and polarized edges of the $ν$=2/3 states at lower and higher magnetic fields, respectively, through spin-dependent interference. A novel multiparticle AB interference between two electrons of opposite spin emerges from spin-charge separation and recombination on the unpolarized edge, featuring a spin swap. Our results establish edge transport as a probe of spin-singlet topological orders, with implications for parafermion platforms in graphene-superconductor hybrids.

The authors identify spin-unpolarized and polarized edges of the ν=2/3 state through spin-dependent Aharonov-Bohm interference and discover a novel multiparticle AB interference between two electrons of opposite spin arising from spin-charge separation on the unpolarized edge, featuring a spin swap.

AI.method: A spin-sensitive probe is developed by using a p-n junction to interface a target FQH state with a probe integer quantum Hall state of opposite polarity. When target and probe edge channels carry the same spin, an Aharonov-Bohm interferometer forms along the interface, enabling spin-dependent interference measurements.

title: Independent Tuning of Surface Acoustic-Waves and Spin-Waves via Buffer-Layer Engineering in Co2FeGe Heusler Thin Films
summary: Understanding and controlling acoustic and spin-wave excitations in magnetic thin films is critical for the development of magnonic and spin-acoustic devices. We report on the use of Cr and W buffer layers to independently modify the acoustic and magnetic excitations in Co2FeGe full-Heusler thin films grown on MgO(001). Using Brillouin light scattering (BLS) spectroscopy and ferromagnetic resonance (FMR), we probed Rayleigh and Sezawa surface acoustic waves (SAWs) alongside Damon-Eshbach and perpendicular standing spin-wave (PSSW) modes. Our results show that acoustic dispersion depends strongly on the buffer material; W-buffered films exhibit a pronounced 16% reduction in Rayleigh SAW frequency compared to buffer-free films, primarily due to mass loading and acoustic impedance shifts. While the buffer layers significantly shift acoustic frequencies, they simultaneously modify the dynamic magnetic response (increasing spin-wave group velocity by ~34%) through different physical mechanisms. Finite-element simulations show excellent agreement with the experimental acoustic data. These findings demonstrate that buffer-layer engineering is an effective strategy for the independent tailoring of elastic and magnetic excitations, providing a versatile platform for hybrid spin-acoustic technologies.

AI.motivation: Controlling acoustic and spin-wave excitations in magnetic thin films is critical for developing magnonic and spin-acoustic devices; however, independently tailoring both elastic and magnetic properties within a single platform remains a challenge.
AI.method: Co2FeGe full-Heusler films were grown on MgO(001) with Cr and W buffer layers. Brillouin light scattering (BLS) spectroscopy and ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) were used to probe Rayleigh and Sezawa surface acoustic waves (SAWs) alongside Damon-Eshbach and perpendicular standing spin-wave (PSSW) modes. Finite-element simulations were used to corroborate acoustic data.

AI.conclusion: Buffer-layer engineering is an effective strategy for independently tailoring elastic and magnetic excitations in full-Heusler thin films, providing a versatile platform for hybrid spin-acoustic technologies.

title: Multiple chiral Majorana states in proximitized magnetic topological insulator heterostructures
summary: Achieving robust topological superconductivity with multiple Majorana channels is a key step for scalable topological quantum computing. To this end, we investigate magnetically doped three-dimensional topological insulator heterostructures proximitized by an s-wave superconductor within a fully three-dimensional extended Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang framework that explicitly accounts for vertical confinement. We show that magnetic exchange coupling, orbital mixing, and bulk band inversion cooperate to generate effective equal-spin p-wave pairing channels supporting multiple chiral Majorana modes. The number of Majorana channels is determined by the confined modes in the vertical direction and the high-Chern-number phases of the normal state, which allows us to derive an analytical criterion for the emergence of the multiple-Majorana topological superconducting phases. The chiral Majorana modes remain robust against strong disorder and moderate symmetry-breaking perturbations. We also demonstrate that a superconducting phase difference defining a vertical Josephson junction acts as a tunable parameter that controls the hybridization, minigap, and effective multiplicity of the low energy Majorana channels. Our results establish magnetic three-dimensional topological- insulator heterostructures as a promising platform for engineering multiple chiral Majorana modes.

It shows that magnetic exchange, orbital mixing, and bulk band inversion cooperate to generate effective equal-spin p-wave pairing channels supporting multiple chiral Majorana modes, with their number determined by confined vertical modes and high-Chern-number phases. An analytical criterion is derived, and robustness against disorder and symmetry-breaking is demonstrated. A vertical Josephson junction phase difference acts as a tunable parameter controlling hybridization and minigap of low-energy Majorana channels.
AI.motivation: Achieving robust topological superconductivity with multiple Majorana channels is a key step for scalable topological quantum computing, motivating the need for platforms that can host multiple chiral Majorana modes.
AI.method: A fully three-dimensional extended Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang framework accounting for vertical confinement is used to model magnetically doped 3D TI heterostructures proximitized by an s-wave superconductor. The study analyzes the interplay of magnetic exchange coupling, orbital mixing, and bulk band inversion, derives an analytical criterion for multiple-Majorana topological superconducting phases, and examines the role of a Josephson junction phase difference as a tuning parameter.

The number of channels is determined by confined vertical modes and the normal-state high-Chern-number phases. The modes are robust against strong disorder and moderate symmetry-breaking. A vertical Josephson junction phase difference controls hybridization, minigap, and effective multiplicity of Majorana channels.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic 3D topological-insulator heterostructures are established as a promising platform for engineering multiple chiral Majorana modes, advancing scalable topological quantum computing.

title: Large Exchange Magnetostriction in a Kagome Antiferromagnet at Room Temperature
summary: The pursuit of high-performance magnetostrictive materials is crucial for advancing technologies in sensing, actuation, and microelectromechanical systems. Although pronounced magnetostrictive effects have been observed in a few ferromagnets, a systematic exploration of magnetostriction across a broader range of antiferromagnets remains limited. Here, we report the observation of large magnetostriction in the kagome antiferromagnet YMn6Sn6. Under a magnetic field, the system undergoes a field-induced evolution from a helical magnetic ground state toward a collinear field-polarized state, accompanied by a large anisotropic lattice strain and a substantial volume magnetostriction exceeding 400 ppm at room temperature. Remarkably, the magnetostrictive response remains nearly fully reversible up to 9 T with nearly hysteresis-free behavior, effectively minimizing the energy dissipation commonly associated with domain-wall pinning. Combined experimental measurements and theoretical calculations reveal that the large, nearly hysteresis-free magnetostriction originates from the competition between intralayer ferromagnetic and interlayer exchange interactions. This exchange-driven magnetoelastic coupling further gives rise to a strongly direction-dependent lattice distortion pathway. This work establishes kagome helimagnets as a tunable platform for low-dissipation magnetoelastic functionalities and responsive magnetomechanical applications.

AI.tldr: The paper reports observation of large magnetostriction exceeding 400 ppm at room temperature in the kagome antiferromagnet YMn6Sn6, which exhibits a field-induced transition from a helical magnetic ground state to a field-polarized collinear state with nearly hysteresis-free, fully reversible magnetostrictive response up to 9 T. The effect originates from competition between intralayer ferromagnetic and interlayer exchange interactions.
AI.motivation: While pronounced magnetostrictive effects have been found in a few ferromagnets, systematic exploration of magnetostriction in antiferromagnets, particularly across broader material classes, remains limited. The authors aim to identify high-performance magnetostrictive materials among antiferromagnetic systems to advance sensing, actuation, and MEMS technologies.
AI.method: Combined experimental measurements and theoretical calculations were used to characterize the magnetostrictive response of the kagome antiferromagnet YMn6Sn6, including measurements of anisotropic lattice strain and volume magnetostriction under magnetic fields up to 9 T, alongside theoretical analysis of the exchange interactions driving the magnetoelastic coupling.
AI.result: Large volume magnetostriction exceeding 400 ppm at room temperature was observed, accompanied by a field-induced evolution from helical magnetic ground state to collinear field-polarized state. The magnetostriction is nearly fully reversible up to 9 T with almost hysteresis-free behavior, minimizing energy dissipation from domain-wall pinning. The effect is attributed to intralayer ferromagnetic versus interlayer exchange competition, producing a strongly direction-dependent lattice distortion pathway.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes kagome helimagnets as a tunable platform for low-dissipation magnetoelastic functionalities and responsive magnetomechanical applications, expanding the search for high-performance magnetostrictive materials beyond conventional ferromagnets into antiferromagnetic systems.

title: Tunneling characteristics of twisted double bilayer graphene heterostructures
summary: Electron tunneling between sheets of bilayer Bernal graphene twisted at different small angles was studied experimentally and theoretically. The current-voltage characteristics exhibit resonant peaks, steps, and regions of negative differential resistance, the origin of which is explained by the intersections of energy- and momentum-shifted electron dispersions of adjacent layers. A theoretical analysis of tunneling transport demonstrated that the key to understanding this phenomenon lies in the competition between two contributions: between like (conductivity-conductivity or valence-valence) and unlike (conductivity-valence) bands of parallel bilayer graphene sheets. A systematic evolution of the tunneling current patterns with increase of the twist angle is investigated. Polarization of electron wave function across graphene sublayers caused by displacement field within bilayer graphene is shown to strongly affect the tunneling probability, thus enhancing negative differential resistance due to Van Hove singularities at the band edges.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally and theoretically investigates electron tunneling between sheets of bilayer Bernal graphene twisted at small angles. Resonant peaks, steps, and negative differential resistance (NDR) in the I-V characteristics are explained by intersections of energy- and momentum-shifted electron dispersions of adjacent layers. The tunneling is governed by competition between like-band and unlike-band contributions, with twist-angle-dependent evolution. A displacement field within bilayer graphene polarizes electron wave functions across sublayers and strongly enhances NDR via Van Hove singularities at band edges.
AI.motivation: To understand the tunneling transport mechanisms in twisted bilayer Bernal graphene systems, particularly the origins of resonant peaks, steps, and negative differential resistance, and to determine how twist angle and displacement field effects can control these phenomena.
AI.method: The study combines experimental measurements of current-voltage characteristics with a theoretical analysis of tunneling transport. The theory accounts for energy- and momentum-shifted electron dispersions of adjacent bilayer graphene layers and examines the competition between like-band (conduction-conduction or valence-valence) and unlike-band (conduction-valence) contributions. The effect of displacement-field-induced wave function polarization across graphene sublayers on tunneling probability is also analyzed.
AI.result: The I-V characteristics exhibit resonant peaks, steps, and regions of negative differential resistance, originating from intersections of energy- and momentum-shifted electron dispersions of adjacent layers. A systematic evolution of tunneling current patterns with increasing twist angle is observed. Displacement-field-induced polarization of electron wave functions across bilayer graphene sublayers strongly affects the tunneling probability and enhances negative differential resistance due to Van Hove singularities at band edges.
AI.conclusion: The key to understanding tunneling transport in twisted bilayer Bernal graphene lies in the competition between like-band and unlike-band contributions. The displacement field provides a tunable mechanism to enhance negative differential resistance through wave function polarization and Van Hove singularities, offering potential pathways for engineering tunnel devices based on twisted bilayer graphene.

title: Antiresonances of Wannier-Stark ladders in Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattices
summary: We demonstrate that Wannier-Stark ladders (WSLs) in one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chains manifest as antiresonance signatures in the electron transmission. We study the quantum transport in the SSH chain in the presence of a periodic potential profile plus a uniform electric field. By employing the global matrix method with non-trivial matching conditions, we find that these WSL antiresonances correspond to states that are exponentially localized at the potential's incident boundary. These findings provide a robust, unified framework for identifying WSLs across diverse scales, ranging from electronic transport in trans-polyacetylene to classical-wave analogs in phononic crystals and surface water waves.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that Wannier-Stark ladders in one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains manifest as antiresonance signatures in electron transmission. Using the global matrix method with non-trivial matching conditions, the authors find that these antiresonances correspond to exponentially localized states at the potential's incident boundary, providing a unified framework for identifying WSLs across diverse scales from electronic transport to classical-wave analogs.
AI.motivation: To establish a robust, unified framework for identifying Wannier-Stark ladders in SSH chains through their manifestation as antiresonance signatures in quantum transport, which can be applied across diverse physical systems.
AI.method: The authors study quantum transport in a 1D SSH chain with a periodic potential profile plus a uniform electric field, employing the global matrix method with non-trivial matching conditions to analyze electron transmission.
AI.result: WSLs in SSH chains produce antiresonance signatures in electron transmission, and these antiresonances correspond to states that are exponentially localized at the potential's incident boundary.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a robust, unified framework for identifying WSLs across diverse scales, including electronic transport in trans-polyacetylene, phononic crystals, and surface water waves.

title: Element priors and target support shape chemical transfer in materials graph networks
summary: Materials graph neural networks must often transfer to chemical regions weakly represented in training data. Such transfer can rely on predefined relations among elements or supervised evidence from target-containing structures, but these pathways are usually entangled. Here, held-out-element splits and incremental target support separate their roles. Without target-containing training structures, formation-energy errors depend strongly on the element representation, particularly for H, O and F. Matched perturbations show that representation-induced sharing matters beyond input dimension or numerical form, while a label-free similarity-graph prior reduces selected zero-shot errors. Adding a few target-containing structures sharply lowers errors and contracts differences among one-hot, k-hot and continuous inputs across ALIGNN and CGCNN. Calibration explains only part of this recovery, and freezing the initial element projection preserves most gains in five of six ALIGNN splits. Target support therefore shifts chemical transfer from reliance on static element relations toward learning from target-containing environments.

AI.tldr: This paper disentangles two pathways for chemical transfer in materials graph neural networks: predefined element relations and supervised evidence from target-containing structures. Using held-out-element splits and incremental target support, the authors show that element representation strongly affects zero-shot errors (especially for H, O, F), while adding even a few target-containing structures sharply reduces errors and contracts performance gaps across different input representations and model architectures, with calibration explaining only part of the recovery.
AI.motivation: Materials graph neural networks must often generalize to chemical regions poorly represented in training data. However, the two potential transfer pathways—reliance on predefined element relations embedded in representations and learning from supervised target-containing structures—are usually entangled, making it unclear which mechanism drives successful transfer.
AI.method: The authors use held-out-element splits and incremental addition of target-containing training structures to separately probe the two transfer pathways. They systematically compare element representations (one-hot, k-hot, continuous) across ALIGNN and CGCNN architectures, use matched perturbations to isolate representation-induced sharing from input dimension or numerical form, and employ a label-free similarity-graph prior for zero-shot contexts. They also analyze the effect of target support on errors, calibration, and whether freezing the initial element projection preserves gains.
AI.result: Without target-containing training structures, formation-energy errors depend strongly on the element representation, especially for H, O and F. Representation-induced sharing matters beyond input dimension or numerical form, and a label-free similarity-graph prior reduces selected zero-shot errors. Adding a few target-containing structures sharply lowers errors and contracts differences among one-hot, k-hot and continuous inputs across both ALIGNN and CGCNN. Calibration explains only part of the recovery, and freezing the initial element projection preserves most gains in five of six ALIGNN splits.
AI.conclusion: Target support shifts chemical transfer in materials GNNs away from reliance on static element relations (embedded in representations) and toward learning from target-containing environments. The findings imply that representation engineering matters most in zero-shot regimes, while even limited supervised target evidence dominates and largely neutralizes representation differences.

title: Weisfeiler-Lehman subtree encoding for Bayesian optimization of atomic configurations
summary: The efficiency of Bayesian optimization (BO) of atomic configurations depends strongly on how configurations are encoded. We introduce the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) subtree kernel, which views configurations as element-labeled graphs and measures their similarity by how many local structural patterns they share, into Bayesian-optimization-based configuration search. Because this kernel is reproduced as the plain inner product of explicit features (L$^2$-normalized histograms of local topological patterns), introducing it reduces to introducing the corresponding features: the encoding enters existing BO frameworks as an ordinary descriptor. In a benchmark ground-state configuration search of cubic BC$_2$N evaluated with a universal machine-learning interatomic potential, the WL encoding reached the ground state almost immediately after a shared random initialization of 100 samples in every one of five independent rounds (108$\pm$5 evaluations on average), whereas the one-hot baseline required 280$\pm$122 evaluations; the WL-driven sampler first exhausted the degenerate ground-state group and then discovered the metastable degenerate groups from the bottom up, in order of increasing energy.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) subtree kernel into Bayesian optimization for atomic configuration search. WL kernel treats configurations as element-labeled graphs and measures similarity via shared local structural patterns, and because it equals an inner product of explicit L2-normalized histogram features, it can be plugged into existing BO frameworks as an ordinary descriptor. In a BC2N ground-state search benchmark with a universal ML interatomic potential, WL encoding reached the ground state in 108±5 evaluations on average across five rounds (versus 280±122 for one-hot baseline), discovering degenerate groups in order of increasing energy from the bottom up.
AI.motivation: The efficiency of Bayesian optimization for atomic configurations strongly depends on how configurations are encoded, suggesting that a better structural encoding could substantially improve BO-based configuration search performance.
AI.method: The WL subtree kernel views atomic configurations as element-labeled graphs and measures similarity by counting shared local topological patterns. Since the kernel is equivalent to an inner product of explicit L2-normalized histogram features, it is implemented as a standard descriptor compatible with existing BO frameworks. The approach was evaluated on cubic BC2N ground-state search using a universal machine-learning interatomic potential, with five independent rounds from a shared 100-sample random initialization.
AI.result: The WL encoding reached the ground state in 108±5 evaluations on average across all five independent rounds, compared to 280±122 evaluations for the one-hot baseline. The WL-driven sampler first exhausted the degenerate ground-state group, then discovered metastable degenerate groups from the bottom up in order of increasing energy.
AI.conclusion: WL subtree kernel-based encoding dramatically improves the efficiency and consistency of Bayesian optimization for atomic configuration search, both hitting the ground state faster and exploring the energy landscape more systematically (discovering degenerate states in ascending energy order).

title: Numerical study of the grain-growth-induced non-parabolic kinetics of a solid-state reaction
summary: Non-parabolic growth of reaction layers is frequently observed in solid-state diffusion couples, but the relationship between microstructural evolution and the resulting kinetics remains incompletely understood. This effect is commonly attributed to grain growth, which can progressively reduce the contribution of fast grain-boundary diffusion, causing the effective diffusivity of a polycrystalline product layer to evolve during reaction. This work develops a moving-boundary diffusion model to describe product-layer growth while accounting for the local grain-growth history of the continuously formed product, as well as both bulk and grain-boundary diffusion. Numerical simulations show that the reaction can pass through three distinct kinetic regimes: an initial approximately parabolic regime dominated by grain-boundary diffusion, a transient sub-parabolic regime associated with strong spatial variation of the effective diffusivity, and a subsequent approximately parabolic regime dominated by bulk diffusion. The magnitude and duration of the sub-parabolic regime depend on the relative grain-boundary and bulk diffusivities and on the kinetics of grain growth. The instantaneous growth exponent therefore evolves continuously and does not represent a unique kinetic constant. Nevertheless, fitting simulated layer-thickness data over finite experimental time intervals produces well-defined apparent exponents, demonstrating how a transient process can appear to obey a single power law.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a moving-boundary diffusion model for product-layer growth in solid-state diffusion couples, accounting for local grain-growth history and both bulk and grain-boundary diffusion. The model reveals three distinct kinetic regimes—grain-boundary-dominated parabolic, transient sub-parabolic, and bulk-dominated parabolic—showing that apparent power-law growth exponents measured experimentally can result from transient processes rather than a single unique kinetic constant.
AI.motivation: Non-parabolic growth of reaction layers in solid-state diffusion couples is frequently observed but poorly understood. The relationship between microstructural evolution (particularly grain growth) and resulting reaction kinetics remains incompletely characterized, motivating a more rigorous modeling framework.
AI.method: The authors develop a moving-boundary diffusion model that incorporates the local grain-growth history of the continuously growing product layer alongside both bulk and grain-boundary diffusion pathways. Numerical simulations track effective diffusivity evolution and product-layer growth kinetics.
AI.result: Simulations reveal three kinetic regimes: an initial grain-boundary-dominated parabolic regime, a transient sub-parabolic regime caused by strong spatial variation in effective diffusivity, and a final bulk-dominated parabolic regime. The instantaneous growth exponent evolves continuously, yet fitting finite experimental time windows yields well-defined apparent exponents that may mask the underlying transient nature.
AI.conclusion: The apparent power-law behavior often extracted from experimental layer-thickness data can arise from transient sub-parabolic processes, meaning measured growth exponents do not necessarily represent a unique kinetic constant. This insight provides a mechanistic explanation for observed non-parabolic growth in polycrystalline diffusion couples.

title: First-Principles Electronic Structure Calculation of Crystals in Laboratory Magnetic Fields
summary: External magnetic fields can qualitatively reshape the electronic structure of crystals, underpinning quantum Hall physics, Landau-level spectra and field-induced topological phases. Their first-principles treatment at laboratory-scale fields is, however, hindered by magnetic-flux quantization, which requires magnetic unit cells with areas inversely proportional to the applied field. Such cells contain a large number of chemical unit cells, rendering real-space and plane-wave calculations prohibitively expensive. Here we, for the first time, construct a magnetic Bloch basis built from linear combinations of gauge-including Gaussian-type atomic orbitals, which incorporate the magnetic-field phase factors required by magnetic translation symmetry. The framework requires far fewer basis functions than real-space or plane-wave representations of the same magnetic supercell and retains the sparsity of an atom-centred basis, together substantially reducing computational cost. We validate the framework by reproducing Landau-level spectrum of graphene from first principles. This approach provides a practical route to simulations of crystalline materials under experimentally accessible magnetic fields.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel magnetic Bloch basis constructed from linearly combined gauge-including Gaussian-type atomic orbitals, enabling first-principles simulations of crystals under experimentally accessible magnetic fields at dramatically reduced computational cost compared to real-space or plane-wave methods.
AI.motivation: External magnetic fields can fundamentally alter electronic structure (quantum Hall physics, Landau levels, topological phases), but first-principles treatment at laboratory-scale fields is hindered by magnetic-flux quantization, which demands magnetic unit cells inversely proportional to the applied field—containing huge numbers of chemical unit cells and making conventional calculations prohibitively expensive.
AI.method: The authors construct a magnetic Bloch basis from linear combinations of gauge-including Gaussian-type atomic orbitals (GIAOs), incorporating magnetic-field phase factors required by magnetic translation symmetry. This basis retains the sparsity of atom-centred representations while requiring far fewer basis functions than real-space or plane-wave approaches for the equivalent magnetic supercell.
AI.result: The framework is validated by reproducing the Landau-level spectrum of graphene from first principles, demonstrating the accuracy and feasibility of the approach.
AI.conclusion: The method offers a practical computational route to simulating crystalline materials under experimentally accessible magnetic fields, overcoming the scaling bottleneck imposed by magnetic-flux quantization in conventional first-principles treatments.

title: Exchange striction determines how fast antiferromagnetic insulators demagnetize
summary: Antiferromagnets combine terahertz spin dynamics with insensitivity to stray fields, and how quickly their order can be manipulated sets the speed limit on device operation. Femtosecond optical pulses demagnetize antiferromagnetic insulators on timescales that span picoseconds to nanoseconds across compounds, and no material parameter is known that accounts for the spread or predicts where a new compound will fall. In a compensated antiferromagnet, no angular momentum needs to leave the spin system, so the rate is set by energy flow from the lattice into the spins. Time-resolved second-harmonic generation experiments show that Cr2O3 demagnetizes within 2 ps once the lattice is driven above the Neel temperature, two orders of magnitude faster than the structurally similar FeBO3. First-principles calculations trace the disparity to exchange striction: short Cr-Cr contacts make the exchange coupling tenfold more sensitive to atomic displacements and widen the phase space for phonon decay into magnon pairs. Spin-lattice simulations with ab initio parameters reproduce the order of magnitude of the measured ratio. The derivative of the exchange coupling with respect to the ionic displacement thus emerges as a computable parameter that predicts how fast an insulating antiferromagnet can be demagnetized. The results advance our understanding of ultrafast control in insulating antiferromagnets, and suggest a practical pathway to screen candidate materials for thermally assisted antiferromagnetic memory before synthesis.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies the derivative of exchange coupling with respect to ionic displacement as a computable parameter that predicts ultrafast demagnetization times in insulating antiferromagnets. Cr2O3 demagnetizes within 2 ps (two orders of magnitude faster than FeBO3) due to exchange striction from short Cr-Cr contacts, validated by first-principles calculations and spin-lattice simulations.
AI.motivation: There is no known material parameter that accounts for the wide spread in demagnetization timescales (picoseconds to nanoseconds) across antiferromagnetic insulators, nor one that predicts where a new compound will fall. A predictive metric is needed to screen candidate materials for applications like thermally assisted antiferromagnetic memory.
AI.method: Time-resolved second-harmonic generation experiments measure demagnetization in Cr2O3 and FeBO3. First-principles calculations trace the timescale disparity to exchange striction (Cr-Cr contacts making exchange coupling tenfold more sensitive to atomic displacements, widening phonon-to-magnon-pair decay phase space). Spin-lattice simulations with ab initio parameters reproduce the measured order-of-magnitude ratio.
AI.result: Cr2O3 demagnetizes within 2 ps once the lattice exceeds the N\'eel temperature, two orders of magnitude faster than structurally similar FeBO3. Spin-lattice simulations reproduce the measured demagnetization ratio. The exchange-coupling derivative with respect to ionic displacement emerges as a computable predictor.
AI.conclusion: The exchange-coupling derivative with respect to ionic displacement is a practical, computable parameter for predicting ultrafast demagnetization rates in insulating antiferromagnets, enabling pre-synthesis screening of candidate materials for thermally assisted antiferromagnetic memory and advancing understanding of ultrafast spin control.

title: Text-guided flow matching enables sample-efficient crystal structure generation
summary: Crystal generators can now propose periodic structures, but their control interfaces remain poorly matched to the mixed descriptors used in materials design. Text provides a compact way to combine composition, symmetry, prototype and property cues, yet it has not been clear whether such information can steer flow-based crystal generation. Here we introduce TFMat, a text-conditioned flow-matching framework that uses structured materials language as a semantic prior for a CrystalFlow generator. Across Perov-5, Carbon-24 and MP-20 crystal structure prediction benchmarks, TFMat improves one-candidate match rates over CrystalFlow and reaches a 92.04% MP-20 match rate with 20 candidates; in de novo generation, it improves element-count and density distribution alignment while retaining coarse property consistency in composition-selected outputs. These results position structured text as an inspectable control layer for translating human-readable materials intent into candidate crystals for downstream simulation and validation.

AI.tldr: TFMat is a text-conditioned flow-matching framework that uses structured materials language as a semantic prior for CrystalFlow, improving crystal structure prediction and de novo generation across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Crystal generators can propose periodic structures, but their control interfaces do not match the mixed descriptors (composition, symmetry, prototype, property) used in materials design. Text could provide a compact way to combine these cues, but it was unclear whether such information can steer flow-based crystal generation.
AI.method: TFMat integrates structured materials language as a semantic prior into CrystalFlow, a flow-matching-based crystal generator. The model is evaluated on crystal structure prediction benchmarks (Perov-5, Carbon-24, MP-20) and de novo generation tasks.
AI.result: TFMat improves one-candidate match rates over CrystalFlow across benchmarks, reaches 92.04% MP-20 match rate with 20 candidates, and improves element-count and density distribution alignment in de novo generation while retaining coarse property consistency in composition-selected outputs.
AI.conclusion: Structured text serves as an inspectable control layer for translating human-readable materials intent into candidate crystals for downstream simulation and validation.

title: Geometry-Controlled Magnetic and Electronic Landscapes in Anisotropic van der Waals Materials
summary: Electronic structure in van der Waals materials is commonly engineered through composition, strain, electrostatic gating and heterostructure assembly. Here we introduce geometronics, a concept in which substrate geometry locally reorients an anisotropic crystal, transforming homogeneous external perturbation into programmable magnetic and electronic landscapes. We demonstrate this concept using a bilayer of the antiferromagnetic semiconductor CrSBr transferred onto an inverted pyramidal nanoindentation, where the local crystal orientation with respect to the external magnetic field drives the coexistence of antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic phases within a single continuous crystal. The resulting magnetic landscape creates a switchable excitonic potential well of up to 10--12 meV, directly visualised by spatially resolved spectroscopy. More generally, geometronics provides a universal route for deterministically programmed electronic and magnetic landscapes without modifying the material itself. It therefore establishes substrate topography as a new design principle that exploits the intrinsic anisotropy of layered van der Waals materials.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "geometronics," a concept where substrate geometry locally reorients anisotropic van der Waals crystals to transform uniform external fields (e.g., magnetic fields) into spatially programmable electronic and magnetic landscapes. Demonstrated using a CrSBr bilayer on an inverted pyramidal nanoindentation, it produces coexisting antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic phases within one crystal and creates a switchable excitonic potential well of 10–12 meV, visualized via spatially resolved spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: Conventional methods for engineering electronic structure in van der Waals materials (composition, strain, gating, heterostructures) are limited in their ability to create spatially programmable landscapes. The authors propose substrate topography as a new, material-agnostic design principle that exploits intrinsic crystal anisotropy.
AI.method: A bilayer of the antiferromagnetic semiconductor CrSBr is transferred onto an inverted pyramidal nanoindentation, causing local reorientation of the crystal lattice relative to an external magnetic field. Local orientation differences drive a phase coexistence (antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic) in the same continuous crystal, producing a spatially varying excitonic potential.
AI.result: The geometric reorientation yields coexisting antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic regions within a single crystal, forming a switchable excitonic potential well of 10–12 meV, directly confirmed by spatially resolved spectroscopy.
AI.conclusion: Geometronics offers a universal, deterministic route to engineering programmable magnetic and electronic landscapes in anisotropic layered van der Waals materials without chemical or structural modification. Substrate topography is established as a new design principle for functional materials.

title: Trap Dynamics and Conductivity Changes in AlGaN/GaN Heterostructures Under Ultrasonic Loading
summary: AlGaN/GaN heterostructures are critical for high-power electronic devices but suffer from electron trapping at defects, limiting reliability. We investigate how ultrasonic vibrations affect electron transport in MOCVD-grown AlGaN/GaN heterostructures by combining temperature-dependent Hall effect and high-resolution X-ray diffraction measurements. Here we demonstrate that ultrasonic loading induces persistent acoustoconductivity and lattice parameter changes, attributed to acoustically driven rearrangement of metastable DX centers. This leads to increased carrier concentration and decreased mobility, reflecting defect state modulation by acoustic strain. These findings provide new insights into trap dynamics under dynamic deformation and suggest ultrasonic treatment as a potential approach to mitigate trapping effects, thereby enhancing the performance and reliability of GaN-based devices.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how ultrasonic vibrations affect electron transport in MOCVD-grown AlGaN/GaN heterostructures using temperature-dependent Hall effect and high-resolution X-ray diffraction. Ultrasonic loading induces persistent acoustoconductivity and lattice parameter changes attributed to acoustically driven rearrangement of metastable DX centers, increasing carrier concentration while decreasing mobility. This suggests ultrasonic treatment as a potential approach to mitigate electron trapping and enhance GaN-based device reliability.
AI.motivation: AlGaN/GaN heterostructures are essential for high-power electronics but suffer from electron trapping at defects, limiting device reliability. Understanding and mitigating trap dynamics is critical for improving device performance.
AI.method: Temperature-dependent Hall effect measurements combined with high-resolution X-ray diffraction were conducted on MOCVD-grown AlGaN/GaN heterostructures under ultrasonic loading to probe changes in electron transport and lattice parameters.
AI.result: Ultrasonic loading induces persistent acoustoconductivity and lattice parameter changes, explained by acoustically driven rearrangement of metastable DX centers. This leads to increased carrier concentration and decreased mobility, indicating defect state modulation by acoustic strain.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide new insights into trap dynamics under dynamic deformation and propose ultrasonic treatment as a viable approach to mitigate trapping effects, thereby enhancing the performance and reliability of GaN-based high-power devices.

title: Polar nanoregions and reentrant-like ferroelectric behavior in SrTiO$_3$
summary: Recent real-space imaging in quantum paraelectric SrTiO$_3$ [Nature 656, 54 (2026)] reveals that local polar textures do not continuously grow upon cooling, but reach a maximum intensity at intermediate temperatures around 60-65~K and weaken again toward the quantum paraelectric ground state. Such a reentrant-like weakening of local polar textures challenges the conventional paradigm in which ordering tendencies generally strengthen as thermal fluctuations are suppressed. Here we employ a self-consistent phase-field theory showing that this anomalous behavior naturally arises from the interplay between intrinsic polar and antiferrodistortiv (AFD) fluctuations. We demonstrate that flexoelectric-like coupling strongly hybridizes the polar and AFD modes. As the uncoupled polar and AFD modes cross near 52~K, their hybridization is maximized, driving the lower hybridized branch to develop a minimum on a finite-wave-vector shell. This finite-$q$ softening triggers a Brazovskii-type instability, strongly enhancing polarization correlations and producing nanoscale polar textures. Away from the crossing temperature, the two modes become increasingly detuned, weakening their hybridization and the associated finite-$q$ softening. These results reaveal the origin of the formation of polar nanoregions in SrTiO$_3$, naturally explaining the unexpected confinement to an intermediate-temperature window and providing a mechanism beyond the quantum-fluctuation-based interpretation suggested by experiment. Furthermore, we predict an unconventional reentrant-like sequence in weakly strained SrTiO$_3$, evolving from ferroelectric to paraelectric, polar-nanoregion, and eventually paraelectric regimes upon heating from zero temperature.

AI.tldr: This paper uses self-consistent phase-field theory to explain the reentrant-like weakening of local polar textures in quantum paraelectric SrTiO3 observed at intermediate temperatures (~60-65 K). The anomalous behavior arises from flexoelectric-like coupling that hybridizes polar and antiferrodistortive (AFD) modes, which maximally hybridize near their crossing at ~52 K, driving a finite-q softening and Brazovskii-type instability that generates nanoscale polar textures. The theory also predicts a reentrant-like sequence in weakly strained SrTiO3 from ferroelectric to paraelectric, polar-nanoregion, and paraelectric regimes upon heating.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments in quantum paraelectric SrTiO3 show that local polar textures peak at intermediate temperatures (60-65 K) and weaken toward the quantum ground state, contradicting the conventional paradigm where ordering strengthens as thermal fluctuations are suppressed. This challenges existing interpretations and requires a new mechanism to explain the unexpected intermediate-temperature confinement of polar nanoregions.
AI.method: The authors employ a self-consistent phase-field theory to model the interplay between intrinsic polar and antiferrodistortive (AFD) fluctuations. They demonstrate that flexoelectric-like coupling strongly hybridizes the polar and AFD modes, and analyze how mode crossing near 52 K maximizes hybridization, producing a minimum on a finite-wave-vector shell that triggers a Brazovskii-type instability.
AI.result: The theory shows that maximal hybridization of polar and AFD modes near their crossing temperature drives finite-q softening and a Brazovskii-type instability, strongly enhancing polarization correlations and producing nanoscale polar textures. Away from the crossing, mode detuning weakens hybridization and the associated softening. The paper also predicts an unconventional reentrant sequence in weakly strained SrTiO3: ferroelectric to paraelectric, then polar-nanoregion, and finally paraelectric regimes upon heating from zero temperature.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal the origin of polar nanoregion formation in SrTiO3, naturally explaining its confinement to an intermediate-temperature window through a mode-hybridization + Brazovskii-instability mechanism, offering an alternative to the quantum-fluctuation-based interpretation suggested by experiment, and predicting a novel reentrant sequence in strained samples.

title: Pressure-regulated mechanochemistry at lithium metal-sulfide electrolyte interfaces
summary: Stack pressure is commonly treated as a means of maintaining physical contact in all-solid-state lithium-metal batteries, but it can also alter the chemistry of reactive solid-solid interfaces. Here, using pressure-aware, charge-resolved machine-learning molecular dynamics validated against DFT, we determine how pressure magnitude and loading geometry regulate interphase formation at Li||Li6PS5Cl interfaces. The response is nonmonotonic: compression at 1 kbar accelerates PS4 decomposition and Li2S-like ordering, whereas 10-100 kbar compression restricts structural rearrangement and long-range crystallization. Charge-resolved dynamics further identify sulfur-centered, lithium-rich early-interphase environments associated with subsequent Li2S-like ordering. Uniaxial loading accelerates interfacial reaction relative to isostatic loading at the same nominal pressure. Pressure also changes void closure and dead-lithium spreading in a defect-location-dependent manner. These results establish applied pressure as a mechanochemical process variable coupling interphase chemistry, ion transport and defect evolution, providing a mechanistic framework for interpreting pressure effects in sulfide solid-state batteries.

AI.tldr: This paper uses pressure-aware, charge-resolved machine-learning molecular dynamics (validated against DFT) to investigate how applied pressure magnitude and loading geometry regulate interphase formation at Li||Li6PS5Cl interfaces in all-solid-state lithium-metal batteries. The response is nonmonotonic: 1 kbar compression accelerates PS4 decomposition and Li2S-like ordering, while 10-100 kbar restricts structural rearrangement and crystallization. Uniaxial loading accelerates interfacial reactions compared to isostatic loading, and pressure also alters void closure and dead-lithium spreading in a defect-location-dependent manner. The work establishes applied pressure as a mechanochemical process variable coupling interphase chemistry, ion transport, and defect evolution.
AI.motivation: To move beyond treating stack pressure merely as a means of maintaining physical contact in all-solid-state batteries, and instead understand how pressure magnitude and loading geometry mechanochemically regulate reactive solid-solid interfaces—specifically interphase formation at Li||Li6PS5Cl interfaces.
AI.method: Pressure-aware, charge-resolved machine-learning molecular dynamics simulations validated against density functional theory (DFT), examining different pressure magnitudes (1, 10, 100 kbar) and loading geometries (uniaxial vs. isostatic) at Li||Li6PS5Cl interfaces, with charge-resolved analysis to track interphase chemical environments.
AI.result: Pressure effects on interphase formation are nonmonotonic: moderate compression (1 kbar) accelerates PS4 decomposition and Li2S-like ordering, while high compression (10-100 kbar) restricts structural rearrangement and long-range crystallization. Charge-resolved dynamics reveal sulfur-centered, lithium-rich early-interphase environments that precede Li2S-like ordering. Uniaxial loading accelerates interfacial reaction relative to isostatic loading at the same nominal pressure, and pressure modulates void closure and dead-lithium spreading depending on defect location.
AI.conclusion: Applied pressure should be regarded as a mechanochemical process variable that couples interphase chemistry, ion transport, and defect evolution in sulfide solid-state batteries, providing a mechanistic framework for interpreting and engineering pressure effects in all-solid-state lithium-metal batteries.

title: Autonomous discovery of new structure-plausibility laws for explainable and rapid crystal diagnosis and screening
summary: Crystal generators and tool-using agents propose structures faster than density functional theory (DFT) energy and phonon calculations or experiments can assess them. Deciding which candidates merit expensive assessment is therefore the bottleneck, yet most screens test little beyond atomic overlap and give no chemical reason for failure. Here, our agents generate, test and actively refute two million candidate laws, leaving eight Plausibility Rules for Inorganic Structures (PRIS). These laws encode five mechanisms: short-range repulsion, ionic contact and packing, electrostatic balance, bond-valence conservation and crystallographic site complexity. Experimental structures satisfy our law sets at 82--99%, but satisfy Pauling's rules 2--5 together at only 6.5%. The strictest set detects 87.9% of damaged crystal structures, whereas distance cutoffs detect only 1.6--3.2%. PRIS plausibility is linearly correlated with synthesizability, so the PRIS-derived synthesis score (PSS) explainably screens 83.7% of hard-to-synthesize structures while retaining 80.7% of experimental structures. In a property-conditioned inverse-design run, PRIS and PSS can reduce the DFT validation queue by up to 67.3% and keep 99.2% of the candidates whose DFT-validated bulk moduli reach the design target. PRIS moves screening from a pass-or-fail verdict to a chemical reason for failure, showing that autonomous agents can discover, by active refutation, physicochemical laws that guide calculations and experiments.

PRIS outperforms Pauling's rules and distance-based cutoffs at detecting invalid/damaged crystal structures, correlates linearly with synthesizability, and reduces DFT validation queues by up to 67.3% in inverse design while retaining 99.2% of target-reaching candidates.
AI.motivation: Crystal generators and tool-using agents can propose structures far faster than DFT or experiments can validate them. Existing screening criteria (mostly atomic overlap tests and distance cutoffs) provide no chemical explanation for failure, making the decision of which candidates merit expensive evaluation the key bottleneck in materials discovery.
AI.method: Autonomous agents employ an active-refutation framework to generate, test, and falsify two million candidate laws, ultimately distilling them into eight Plausibility Rules for Inorganic Structures (PRIS). These laws encode five physical mechanisms: short-range repulsion, ionic contact and packing, electrostatic balance, bond-valence conservation, and crystallographic site complexity. The rules are validated against experimental datasets, damaged structures, and used to derive a synthesis score (PSS) and a property-conditioned inverse-design screening workflow.

The strictest set detects 87.9% of damaged structures versus 1.6–3.2% for distance cutoffs. PRIS also explains biases in GNoME toward rare low-symmetry structures and reveals why wrong-element assignments in falsified crystal reports hide behind plausible coordinates.
AI.conclusion: PRIS transforms structure screening from a binary pass/fail check into an explanatory chemical diagnosis. It demonstrates that autonomous agents can discover, through active refutation, physicochemical laws that meaningfully guide both computational and experimental materials research. This approach provides chemically transparent filters that reduce computational cost and improve candidate selection in inverse design.

title: Simulating Continuous-Rotation 3D Electron Diffraction: A Multislice and Bloch Wave Framework
summary: To improve the agreement between measured and calculated intensities of three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED) experiments, a simulation pipeline is needed to assess and quantify the influence of various structural and experimental parameters. We present a computational pipeline, built upon the abTEM Python package, to simulate continuous-rotation 3D electron diffraction data based on either the Bloch wave or the multislice formalism. Multislice calculations in arbitrary orientations are achieved through large supercells and windowing. We investigate the convergence of key simulation parameters and test their consistency, establishing suitable parameters for accurate and efficient simulations. The pipeline's applicability and robustness are demonstrated through case studies on cubic silicon as well as stretched and sheared variants, analyzing the influence of electron kinetic energy, sample thickness, orientation, and symmetry on simulated diffraction intensities. Finally, we investigate a representative selection of seven compounds, including cubic $\mathrm{SrTiO_3}$, monoclinic $α$-glycine $\mathrm{C_2H_5NO_2}$, and triclinic kyanite $\mathrm{Al_2SiO_5}$ to validate the method. This framework for the simulation of 3D electron diffraction data establishes an approach to investigate the dependence of diffracted intensities on experimentally relevant parameters which are difficult to systematically investigate in experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a computational pipeline built on the abTEM Python package to simulate continuous-rotation 3D electron diffraction (3D ED) data using either Bloch wave or multislice formalisms, systematically investigating convergence of simulation parameters and validating the approach on silicon and seven representative compounds.
AI.motivation: There is a need to improve agreement between measured and calculated intensities of 3D ED experiments, requiring a simulation framework to assess how structural and experimental parameters influence diffracted intensities, which are difficult to systematically investigate experimentally.
AI.method: A computational pipeline is built on the abTEM Python package to simulate continuous-rotation 3D ED data using Bloch wave or multislice formalisms. Multislice calculations in arbitrary orientations are achieved via large supercells and windowing. Convergence of key simulation parameters is investigated, and case studies on cubic silicon and stretched/sheared variants analyze the effects of electron kinetic energy, sample thickness, orientation, and symmetry.
AI.result: Suitable parameters for accurate and efficient simulations are established through convergence testing. The pipeline is validated on seven compounds spanning different crystal systems (cubic SrTiO3, monoclinic α-glycine, triclinic kyanite), demonstrating its applicability and robustness.
AI.conclusion: This framework provides a systematic approach to simulate 3D electron diffraction data and investigate how experimentally relevant parameters affect diffracted intensities, enabling quantitative comparison and improvement between simulations and experiments.

title: A relational fabrication-to-modeling database for memristor devices
summary: Resistive random access memory (RRAM) devices, also known as memristors, are highly dependent on fabrication, location on the wafer, and measurement protocols. However, openly available large-scale memristor datasets remain scarce, particularly those that combine experimental metadata with electrical measurements and preserve explicit links across the experimental workflow. Here, we present a comprehensive relational database of automated electrical characterization data from oxide-based memristors. The database links 6,190 memristor devices across TiN/HfOx/TiN, Pt/TiOx/AlOy/Pt, and Pt/TiOx/Pt stacks to 161,006 validated experiments and over 169 million electrical point records. It integrates fabrication, wafer mapping, electrical characterization, and modeling to describe electroforming, current-voltage non-linearity, memory windows (R_off/R_on), switching dynamics, and short-term volatility. Released as a normalized and indexed SQLite database with schema documentation, graphical user interfaces, and examples of empirical modeling, this resource supports provenance-aware querying, statistical analysis, and data-driven applications for the development of future memristor technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a large-scale relational database of automated electrical characterization data from oxide-based memristors, linking 6,190 devices across three stack types to 161,006 validated experiments and over 169 million electrical point records, released as a normalized SQLite database with GUIs and modeling examples.
AI.motivation: RRAM/memristor devices are highly dependent on fabrication, wafer location, and measurement protocols, yet openly available large-scale memristor datasets that combine experimental metadata with electrical measurements and preserve explicit workflow links remain scarce.
AI.method: The authors constructed a comprehensive relational database integrating fabrication details, wafer mapping, automated electrical characterization, and modeling across TiN/HfOx/TiN, Pt/TiOx/AlOy/Pt, and Pt/TiOx/Pt stacks. The database is released as a normalized and indexed SQLite file with schema documentation, GUI tools, and empirical modeling examples.

title: No source-free exchange-correlation magnetic fields in non-collinear spin DFT
summary: We show that the Maxwellian equation $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{xc}}=0$, where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{xc}}$ is the exchange-correlation (xc) magnetic field, is not an exact condition of non-collinear spin density functional theory: it violates global spin-rotation symmetry, the operation which turns the electron spins. How much does this matter in practice? To find out we impose the condition anyway, in the best way we can: we modify any parent xc functional so that the Kohn-Sham procedure yields a divergence-free $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{xc}}$ that is a functional derivative, stays exact for the homogeneous gas, and exerts the local torques a locally collinear functional cannot. Any non-physical result from the calculation must be due to the spurious condition, not the implementation. On Mn$_2$ with LSDA as parent, the source-free (SoF) construction and locally collinear (LoC) LSDA both give too short a bond and too large a bond energy, but differ on the magnetic exchange coupling and on the state itself: SoF finds the experimentally observed $^1Σ^+_g$ antiferromagnet, with a coupling of the right sign and roughly the right size, while LoC finds a high-spin $^{11}Π_u$ ferromagnet and the wrong sign. Despite this seeming success, breaking the symmetry has serious consequences: a rigid spin rotation of the magnetization changes $E_{\mathrm{xc}}$ by about 1 eV (it should not change at all), and the magnetization induced by a weak uniform field points perpendicular to the field (it should be antiparallel to it).

AI.tldr: The paper examines whether the divergence-free condition on the exchange-correlation magnetic field (∇·B_xc = 0) is an exact condition in non-collinear spin density functional theory. The authors show it violates global spin-rotation symmetry and then test its practical consequences by imposing it in a principled way on LSDA for Mn₂. The source-free construction predicts the correct antiferromagnetic ground state and exchange coupling, while the locally collinear functional gives a ferromagnet with wrong sign. However, the symmetry breaking causes severe artifacts: spin rotations change E_xc by ~1 eV and field-induced magnetization is perpendicular (not antiparallel) to the applied field.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to determine whether the Maxwellian condition ∇·B_xc = 0 is an exact physical constraint of non-collinear spin density functional theory, and if not, to assess how seriously its imposition distorts practical calculations.
AI.method: The authors prove ∇·B_xc = 0 violates global spin-rotation symmetry. They then construct a source-free (SoF) correction to any parent xc functional that enforces divergence-free B_xc while remaining a functional derivative, staying exact for the homogeneous gas, and providing local torques beyond locally collinear (LoC) functionals. This is applied to Mn₂ with LSDA as the parent functional and compared against LoC results.
AI.result: On Mn₂, SoF-LSDA yields the correct experimental ¹Σ⁺g antiferromagnetic ground state with the right sign and approximate magnitude of exchange coupling, whereas LoC-LSDA gives a high-spin ¹¹Πu ferromagnet with the wrong coupling sign. However, the SoF construction breaks spin rotation symmetry: rigidly rotating the magnetization changes E_xc by ~1 eV, and the magnetization induced by a weak uniform field is perpendicular rather than antiparallel to the field.
AI.conclusion: The source-free condition on B_xc is not exact and, when enforced, produces severe symmetry-breaking artifacts (spin-rotation non-invariance of the energy and unphysical perpendicular response to a magnetic field). Consequently, source-free xc magnetic fields should be avoided or handled with great caution in non-collinear spin density functional theory.
